LLDP neighbors ride the systemInfo detail retention since they're current-state, not time-series. `dropChunks(cutoff)` is the O(1) pre-filter for whole aged chunks; the residue row-DELETE is compression-frontier-safe — `pruneTierByDays` routes through `tieredPruneWindow` (skips the DELETE entirely when the whole delete set is past the compress-after frontier, the common rollup case) and `pruneSelectionAwareDetail` through `unselectedSlowPruneWindow`, so a row-DELETE never decompresses a compressed chunk (prod incidents 2026-06-08, 2026-06-17). The old in-memory `lastPruneAt=0` trigger fired the prune on every process boot and, under a monitor restart loop, fanned into the 2026-06-17 hourly-table DELETE pile-up that pinned the xmin horizon. **Sample writes are async-buffered**: every `record*` function (`recordProbeResult` / `recordTelemetryResult` / `recordSystemInfoResult` / `recordFastFilteredResult`) hands sample rows to `sampleWriteBuffer.enqueue*` instead of issuing per-call `prisma.<table>.create*` — those are batched into one `createMany` per 2 s flush window. **The probe-path Asset.update (status/counters/last*At) is also buffered** via `probePatchBuffer.enqueueProbePatch` — one bulk `UPDATE … FROM (VALUES …)` per 2 s window covers every asset's state write instead of one `prisma.asset.update` per probe. The five-state machine reads its own writes via `getPendingProbePatch(assetId)`: `recordProbeResult` overlays the in-flight patch onto the loaded Asset row BEFORE computing the next state, so the threshold counters advance correctly across same-window probes. Telemetry/systemInfo cadences still issue per-asset `prisma.asset.update` for `lastTelemetryAt` / `lastSystemInfoAt` — those run on slower cadences (60 s / 600 s+) where per-tick connection pressure is much lower; if needed, the same buffer pattern applies straightforwardly. Three writes stay synchronous because they need per-asset replace semantics: the `$transaction` for `assetAssociatedIp` (delete-non-manual + createMany inside `recordSystemInfoResult`), `persistLldpNeighbors` (per-asset full-replace of the LLDP neighbor table with a 48 h stickiness grace), and `persistWirelessStations` (per-scrape full-replace of the connected-client table; no stickiness because clients are transient by design — its endpoint `lastSeenAp` stamp is now edge-triggered: one bounded pre-read of the matched endpoints, only the rows whose AP actually changed are updated (a steady station set issues zero UPDATEs per scrape), and each real move emits an `asset.wireless_ap.changed` audit row AFTER the transaction commits. The id-sorted `$transaction` ordering is a documented 3-way-deadlock fix and survives the filter, which is applied before the sort). The LLDP and wireless paths use a single bulk `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` raw-SQL statement (plus a separate `deleteMany` for stale rows) so the connection isn't held across N pipelined updates inside a transaction — caller pre-assigns ids in JS so insert-vs-update is controlled by id collision, not by the business-key unique constraint which can't be used as a conflict target since Postgres treats NULL as distinct in unique indexes. **Probe path issues exactly one Asset findUnique** — `probeAsset(assetId, out?)` stashes its loaded asset row into the caller's optional out-object so `recordProbeResult(assetId, result, preloadedAsset?)` can skip its own findUnique on the state-machine update path. The hot loop (runProbeFor) and pg-boss probe workers both pass the out-object; the /probe-now route doesn't bother (one operator-triggered request per click). **LLDP asset match index is module-cached** with a 60 s TTL — `persistLldpNeighbors` used to call `buildLldpAssetMatchIndex` on every system-info pass (`findMany` over every Asset row plus its associatedIpRows + macAddressRows), now goes through `getLldpAssetMatchIndex()` which dedups concurrent rebuilders via an inflight Promise and returns the cached map within the TTL window. Worst-case stale-cache effect is one cycle of "LLDP neighbor matched to wrong asset" which self-corrects on the next scrape; `invalidateLldpMatchCache()` is exported for future callers that want explicit refresh after a bulk asset write. **FortiSwitch port-VLAN overlay**: in the SNMP systemInfo path on `assetType="switch"` assets with a Fortinet source AND a resolvable `controllerFortigate`, `collectSystemInfo` calls `fetchFortiswitchControllerPortsCmdb(integration, controllerName, timeoutMs)` after `collectSystemInfoSnmp` returns and overlays per-port `nativeVlan` + `taggedVlans` onto matching `InterfaceSample` rows by ifName == port-name. The fetcher hits the parent FortiGate's `/api/v2/cmdb/switch-controller/managed-switch?datasource=1` once per (integration, controller) per 30 s (`fortiswitchControllerPortsCache` mirrors the `fortinetControllerCache` TTL); the response carries every managed switch's full ports table including `vlan` / `allowed-vlans` / `untagged-vlans`, parsed via `parseFortiosVlanList` which handles FortiOS's three shapes (array of `{vlan-id}` objects, raw number array, comma+range string) and drops `"all"` placeholders. Tagged set is `allowed-vlans − untagged-vlans` so a port carrying only its native isn't duplicated as tagged. The **same CMDB fetch also carries trunk membership** (a `ports[]` entry that lists `members` IS a trunk — the auto-ISL FortiLink uplink is named after the switch serial and has exactly one member): `overlayFortiswitchTrunkMembers` stamps `ifParent=<trunk>` + `ifType="physical"` onto each member's `InterfaceSample` row (synthesizing the row when IF-MIB omitted the subordinate port) and marks the trunk row `ifType="aggregate"`, mirroring the FortiGate-side aggregate back-fill in `collectSystemInfoFortinet`. This parent/member linkage lets the topology layer (`interfaceTopologyService.preferPhysical` + the single-member swap in `topologyGraphService.ts`'s `ifDetail`) render a single-member trunk as its physical port — so the Device Map FortiLink tooltip shows the real cable port (e.g. `port52`) instead of the opaque serial-named trunk. The member-list parser (`parseFortiosMemberList`) is deliberately permissive across FortiOS shapes (array of `{member-name}`/`{q_origin_key}`/`{name}` objects, bare-string array, or space/comma string); the exact CMDB field still wants confirmation on a live FortiOS 7.x device, so the overlay is best-effort and degrades to "no trunk resolved" on an unexpected shape. Best-effort — any overlay failure leaves both VLAN fields null/empty on every row and the interface scrape proceeds. Strictly additive to the SNMP IF-MIB walk. **Interface MAC fold**: when the scrape returns interfaces, EVERY interface MAC (monitored or not) is reconciled into `AssetMacAddress` (source="monitor-interface") via `reconcileInterfaceMacs` — contiguous MACs coalesce into `[mac, macEnd]` range rows (a 48-port switch stores one row), full-replace scoped to that source only so rows owned by discovery/agent/manual writers are never touched. Gated on the scraped-MAC set being non-empty, so the no-MAC case costs zero extra round-trips.
│   │   ├── sampleWriteBuffer.ts     # Periodic batch-flush buffer for the six append-only monitor sample tables (asset_monitor_samples / asset_telemetry_samples / asset_hardware_sensor_samples / asset_interface_samples / asset_storage_samples / asset_ipsec_tunnel_samples). Per-table in-memory arrays + a 2 s `setInterval` flush + a 5,000-row size threshold for burst publishers (e.g. a manual probe-all-now). `flushTable` snapshots the array up front so concurrent enqueues during the awaited `createMany` land in a fresh buffer; on flush failure the snapshot is re-prepended for the next tick's retry. Deadlock retries go through `retryOnDeadlock` (3 attempts, 25-75 ms jitter — same as `reconcileMacAddresses`). Flush duration is observed via the existing `polaris_sample_write_duration_seconds{table}` histogram; current depth per table is exported as `polaris_sample_buffer_depth{table}`. Trade-off: up to 2 s of sample rows are lost on a hard crash — acceptable because samples are an append-only time series and the next cadence tick re-supplies fresh data. **State-side writes (Asset.monitorStatus / counters / lastMonitorAt / monitorStatusChangedAt) live in the companion `probePatchBuffer` with last-write-wins-with-stamp-preservation semantics** instead of this append-only buffer; same 2 s window but different shape because state needs replace semantics and the buffer needs to serve reads (the state machine's threshold counters require read-your-writes). `shutdownFlushSampleBuffers()` is awaited from the SIGTERM/SIGINT hook in `src/app.ts` so a graceful restart doesn't drop the in-flight buffer. **The buffer covers only the six DETAIL tables — the twelve rollup tables (`*_hourly` / `*_daily`) use `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` from `sampleRollupService.ts` instead** because rollup writes need upsert semantics (idempotent re-runs over the same window must rewrite buckets in place); the append-only buffer contract intentionally has no upsert path.. **The monitor rollup scans ALL probeKinds but keeps its row-count and RTT columns PRIMARY-only** (a `PRIMARY` fragment FILTERed onto every one of them). The two column families describe different transports: sampleCount / successCount / failureCount / dependencyFailureCount are the operator's configured status poll — `probeOutageService` reads them to decide what an outage looked like — while `packetsSent` / `packetsReceived` sum the ICMP burst sweep. The WHERE clause used to exclude `probeKind='icmp'` outright, for a reason that expired with the per-asset SAMPLER it was written for: that ran only during warning/recovering windows, so folding it into 400-day aggregates counted quiet and incident-heavy months at different sampling rates. The sweep that replaced it is UNIFORM (business rule 29), which is exactly what makes it comparable across time and worth rolling up. Packets are SUMMED, never averaged, so a long range stays a true packets-lost/packets-sent ratio rather than a mean of per-bucket percentages; and they stay **NULL rather than 0** where no sweep row exists — including in the daily roll-up, deliberately unlike `dependencyFailureCount`, whose 0 is a truthful "none" where 0 packets sent would claim a 0%-loss day for a day nobody measured
│   │   ├── probePatchBuffer.ts      # Companion to sampleWriteBuffer for the STATE-side write inside `recordProbeResult`. Replaces the per-probe `prisma.asset.update` (one Prisma pool connection per probe; the dominant remaining per-tick connection draw on the monitor hot loop at 2000+ assets) with an in-memory `Map<assetId, ProbePatch>` flushed as one bulk `UPDATE … FROM (VALUES …)` statement per 2 s window. Last-write-wins per asset within the window EXCEPT `monitorStatusChangedAt`, `lastUptimeSec`, `lastRebootAt`, `lastSeen`/`lastSeenSource`, `recoveryStartedAt` (the packet-loss recovery anchor -- an ordinary probe merging onto the recovery probe must not erase it, or the loss ratio keeps counting the outage), and `awaitingRecoveryConfirm` (the recovery confirmation run's one bit of memory, business rule 36 -- note it is a BOOLEAN, so the merge and the flush both use `??` / COALESCE rather than truthiness: `false` is a real value that has to land), which are preserved on merge (and COALESCE'd in the flush SQL) so a transition stamp / SNMP uptime reading / reboot stamp isn't NULL-erased by a subsequent same-window probe that didn't carry one (e.g. a non-SNMP probe has no uptime). The state machine reads its own writes via `getPendingProbePatch(assetId)` — `recordProbeResult` overlays the in-flight patch onto the loaded Asset row BEFORE computing the next state, so two failed probes in the same window correctly advance `consecutiveFailures` to 2 instead of both computing it as 1 against the on-disk 0. On flush-retry-exhausted failure, the snapshot is conditionally re-prepended (only entries the buffer no longer holds — concurrent enqueues represent fresher state and win). Trade-off: up to 2 s of state writes lost on hard crash, and the `monitor.status_changed` Event / `propagateAfterStatusChange` / `triggerRetryAfterStatusChange` side effects that fire on transitions run against in-memory `(previousStatus, nextStatus)` values and don't wait for the flush — propagate/retry hooks then read the DB before the buffer lands, so their effects can lag by up to one flush window before the 60 s `dependencyReconciler` and `retryQueuedReservationPushes` ticks catch up as the sources of truth. Acceptable because the state machine is self-healing within one additional probe cycle. Exports `polaris_probe_patch_buffer_depth{table=assets:probe}` gauge + `polaris_probe_patch_write_duration_seconds` histogram. `shutdownFlushProbePatchBuffer()` awaited from the SIGTERM/SIGINT hook so a graceful restart doesn't drop in-flight state.
│   │   ├── sampleRollupService.ts   # Tiered sample-retention rollup writer. Builds twelve `INSERT...ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` statements (6 source tables × hourly + daily) that aggregate raw detail samples into per-hour and per-day rollup tables. Portable across plain Postgres + TimescaleDB via `date_trunc('hour' | 'day', ts)` — single code path on both deployments. Gauge tables (monitor, telemetry, temperature, storage) emit `sampleCount + avg/min/max` per bucket; counter tables (interface, ipsec) emit per-bucket `first/last` counter endpoints + `lastBucketSampleAt` so the read layer derives rate as `(last - first) / (lastBucketSampleAt - bucketStart in seconds)` with negative-delta-as-counter-reset behavior matching the detail-tier client-side diff. IPsec additionally counts per-status sample-bucket occurrences so the chart distinguishes flapping from steady-state. Daily reads from `*_hourly` (not detail) so the daily tick stays bounded on big fleets. Driven by `src/jobs/runSampleRollup.ts`.
│   │   ├── sampleQueryRouter.ts     # Tier router. `pickSampleTier(since, retention)` returns `{tier: "detail"|"hourly"|"daily", bucketSeconds}` based on which tier still covers the requested window. `pickSampleTierForAsset(assetId, entity, since)` is the async hot-path helper used by the six chart history endpoints — resolves the configured retention for the given entity (`assets` / `cpuMem` / `temperature` / `interfaces` / `storage` / `ipsec`) from `sampleRetentionService` and applies `pickSampleTier` (which treats `FOREVER`(-1) as full coverage, `0` as tier-off). `assetId` is retained in the signature for the forthcoming selection-aware read (unselected interfaces have no rollup beyond 24h) but isn't consulted for tier selection today.
│   │   ├── sampleHistoryService.ts  # Tier-aware readers for the six chart history endpoints. Each function takes (assetId, since, until, tier[, extraKey]) and returns `{samples, [meta], [stats]}` in a shape the existing chart renderers consume. Detail tier returns raw sample columns; rollup tiers translate aggregate columns back to the source-table field names so gauge charts (monitor, telemetry, temperature, storage) render unchanged — values become bucket averages with `min*` / `max*` siblings + `sampleCount` for tooltips. Counter tables (interface, ipsec) pre-compute `inBytesPerSec` / `outBytesPerSec` / `inErrorsPerSec` / `outErrorsPerSec` (and IPsec analogs) on rollup tiers so the frontend can branch on `bucketSeconds > 0` and read rates directly instead of diffing cumulative samples.
│   │   ├── probeOutageService.ts    # "When was this device unreachable?", read from the response-time probe stream for the charts of streams that have none of their own. The heavy cadences (telemetry / sensors / interfaces / storage / processes) do not RUN while an asset is down — `runsHeavyCadences` gates them on `up` — so a skipped poll leaves no row and there is nothing in those tables to mark; the probe keeps running in every state and writes a real `success:false` row per interval. `foldProbeOutages` (pure) folds a run of probe verdicts into contiguous `{from, to}` failure windows, splitting whenever the KIND changes (`"outage"` red / `"dependency"` grey / `"missed"` amber — the last only when a caller supplies the covering automation's count, since a miss short of it is not yet a verdict); `replayProbeStates` (pure) replays the monitor state machine over the same verdicts and is a deliberate mirror of the browser's shared `PolarisMonitorStates.replay` (`public/js/monitor-states.js`, read by the Last-30-min strip, the desktop response-time chart and the phone's), so the alert email's response-time chart and the device page cannot disagree about which miss was already Down or which answer was still climbing — `foldProbeRecoveries` reads its `recovering` runs straight off it, which is what carries the automation's RESET into the picture (business rule 36: "up after 5 received" stays blue for five answers, not the three the bucket's drain costs). Parity between the two copies is pinned by tests/unit/assetIntermittencyBar.test.ts; `readProbeOutages` picks the `assets` retention tier and reads detail rows or the hourly/daily rollups (where only `successCount === 0` counts — a partial-loss bucket still plots its average). Served as `outages` on the telemetry / storage / interface history endpoints, consumed by `_outageMarkers` in public/js/assets.js and its mobile + compare ports. Replaced a 2.5×-median-cadence gap heuristic that could not tell an outage from an unmounted disk, an uncollected metric or a widened cadence, and drew red dives through maintenance windows. Deliberately read-only: writing synthetic failure rows into the sample tables was rejected because the alert engine, the rollups and the vanished-state sweep all read those tables raw.
│   │   ├── sampleRetentionService.ts # Global sample-retention policy. `Setting("sampleRetention")` holds a per-ENTITY shape `{assets|cpuMem|hardware|interfaces|storage|ipsec|perfSla|process: {detail, hourly, daily}}` (8 tiered entities × 3 tiers) PLUS a parallel FLAT dimension for tables that are current-state-with-age rather than tiered time-series, where detail/hourly/daily would be meaningless: `FLAT_RETENTION_ENTITIES` = `{appMapConnections: {days}}` (`asset_process_connections`, the Application Map socket facts). `SampleRetention` is the INTERSECTION of the two records, so `retention[tieredEntity][tier]` keeps working untouched while flat entities read `retention.appMapConnections.days`; `parseSampleRetention`/`mergeRetention` loop both lists, so a stored blob that predates a flat entity simply inherits the default on read — no migration needed. The flat window also bounds its READING surface: `getAppMapConnectionRetentionDays()` feeds both the nightly prune and the Application Map graph query, so the page's "Seen within" range can't promise history that was already pruned. `POLARIS_PROCESS_CONN_RETENTION_DAYS` is the default seed for `appMapConnections.days`, not an override. Encoding per tier: positive = N days, `0` = tier off (pruned away), `FOREVER`(-1) = keep forever. Defaults 7/30/365. `getSampleRetention()` reads with a 5-second in-process cache; `updateSampleRetention(input)` merges partial updates + invalidates the cache; `getRetentionDays(retention, entity, tier)` is the keyed accessor. `SELECTION_AWARE_ENTITIES` = interfaces/storage/ipsec — for those the configured retention applies to OPERATOR-SELECTED (monitored, `cadence="fast"`) rows; UNSELECTED bulk rows are kept a fixed `UNSELECTED_DETAIL_HOURS` (24h), no rollup (the class axis — default/switch/accessPoint — was retired in favor of this selection split). Edited from Server Settings → Retention card; consumed by the prune layer (`monitoringService.pruneXxxSamples`) and the chart tier router. Legacy class-shaped Setting values migrate forward via `migrateSampleRetentionToEntities` on first boot.
│   │   ├── capacityService.ts       # Capacity snapshot: host (cpu/ram + per-volume disk free), DB sample-table breakdown, monitoring workload + steady-state size projection, severity grading (ok/watch/amber/red). Volume scan walks every distinct filesystem Polaris/Postgres write to (app dir, state dir, backups dir, plus the PostgreSQL data directory when DB is co-located — resolved authoritatively via `SHOW data_directory`, falling back to platform-conventional paths like `/var/lib/pgsql/...` when SHOW fails because the application's DB role lacks `pg_read_all_settings`), deduped by stat.dev so single-LV installs collapse cleanly and STIG-style multi-LV layouts surface each filesystem once. `recordCapacityTransition()` compares against a stored `capacity.lastSeverity` Setting and writes one `capacity.severity_changed` Event on each transition (any direction), routed out through eventArchiveService → syslog/SFTP so an alert reaches on-call before the DB dies. Feeds the Maintenance tab Capacity card and the sidebar critical alert via the /server-settings/pg-tuning endpoint. Snapshot also carries `database.timescale: { extensionInstalled, hypertableTables[] }` and a `timescale_recommended` watch-severity reason that fires when sample tables exceed 1 GB without the extension installed; reason text adapts via `deploymentContext` heuristics (local-DB vs remote/managed, bare-metal vs container). Also carries `database.connectionPool: { currentInUse, peakObserved, prismaPoolSize, pgbossPoolSize, maxConnections }` — `currentInUse` from `pg_stat_activity` at snapshot time; `peakObserved` is a rolling high-water mark tracked in module-local memory (resets on process restart); `prismaPoolSize` and `pgbossPoolSize` are the configured Polaris pool capacities (DATABASE_POOL_SIZE / POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE; pgboss is null in cursor mode); `maxConnections` from `SHOW max_connections`. Drives the `db_pool_undersized` watch-severity reason that fires when peak ≥80% of the combined Polaris pool capacity; suggestion text points operators at the Capacity Advisor card for the actual recommended pool sizes. The three advisor-driven reasons — `monitor_workers_undersized` (watch — single rollup naming the worst worker gap), `max_connections_undersized` (amber — fires when the advisor recommends a higher max_connections than is currently set), and `monitor_handler_timeout_pressure` (watch — fires when observed p90 ≥ 70% of `pgboss.queue.expire_seconds` on any monitor cadence) — are populated by `getCapacitySnapshotWithAdvisor()`, the two-pass orchestrator helper that builds an initial snapshot, runs the Capacity Advisor against it, then rebuilds with the advisor's gap data in scope so the reasons fire. The legacy `pgboss_recommended` / `pgboss_overdue` / `pgboss_pending` reasons + their inline manual "Enable on next restart" buttons were folded into the Capacity Advisor's QUEUE_MODE lever and removed from this service. The local `SAMPLE_TABLES` enumeration (capacity-domain, distinct from `timescaleService.SAMPLE_TABLES`) lists all 21 tables — 7 detail + 7 hourly + 7 daily — each tagged with `(entity, tier, countKey)` for the steady-state projection. **DETAIL tiers that never compress** (retention ≤ compress-after — all detail at the 7d/7d default) are projected from a **measured uncompressed daily byte-rate** (`measureDetailDailyBytes` → median size of recent settled, uncompressed chunks ÷ span, × retention) via the pure helper `projectDetailBytes` — this captures real index + page overhead and the true pinned-interface/cadence/asset mix that the hardcoded `count × rows-per-asset-per-day × bytes/row` workload model can't see (the workload model underprojected interface detail ~33× on a real fleet: 2026-06, assumed 20 ifaces/24h-cap/395 B-row vs. 9,418 pinned interfaces/7d/~1.1 kB-on-disk-row). **Rollup tiers** (hourly/daily, mostly compressed at steady state) keep the workload model — `monitored asset count × rows-per-asset-per-day × retentionDays × bytes/row` — using the CALIBRATED `DEFAULT_BYTES_PER_ROW`. It still NEVER uses the live-measured `avgBytesPerRow` (relpages ÷ pg_stat tuples): unreliable for compressed/bloated hypertables (relpages count bloated/empty pages + compressed TOAST; swings under write load), which once produced phantom 14–218 TB steady-states. The chunk measurement instead reads only dense, settled, uncompressed chunks and takes the median (robust to a single decompression-bloated outlier). Fallback to the workload model when a detail table has no settled chunk yet (fresh install) or its retention reaches past the compress frontier. `projectSteadyStateSize` + `projectDetailBytes` are exported for the unit tests that lock this. Retention values come from `Setting("sampleRetention")` via `getSampleRetention()` (per-entity per-tier — projection reads `retention[entity][tier]`) instead of the legacy single-tier `monitor.sampleRetentionDays` etc. Snapshot also carries `database.rollupLastSuccess: { hourly, daily }` (timestamps from `Setting("sampleRollup.<tier>.lastSuccess")`) which drives the new `sample_rollup_lagging` watch reason — fires when hourly is >6 h stale or daily is >36 h stale AND any sample table has rows, catching a wedged rollup before long-range chart queries silently fall back to detail-table scans. Snapshot also carries `database.io: { trackIoTiming, measured, avgBackendsBlockedOnDisk, windowSeconds }` — measured disk-read pressure from `pg_stat_database.blk_read_time` sampled between snapshots (rate via module-local `prevDbIo`, not the cumulative counters; pure math + thresholds live in `capacityDbIo.ts`, read through the PgBouncer-aware `getDirectStatsPool()`). This replaced the old size-based `ram_insufficient` heuristic and its prescriptive "recommended N GB" figure: the `db_io_pressure` reason (family `db_ram`; **warning** at ≥2.0 / **watch** at ≥0.5 avg connections continuously blocked on storage reads, guarded on DB > host RAM) fires only when PostgreSQL is genuinely waiting on storage — medium-aware (HDD vs SATA vs NVMe) and OS-page-cache-aware for free, since an in-cache read returns from read() in ~0 ms. When `track_io_timing` is off blk_read_time stays 0 so we can't measure; the `track_io_timing_off` watch (own family `pg_io_timing`, fires only when DB > RAM) nudges the operator to enable it instead of guessing.
│   │   ├── capacityDbIo.ts           # Pure disk-read-pressure rate math, split out of capacityService so it's unit-testable without the service's heavy import graph (prisma / queueService → pg-boss optional dep). `deriveDbIoVerdict(prev, current)` turns two `pg_stat_database` readings into `{ measured, avgBackendsBlockedOnDisk, windowSeconds }`; returns measured:false on first call / window < `MIN_IO_WINDOW_MS` / counter reset (so callers never alarm on bad data). Exports the tunable thresholds `DB_IO_WATCH_BACKENDS` (0.5) + `DB_IO_WARNING_BACKENDS` (2.0) and `IO_VERDICT_STALE_MS`.
│   │   ├── capacityAdvisorService.ts # Capacity Advisor: derives recommended values for connection-pool sizes, monitor worker counts (per-cadence: probe / fastFiltered / telemetry+systemInfo / **lldp** / **storage** / floating — LLDP and Storage levers added in Phase 2 alongside the queue carve-out), queue mode (cursor ↔ pg-boss), PostgreSQL `max_connections`, and PostgreSQL tuning settings from observable workload (monitored asset count, monitored interface count, per-class FortiGate count, per-cadence pass-duration P90 read from the `polaris_monitor_work_duration_seconds` histogram, observed peak connections, host RAM). Also reads `pgboss.queue.expire_seconds` for the six monitor cadences (live from the DB, so the advisor reflects what's actually in effect — not just what `EXPIRE_BY_QUEUE` in queueService.ts would write on a fresh install); surfaces the value alongside p90 in each per-cadence worker tooltip, and rolls cadences whose p90 ≥ 70% of expire_seconds into `handlerTimeoutPressure` for the capacity reason of the same name. `buildAdvisorState(inputs)` is the pure calc; `recomputeAdvisorFromSnapshot(snap, pgTuning)` is the async wrapper that loads integration counts + cadence percentiles + applicable-asset SQL counts + queue timeouts and calls into it. Cached in module memory with a 10-min TTL refreshed by `capacityWatch` and on demand by the GET endpoint. **Advisory-only** — operator clicks Stage in the UI to write env-driven recommendations to `.env` via `setEnvVar` (restart-required to take effect). `max_connections` and PostgreSQL settings stay display-only because they require a PostgreSQL restart Polaris can't trigger. Calc chain (also covered in the plan file): `workersNeeded[c] = ceil(applicable × p90 × 1.5 / cadenceInterval)`, floored at `perCadenceFloor = clamp(ceil(monitoredAssetCount × 0.5), 4, 24)` per cadence (so 6-asset installs floor at 4, 48+-asset installs cap at 24 — the floor is a "modest burst absorber" sized to the fleet rather than a fixed 24); `floatingWorkers = max(floatingFloor, ceil(0.25 × Σ))` where `floatingFloor = clamp(ceil(monitoredAssetCount × 0.5), 4, 32)`; `prismaTarget = workerCeiling + discoveryReserve + httpOverhead`; `DATABASE_POOL_SIZE = roundUpToNearest(max(prismaTarget, current), 50)`; `POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE = roundUpToNearest(max(pgbossTarget, current), 50)`; `recommendedMax = roundUpToNearest(ceil((effectivePrisma + effectivePgboss) / 0.65), 50)`. Cold start substitutes `COLD_START_P90_SEC = { probe: 0.4, fastFiltered: 0.6, telemetry: 0.8, systemInfo: 1.0 }` when histogram sample count is < 100 per cadence; the UI shows a "cold-start" badge per affected row. Never recommends shrinking — `changeRequired` is true only when recommended > current. **Operator override:** the advisory-only PG-tuning levers (`work_mem` / `shared_buffers` / `effective_cache_size` / `random_page_cost`) carry an `operatorOverride` flag — true when the current value was set explicitly via `ALTER SYSTEM` (detected in `computePgTuning` via `pg_settings.sourcefile` ending in `postgresql.auto.conf`). When set, `changeRequired` is forced false (`ok=true`) and the UI renders an "Operator-set" pill instead of "Stage", because the operator deliberately overrode the heuristic — e.g. lowering `work_mem` below the `RAM/128` recommendation to stop swapping — and staging would write to `postgresql.conf`, which `postgresql.auto.conf` overrides anyway (the prior behavior nagged "Stage" forever on such a value).
│   │   ├── timescaleService.ts      # TimescaleDB detection + hypertable utilities. `detectTimescale()` runs once at startup (warmed in src/app.ts) and queries `pg_extension` + `timescaledb_information.hypertables` to populate a module-level cache; `isTimescaleAvailable()` and `isHypertable(name)` are sync getters used by the prune layer and capacityService. `dropChunks(table, olderThan)` is the chunk-granular fast path used as a pre-filter before the per-class `deleteMany` in `pruneOneTable` — no-op when the target table isn't a hypertable, so callers don't need to branch. `migrateToHypertables()` runs at boot (after detection) and idempotently converts all twenty-two managed tables — the 21 tiered sample + rollup tables plus the standalone `asset_custom_widget_samples` — to hypertables (`create_hypertable(if_not_exists => TRUE, migrate_data => TRUE)`). Source tables partition by `timestamp`; rollup tables partition by `bucketStart`. Each table gets column compression with `compress_segmentby = "assetId"` + `compress_orderby` matching the partition column, and the compression policy with the `TIMESCALE_COMPRESS_AFTER_DAYS` window (default 7). **The compression policy is only removed + re-added when the window actually changed** (`compressionPolicyMatches` introspects the existing policy's `compress_after`); an unconditional recreate every boot resets the policy's 12h `next_start`, so a frequently-restarted host (in-app updates cycle `polaris.target`) would never let it fire — the failure mode that left compression off in prod and ballooned `asset_interface_samples` to 114 GB (a single 63 GB uncompressed chunk). **After the conversion loop a self-heal pass (`compressEligibleBacklog`) immediately compresses any chunk already past its window but still uncompressed** — sequential, oldest-first, capped at 8/table/boot — so a restart-cycled host self-heals instead of accumulating uncompressed delete-churn bloat. Source tables carry a composite PK on `(id, timestamp)` and rollup tables on `(id, bucketStart)` to satisfy Timescale's "all UNIQUE/PK constraints must include the partitioning column" rule — works fine on plain Postgres too. The canonical lists are exported as `SAMPLE_TABLES` (7 sources), `ROLLUP_TABLES` (14 rollups), `STANDALONE_SAMPLE_TABLES` (detail-only, no rollups — currently just `asset_custom_widget_samples`), and `ALL_HYPERTABLE_CANDIDATES` (the union of all three); capacityService consumes the union for `database.timescale.hypertableTables` enumeration, and `tests/unit/timescaleTables.test.ts` drift-guards the lists against the rollup writer, the prune layer, and the schema.
│   │   ├── queueService.ts          # Monitor work queue mode + pg-boss runtime. Two implementations: `cursor` (default — in-process worker pool inside runMonitorPass; fits small/medium fleets fine after the Step 4a split-tick fix) and `pgboss` (durable queue with per-cadence worker pools — recommended once the fleet crosses ~500 monitored assets). Queues include `polaris-monitor-losssample` for the ICMP loss sampler (own pool via `POLARIS_MONITOR_LOSS_SAMPLE_WORKERS`, 15s job expiry, 2s polling - a sample later than its 10s cadence is worthless; deliberately absent from `FLOAT_PRIORITY` so it can never borrow the floating pool from real monitoring work). Active mode lives in `Setting.monitor.queueMode`; captured at boot via `initializeQueue()` and frozen as the running process's mode regardless of subsequent Setting writes (operator changes take effect on next restart). `startPgbossWorkers()` boots pg-boss (only when boot-time mode is `pgboss`), creates **six** queues with `policy: "stately"` + per-asset singletonKey for natural coalescing (at most one QUEUED and one ACTIVE job per `(assetId, cadence)`: a duplicate of a still-queued job is absorbed silently, and the next round may queue behind a running one; different assetIds run in parallel up to `localConcurrency`. Was `policy: "singleton"` until 2026-09 — which SOUNDS like that contract but is not: pg-boss 12's singleton unique index constrains state=active only, so every 5s tick re-queued a still-queued due asset and a backed-up queue accumulated created-state duplicates bounded only by retentionSeconds; verified empirically, send() and insert() alike. ensureQueues detects a queue stored with the old policy and recreates it once at boot — safe because monitor jobs are stateless and the next tick republishes), and registers worker handlers that call back into the same `runFooFor()` functions the cursor pass uses. **Phase 2 carve-out**: LLDP and Storage each get their own queue (`polaris-monitor-lldp` / `polaris-monitor-storage`) and dedicated worker pool (default 12 workers each, env `POLARIS_MONITOR_LLDP_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_STORAGE_WORKERS`) running `runLldpFor` / `runStorageFor`. The publisher in `monitorAssets.ts` checks `Asset.lastLldpAt + lldpIntervalSeconds` / `Asset.lastStorageAt + storageIntervalSeconds` against the per-asset resolved cadence to decide when each is due. The legacy `collectSystemInfo` still walks LLDP and storage as session-coalesced side effects when interfaces + LLDP / storage resolve to the same polling method; the dedicated queues drive their own independent cadence and `persistLldpNeighbors` / `enqueueStorageSamples` are idempotent against double-walks. Cursor-mode installs keep LLDP + Storage on the legacy systemInfo path — the dedicated queues are pg-boss-only. `publishMonitorJobsBulk(cadence, jobs[])` is the publisher entry point — `monitorAssets.ts` accumulates the due set per cadence inside its loop and flushes one bulk INSERT per queue per tick (2000 per-asset awaited `send()` round trips measured 3.7s against a LOCAL Postgres, most of the 5s probe-tick budget; the bulk insert is ~260ms). `publishMonitorJob(cadence, assetId, transport?)` remains the single-job form. `monitorAssets.ts` runs the same two ticking loops it uses for cursor — only the dispatch differs. Worker architecture: 24 dedicated workers per queue (probe / fastFiltered / telemetry / systemInfo, configurable via `POLARIS_MONITOR_PROBE_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_FAST_WORKERS` / `POLARIS_MONITOR_HEAVY_WORKERS` — the heavy var sets both telemetry and systemInfo) plus a **floating worker pool** (default 32, env `POLARIS_MONITOR_FLOATING_WORKERS`) that polls all four queues in priority order via `boss.fetch()`. The floating pool flows idle capacity to wherever the backlog actually is — when telemetry is chronically backed up while fastFiltered sits empty, floating workers drain telemetry instead of slots being wasted on idle queues. Total ceiling stays at 96+32=128 (same DB pool pressure as the prior flat 32×4). Implemented in `startFloatingWorkers(boss, maxFloat)` with module-level `floatingInFlight` (soft cap counter) and `floatingLoopRunning` (shutdown signal); the loop fires per-queue `boss.fetch()` calls in `FLOAT_PRIORITY` order (probe > fastFiltered > telemetry > systemInfo), dispatches each fetched job to the matching `runFooFor()`, and explicitly calls `boss.complete(name, id)` / `boss.fail(name, id, ...)`. Singleton-key dedup at the publish layer means floating workers never collide with dedicated workers on the same `(assetId, cadence)` — pg-boss already coalesces those into a single in-flight job. `POLARIS_PGBOSS_POOL_SIZE` defaults to 20 at runtime but the Capacity Advisor now scales the **recommended** value with the configured worker count: `roundUpToNearest(max(20, ceil(workerCeiling × 0.25)), 50)` — at the 128-worker default that rounds up to 50. The pool is used only for pg-boss's internal queue mechanics (boss.fetch / boss.complete / boss.fail); a too-small pool serializes the simultaneous boss.complete() calls that fire when a heavy cadence finishes a batch of work, which the operator can then see as failed jobs and stalled queue depth. The configured count per queue plus `queue="floating"` is exposed as the `polaris_monitor_workers{queue}` gauge so operators can confirm restart-pickup without reading logs. **Stable per-worker slot IDs** are assigned via [src/utils/workerSlotPool.ts](src/utils/workerSlotPool.ts) — `probe-W01..W24`, `fast-W01..W24`, `telemetry-W01..W24`, `sysinfo-W01..W24`, `floating-F01..F32`. The slot is acquired on handler entry and released on exit (try/finally) so a slot is reused across jobs and an operator can follow one slot's lifecycle through journalctl. The pickup/finish lines emit at info level ONLY when the job payload carries `verboseDebug: true` (set by the publisher when the asset's source integration has `config.verboseLogging` on); slot bookkeeping itself runs every tick regardless. Naming convention `polaris-monitor-*`; future `polaris-discovery-*` queues should be added when discovery moves under pg-boss and worker tuning revisited together.
│   │   ├── assetSightingService.ts  # DHCP-only sighting recorder: recordSightings() batch-upserts AssetFortigateSighting rows (deduped by (assetId, fortigateDevice)); getQuarantineCandidates(assetId) returns sightings within max-age; getSightingSettings/updateSightingSettings backed by Setting key "quarantineSightingSettings". Default max-age: 180 days. Also owns the **gateway-change audit**: `computeFreshestGateChanges(current, incoming)` (pure, unit-tested) decides when an asset's FRESHEST sighting moves to a different gate — freshest = max `lastSeen`, the same rule `syncEndpointDependencyEdges` uses to pick an endpoint's parent, so the event tracks the value that drives dependency suppression (a move INSERTS a row and nothing prunes the old one, hence "freshest" not "only"). `recordSightings` runs one bounded pre-read over the deduped asset ids and emits `asset.gateway_firewall.changed` per real move. Three deliberate silences: no prior rows = first sighting; names compare through `bareFortinetDeviceName` + case-fold; and the **takeover guard** — nothing fires while the incumbent gate is also refreshed in the same batch, because a device holding live leases on two gates has both rows stamped to ~now every run and would tie-flip an event every cycle forever (cost: a real move reports once the old gate stops handing out the address). `SightingInput.assetHostname` is passed by the caller purely to name the audit row, so this service never queries assets.
│   │   ├── assetUpstreamService.ts   # Resolves the three UPSTREAM devices the asset-details General tab names (Last Seen Switch / AP / Firewall) from the display strings discovery stores to the Asset rows behind them, so those rows carry verbs instead of being dead text. `resolveAssetUpstream(assetId, {includeFirewall})` reads `Asset.lastSeenSwitch` (`splitLastSeenSwitch` splits `"<switch>/<port>"` — the device name becomes the clickable half, the port stays text), `Asset.lastSeenAp`, and the FRESHEST `AssetFortigateSighting.fortigateDevice`; ONE candidate query (`parentAssetWhereOr` branches, type-scoped per kind) then the shared `resolveInfraParentAsset` precedence per kind — serial → the candidate's own FMG device-name stamp → hostname → name-as-serial, never a bare hostname match (see utils/fortinetParentKey.ts). Indexes per KIND, since `buildInfraParentIndex` is first-writer-wins per key and a switch sharing a gate's hostname would otherwise shadow it. The displayed NAME never changes: the firewall half resolves the most recent sighting's device rather than walking for the first name that matches something. Unresolved ⇒ `{name, asset: null}`, never an error. Management access rides each resolved device through `shapeManagementAccessForClient`. Backs `GET /assets/:id/upstream`; read-only.
│   │   ├── assetQuarantineService.ts # FortiGate MAC quarantine push/pull. quarantineAsset()/releaseQuarantine() orchestrate per-FortiGate pushes using buildTransportForIntegration() (supports both FMG proxy/direct and standalone FortiGate). Writes the `user.quarantine` object via ONE `PUT /api/v2/cmdb/user/quarantine` carrying the whole `targets` array — that child table has no collection resource to POST to (the parent is a COMPLEX object with no mkey), so create, release and rollback all share the mechanism; read-modify-write preserves entries Polaris does not own and every MAC carries `drop: enable`. quarantineTargets JSON array tracks per-target status (synced|drift|failed). verifyAssetQuarantine() drift-checks all targets without writing. statusBeforeQuarantine + monitoredBeforeQuarantine preserve the prior status AND the `monitored` flag for restore on release — quarantined is an unmonitorable status (business rule 10), so the quarantine write itself turns polling off and the release write stages the restored status and monitored together (one write, so the clamp judges the RESTORED status). Auto-quarantine fires from discovery when a quarantined asset is sighted on a new FortiGate.
│   │   ├── apiTokenService.ts       # Bearer-token auth for external callers. createToken/listTokens/revokeToken/deleteToken/verifyToken. Wire format: polaris_<32-char-base64url>. argon2id hash + tokenPrefix-indexed candidate lookup. Each token is bound to a Role at mint time (roleId); requirePermission resolves the token's role matrix like a session snapshot. integrationIds required when the role grants assetsQuarantine >= write. Admin-equivalent binding logs an api_token.admin_equivalent warning Event. lastUsedAt/lastUsedIp bumped on successful verify.
│   │   ├── agentInstallService.ts   # Polaris Agent remote install/upgrade/uninstall over SSH (SFTP push + installer script) / WinRM (cert-pinned HTTPS binary pull + PowerShell). State machine pending→uploading→enrolling→active. The install-method variant (ManagedAgent.installScriptId) selects which script `installerScript`/`uninstallerScript` upload; `runInstall` re-validates the OS-lock via resolveInstallScriptId before executing. See ARCHITECTURE.md → Monitoring Architecture.
│   │   ├── agentInstallScripts.ts   # Curated catalog of agent install-method VARIANTS (metadata only: id/osPlatform/label/description/isDefault — one vetted variant per OS today: linux-systemd / darwin-launchd / windows-service). `resolveInstallScriptId(os, scriptId?)` is the server-side OS-LOCK (throws when a variant's OS ≠ the target's, or on unknown id; returns the per-OS default when none picked). Script BODIES stay inline in agentInstallService.ts (version-coupled to the binary); this module owns the picker vocabulary + validation. Curated, NOT operator-authored — adds no RCE surface beyond what agent deploy already does. Exposed at GET /assets/agent-install-scripts for the deploy modal.
│   │   ├── windowsSshOnboardingService.ts # "Windows SSH Deployment" card (Integrations → Polaris Agent). Generates the ed25519 deployment keypair via ssh2's `utils.generateKeyPairSync` (OpenSSH private-key format, exactly what ssh2.connect accepts — no conversion, no shelling out), owns the Polaris-managed `ssh` Credential that holds it, and persists the card's non-secret config in the `windowsSshOnboarding` Setting. Private half is written into Credential.config (sealed at rest by db.ts) and NEVER returned by any read path — the VAPID precedent; only the public half + `SHA256:` fingerprint come out. Rotation REPLACES the credential config rather than going through updateCredential(), because mergeConfigPreservingSecrets reads an empty string as "keep the stored secret" and so cannot clear a stale `password`. `credential.ssh_keypair_generated` is stamped at WARNING level: rotating locks Polaris out of every endpoint until the onboarding script re-runs.
│   │   ├── intunePublishService.ts # Publishes the WINDOWS SSH onboarding pair to Intune as a Remediation (deviceHealthScript). Upserts by displayName (paged, bounded) so re-publishing updates one policy instead of accumulating duplicates. **NEVER calls /assign** — that is the human review gate for a script granting fleet-wide administrative SSH, and two tests pin it. The Graph API version is PROBED at first use (v1.0 then beta, cached per process): a 404 means wrong version, a 403 means the endpoint EXISTS and permission is missing, so that base is the right one. Opt-in per integration via `EntraIdConfig.publishToIntune`, which needs the Graph application permission DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All + admin consent. Audits `intune.script_published` at warning level.
│   │   ├── arcPublishService.ts    # Runs the SSH onboarding script on Azure Arc machines via Run Command (azureArcService.dispatchRunCommand). The Arc counterpart to intunePublishService, shaped differently because Arc has NO inert state — a run command EXECUTES on creation, so the review gate is the operator's explicit target selection rather than assignment; there is deliberately no 'all machines' affordance and ids are re-resolved against the LIVE roster (the subscription/resourceGroup/region reaching ARM come from Azure, not a request body). Sends BOTH platform scripts so each machine gets the one matching its osType; capped at 200 targets per run. Opt-in per integration via `AzureArcConfig.allowRunCommand`, which needs an Azure RBAC role carrying Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines/runCommands/write — a role ASSIGNMENT, not a Graph permission. Audits one warning-level `arc.run_command_executed` per batch with the per-machine roll-up. This is what covers Linux and Windows Server, which Intune does not reach.
│   │   ├── sshHostKeyService.ts     # Trust-on-first-use pinning for SSH SERVER host keys (`SshHostKey` table, one row per dialed host:port). `verifyOrPin` = no pin → store + accept (`ssh.host_key.pinned`); match → accept + hourly-throttled `lastSeen`; DIFFERS → refuse + warn-level `ssh.host_key.mismatch` carrying both fingerprints. Fingerprints are `SHA256:<unpadded base64>` — byte-identical to `ssh-keygen -lf` so operators can compare by eye. Opt-in per credential via `SshConfig.verifyHostKey` (default OFF, mirroring WinRM's `verifyTls`), because before this Polaris passed NO `hostVerifier` and accepted any host key on every SSH path. Lookup is served from a module-level Map (the `bumpRoleVersion` cache shape) since `withSshClient` runs on the per-minute agentless-processes cadence. `deleteHostKey` is the audited recovery for a legitimately rebuilt host.
│   │   ├── sshOnboardingScript.ts   # Pure generator for the SSH onboarding scripts, TWO PER PLATFORM. **Windows**: `buildWindowsOnboardingScript` (REMEDIATION — installs the OpenSSH Server capability, starts sshd, optionally creates the local admin account, writes the public key to %ProgramData%\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys with the Administrators+SYSTEM ACL sshd demands, optionally scopes inbound TCP/22) + `buildWindowsOnboardingDetectionScript`. **Linux**: `buildLinuxOnboardingScript` (writes the key into the USER's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys at 700/600 with correct ownership, `restorecon`s the SELinux context, and installs a **NOPASSWD sudoers drop-in** at /etc/sudoers.d/polaris-agent — validated with `visudo -cf` BEFORE install, since a malformed drop-in locks sudo out for every user on the host; deliberately does NOT install openssh-server, which would need distro-specific package management) + `buildLinuxOnboardingDetectionScript`, which unlike the Windows one ALSO checks the account and the sudoers drop-in, because both are prerequisites the agent install genuinely fails without. Each platform's key-presence predicate is emitted into BOTH its scripts from one constant so detection can never drift from what remediation writes. Emitted scripts are idempotent and delivery-neutral. `assertValidUsername` / `assertValidLinuxUsername` (stricter: POSIX charset, no DOMAIN\user) / `assertValidPublicKey` / `assertValidServerIp` are hard REJECTS, not escapes — these values are interpolated into a script an admin runs fleet-wide as root/SYSTEM.
│   │   ├── agentBuildService.ts     # In-app `go build` of the six agent platform binaries (linux/darwin/windows × amd64/arm64); writes data/agents/<version>/ + manifest.json atomically; FIFO build queue + cancellation + per-version retention; post-build Windows binary signing via agentSigningService (fail-open).
│   │   ├── agentSigningService.ts   # Internal-CA code signing of the Windows agent binaries (jsign via `java -jar` against a PKCS#12 keystore, password via env — never argv). Owns the masked `agent.codeSigning` Setting, the EXPLICIT RFC3161 timestamping (a PKCS12 store gets none automatically, so a missing countersignature would invalidate the whole fleet at cert expiry), the keytool-backed keystore/alias verification behind the Test button (resolved bare-name-then-`java.home`, because java-17-openjdk-headless ships keytool beside the JVM rather than necessarily on PATH — a PATH miss is not the tool being absent; a genuine absence degrades the Test message and nothing else, since signing itself only ever runs `java -jar jsign.jar`), the signingAvailability() probe, the operator KEYSTORE UPLOAD (validate-then-promote: the .pfx lands on a temp path in the same directory, is opened with the supplied password, and is only renamed over the managed path once it answers — so a wrong password can't replace a working keystore with one that fails at the next build; a keystore with no PrivateKeyEntry is refused outright, a missing keytool stores it UNVERIFIED since jsign needs no keytool), the `keytool -list -v` cert-metadata read behind the card's expiry countdown + Defender-indicator fingerprint, and the `agent.signing.lastFailure` stamp behind the assets:write sidebar alert.
│   │   ├── agentChannelService.ts   # Agent ↔ Polaris outbound WebSocket channel: heartbeat tracking + on-demand config push (`refreshConfig`) + command-dispatch wake (`wakeCommands` → `commands-pending` frame). Also runs the cross-process command-wake LISTENer (`startCommandWakeListener`, web/all role) on a dedicated direct-URL pg session.
│   │   ├── agentCommandWake.ts      # Cross-process "wake this agent" signal. `publishCommandWake(managedAgentId)` emits a Postgres NOTIFY (`CMD_WAKE_CHANNEL` = polaris_agent_cmd_wake) so the process holding the agent's WS session pushes a `commands-pending` frame. Best-effort latency optimization; the ≤20s command poll is the guaranteed floor.
│   │   ├── agentTokenService.ts     # Agent enrollment-token / bearer-token mint + argon2id hashing; consumeEnrollmentToken swaps one-shot token for long-lived bearer, stamps the asset's per-stream polling to "agent", and auto-enables `monitored` (status-permitting; shouldEnableMonitoringOnEnroll) with a monitorOverride recompute.
│   │   ├── agentCommandService.ts   # The agent command queue (run_script only — process/service control was removed in the Satellite-posture change). `fetchPendingCommands(agentId)` (agent poll; marks sent, includes `payload`, and flips linked run_script AutomationScriptRuns pending→running), `recordCommandResult(...)` (agent report → succeeded|failed; run_script results complete the linked AutomationScriptRun with exitCode/stdout/stderr ≤64KB and stamp `automation.script.run`; a stale/foreign non-run_script row is audited generically). Script runs are enqueued by `automationScriptService.requestScriptRun`, not here.
│   │   ├── agentlessProcessService.ts # Agentless (SSH/WinRM) collection for the `processes` stream — the previously-missing server-side collector (the matrix advertised ssh/winrm but only the agent path existed). Two orchestrators called from monitoringService.runProcessesFor: `collectProcessesSsh(host, credConfig, opts)` (one SSH session: `LC_ALL=C ps -eo pid=,pcpu=,rss=,etimes=,user:32=,comm=` for inventory + pinned telemetry — pcpu is lifetime-average, accepted tradeoff; `ss -tunapH | grep -F -e '"<name>"' …` for mapped-process connections, filtered ON-HOST, grep exit 1 = empty scrape; `ss -p` attribution needs root/sudo) and `collectProcessesWinrm(conn, opts)` (two compact `-EncodedCommand` PowerShell scripts kept under the 8191-char cmd ceiling: Get-Process + Win32_PerfFormattedData_PerfProc_Process per-PID JSON; Get-NetTCPConnection/Get-NetUDPEndpoint filtered by OwningProcess ∈ mapped PIDs). Everything below the transport calls is a pure parser (parseLinuxPs / parseLinuxSs / parseWindowsProcessJson / parseWindowsConnectionsJson / aggregatePsRows / buildConnectionRows — the server-side mirror of the agent's direction heuristic), unit-tested against fixtures. Mapped names are charset-sanitized (isShellSafeProcessName) before embedding in any remote command line — never raw shell interpolation. Result contract AgentlessProcessResult { inventory?, telemetry?, connections? }.
│   │   ├── agentlessHostService.ts # CPU/memory, interfaces and storage from a Linux or Windows host over SSH or WinRM, no agent installed — the missing half of three streams that accepted `ssh`/`winrm` at every validator and then returned `{supported:false}`, which `runTelemetryFor` records as a SUCCESSFUL tick. Same shape as its processes sibling: shipped-and-fixed command constants, pure parsers as the unit-test surface, thin transports. Linux reads `/proc/stat` TWICE a second apart in one command (CPU is a rate, so a single read cannot produce it) plus `/proc/meminfo` (**MemAvailable**, not MemFree — page cache is not "used" and MemFree makes every healthy box look full), `/sys/class/net/*` (stable across distros, unlike `ip`/`ifconfig` output) and `df -PkT` (pseudo-filesystems dropped). Windows uses `Win32_OperatingSystem` + the `_Total` processor counter, `Get-NetAdapter` + `Get-NetAdapterStatistics` (LinkSpeed is a DISPLAY string — `parseWindowsLinkSpeed`; MAC normalised from dashes to colons, which the downstream identity joins assume) and `Get-Volume`. **One SSH connection per host per tick** — at 2000 assets the handshake dominates, not the parse; WinRM is stateless per call and batches one script per stream against the WinRS length ceiling. A failed command leaves its stream `undefined` (persist layer keeps stored rows) rather than `[]` (wipe).
│   │   ├── notificationTypes.ts     # Automations vocabulary: the discriminated `trigger` Zod union (asset_metric | asset_state | host_metric | event | change), the asset `scope` schema (allAssets / assetTypes / tags / assetIds / integrationIds / manufacturers + models — case-insensitive CONTAINS per entry / subnetCidrs — CIDRs or bare IPs validated at save, matched via ipInCidr with bare-IP→host-route via `scopeCidrOf` / `condition` — a nested AND/OR/NONE/NOT-ALL rule tree over assetType/manufacturer/model/hostname/os/tag/subnet/**interfaceName**/status/assetId with per-field operator whitelists (SCOPE_FIELD_OPS), recursive Zod via z.lazy, ≤5 deep + ≤100 rules, evaluated by the pure exported `evaluateScopeCondition`. `interfaceName` — "Device interface", the field that pairs with a device type to select "switches that have a fortilink port" — is the only one backed by a RELATION rather than a column, and the only MULTI-VALUED one besides the device-filter-only `fortigate`: both go through the shared `matchMultiValue`, where a positive operator is satisfied by ANY value and a negative one must hold for EVERY one, and an empty inventory reads as absence. It is deliberately NOT restricted to pinned interfaces the way every interface TRIGGER is — a trigger reads a metric, which only exists for a pinned interface, whereas this asks what the device HAS — and it deliberately contributes NOTHING to `scopeRank`, since an interface is a component of a device, not a statement of which devices a rule is about. Fleet-scale callers never join the relation: they prefetch through `scopeInterfaceIndex.decorateInterfaceLeafHits` and the evaluator reads `asset.interfaceLeafHits`), and the RULE-SHAPE-V2 layer — `resetSchema` ({mode manual|auto|timed|condition|event, clearThreshold? (hysteresis), sustainSec? (clear-sustain), afterSec?, condition? (a custom AND/OR reset tree over the composite leaf vocabulary — allowed on any trigger in `TRIGGER_TYPES_WITH_RESET_CONDITIONS`, i.e. everything but event/change, with leaves restricted to the trigger's own kind; business rule 32), resetEvent? ({actionPattern glob, resourceType?} — the counterpart audit Event that clears the alert, allowed on exactly the complement set `TRIGGER_TYPES_WITH_RESET_EVENT` = event/change; `RESET_EVENT_SUGGESTIONS` maps a trigger pattern to its known recovery pattern and rides the catalog as `resetEventSuggestions` so the wizard prefills it; business rule 32(e))}), the `actionSchema` discriminated union (notify {channelId, recipients, per-action emailComposition?} | api_call {method, static http(s) url, headers ≤20 UNMASKED — no secrets, bodyTemplate {token}s, timeoutSec ≤60} | script {scriptId, runOn server|agent, argsTemplate, timeoutSec ≤600}), escalation v2 (tiers of actions; input accepts either shape), `escalatableActionSchema` (top-level + severity-band actions may carry their own per-action escalation chain; tier actions + resolvedActions stay bare), notify's `recipientDeviceRegion` flag, and the canonical action walk + chain selection (`allRuleActionRefs`, `ruleHasAnyEscalation`, `escalationChainsForSeverity`/`escalationTierStateKey`). `ruleInputSchema` accepts v2 AND legacy bodies (transform folds clearBehavior/clearAfterSec/targets → reset/actions; superRefine validates timed-needs-afterSec + hysteresis threshold ordering per operator); `previewInputSchema` additionally defaults name + makes trigger optional (scope-only preview). Pure converters shared by every reader/writer: `normalizeRuleToV2` (stored row → v2 view), `normalizeReset`, `targetsToNotifyActions`/`actionsToTargets`, `legacyMirrorOfV2` (v2 → the legacy columns kept mirrored at save), `normalizeEscalationToV2`. Plus `emailCompositionSchema`, legacy `escalationSchema`, severities/clearBehaviors/comparators/aggregations, the metric/state/change catalogs, and `buildSchemaCatalog()` (drives the builder/wizard via GET /automations/schema — v2 adds schemaVersion, resetModes/-Meta/-ByTriggerType/resetDefaults, actionTypes, apiCallMeta, scriptMeta, escalationMeta, the sentence-builder comparatorPhrases/inverseComparators/aggregationPhrases/dimensionPhrases, and the per-dimension alerting vocabulary `stateFieldDimensions` (STATE_FIELD_DIMENSIONS — which asset-state fields report per dimension, the state-side counterpart of METRIC_DIMENSIONS) + `dimensionNouns` (DIMENSION_NOUNS — what one dimension is called, so a surface can say "one alert per interface" without hardcoding it)). Single source of truth so the engine, routes, and frontend never hardcode the vocabulary.
│   │   ├── scopeRelationIndex.ts    # The SQL half of the device-filter condition tree's RELATION-backed fields — `interfaceName` ("Device interface", AssetInterface.ifName) and `ssid` ("Broadcast SSID", AssetApVap.ssid), the two fields backed by a relation instead of a scalar column. `decorateRelationLeafHits(rows, trees)` walks the trees for leaves whose field is in `RELATION_CONDITION_FIELDS`, dedupes them by `relationLeafKey` (the FIELD + POSITIVE operator + value, so `equals port9` and `notEquals port9` are one query), runs ONE `assetInterface.groupBy({by:["assetId"]})` per distinct leaf scoped to the rows it was handed, and stamps each row's `interfaceLeafHits` verdict map. The tree evaluator then reads that map instead of an `interfaces` relation — `AssetInterface` is the largest current-state table in the schema (tens of thousands of rows at 2000 devices, an order of magnitude past the fleet), and `loadScopeAssets` re-resolves every DISTINCT scope on the 60s engine tick (memoized per pass, so the ~30 seeded automations' identical `allAssets` scopes share ONE read; the memo is armed only while a pass owns it, because the operator-triggered previews call the same loader and must stay live), so joining it is the anti-pattern the 2000-asset rule exists to catch. Three deliberate details: **groupBy, not findMany+distinct** (a client-side dedupe would ship every matching row, which for `contains "port"` is the whole table); **decoration MERGES**, because the engine decorates a rule's own scope first and its carve-out peers' second; and an ABSENT key means unknown, not false, so `matchScopeRule` falls back to the relation rather than silently answering no. The `matches` wildcard is the one operator with no SQL form — narrowed by the pattern's literal prefix, then regex-tested here; only the wider DEVICE_FILTER vocabulary offers it, so the engine tick never takes that path. Callers: `notificationEngine.loadScopeAssets` + its carve-out pass, `contactService`'s condition preview, `downDetectionService`'s index build. The SINGLE-asset paths deliberately do NOT use this — they join `interfaces` on the one row, which beats a second round trip
│   │   ├── notificationService.ts   # Triggered-notification read + lifecycle (View tab + asset tab). `listNotifications({viewerRegionTags, filters, sort, paging})` (server-side, region-scoped — empty viewer tags = unrestricted, else regionTags intersect + unscoped rows), `acknowledgeNotifications(ids, actor, note)` / `clearNotifications(ids, actor)` (batch updateMany, audited), `getAssetNotifications(assetId)` ({active, matchingRules}), `activeAlertSummaryByAsset(assetIds)` → Map<assetId, {severity, count, unacknowledged}> — "does this device have an active alert and how bad is the worst one", for the Assets list's per-row indicator: ONE indexed findMany over the ids on screen (never a count per row — the list ships up to 10 000 rows on the export path), reduced in JS through `higherAlertSeverity`. Deliberately UNFILTERED by automation relevance (unlike the NOC widgets' pills, this answers "is anything wrong with this device") and unscoped by region (the assets list is, so scoping only the indicator would mark a row quiet the operator can open and find noisy); `unacknowledged` rides along because it decides whether the indicator strobes or sits still, `clearSuppressedAlerts(assetIds?)` (the suppression sweep — retires every ACTIVE alert whose asset is in a maintenance window or dependency-suppressed: soft-clear `system:maintenance` / `system:dependency-suppressed`, `NotificationRuleState` released, one `notification.suppressed` Event each, NO reset actions; sweeps Notification rows rather than state rows because event/change alerts have none, business rule 16), `stripRegionPrefix` + `REGION_TAG_PREFIX`.
│   │   ├── notificationRuleService.ts # Notification RULE business logic: `getMetricSeverityTiers(assetId, metric, dimension?)` (the severity thresholds that would fire on one asset's charted metric — every scope-matching enabled automation's `resolveTierLadder` for a numeric single trigger, plus each composite leaf on that metric at the rule's severity; hwSensorValue tiers are filtered by `hwSensorFilterMatches` so a temperature automation can't shade a fan's chart, one tier per (severity, direction) keeping the MORE SENSITIVE threshold, and deliberately NO rule-18 carve-out since precedence decides who notifies, not what a reading means — backs `GET /assets/:id/metric-thresholds`), `scopeMatchesAsset(scope, asset)` (AND across dimensions, OR within a list; allAssets short-circuits), `findRulesMatchingAsset(assetId)` (asset-tab "automations that can trigger for this asset" — rows go out through `withV2` like every other read path, because clicking a name in that table opens the same edit wizard and a pre-v2 row handed over with NULL reset/actions would open with its actions missing and save them away), rule CRUD (createRule/updateRule/deleteRule/listRules/getRule — audited, bumps the subscription cache; updateRule clears active alerts + drops state rows on trigger-identity change OR disable, deleteRule clears active alerts before the cascade — a rule leaving evaluation must never strand uncleared alerts), and the change-type subscription cache (`getSubscribedChangeActions`/`isChangeActionSubscribed`/`bumpChangeSubscriptions`) so the persist* change-detectors do zero work when no change rule subscribes.
│   │   ├── notificationDimensionService.ts # Values the automation builder's dimensionFilter pickers offer: `listDimensionValues(metric, dimension, scope, narrow?)` (`metric` may also name an asset_state FIELD, the two namespaces being disjoint; applicability is `triggerDimensionApplicable` — METRIC_DIMENSIONS / FIELD_DIMENSIONS, or any asset metric/field for the device-identifier dims) resolves the draft's scope through `notificationEngine.loadScopeAssetIds` (same loader the tick uses, so the picker can't offer a value from a device the automation wouldn't evaluate), then GROUP BYs (value, assetId) on the backing sample table (or reads the operator's pin arrays for ifNamePattern / mountPathPattern / tunnelName — the first and last are what the engine's `interfaceIsPinned`/`tunnelIsPinned` gates match on) and folds it to per-value DEVICE counts (`foldValuePairs`, pure). One source per dimension: sensorClass + stateProbeId (strict → select) / sensorNamePattern / ifNamePattern / mountPathPattern / sdwanRulePattern / healthCheck / link / tunnelName / stateRowPattern (substring-matched → combobox suggestions + a match cue), plus the five device-identifier dims (hostnamePattern / ipPattern / macPattern / manufacturerPattern / modelPattern — valid on every asset metric and state field, backing the wizard's filter rows; they list the SCOPED devices' own Asset columns, no sample table and no window); `widgetId` deliberately has none (opaque registry UUIDs). `stateProbeId` IS offered despite also being a UUID, because a source may declare `labelOf()` — a value→display-name lookup built ONCE per request (not per value) that `foldValuePairs` attaches as an optional `label`, so the picker shows "Hardware sensor alarm (Fortinet)" from `manufacturerProfileService.listStateProbes()` and stores the id; an id that no longer resolves keeps working as a bare value rather than vanishing from the list. `narrow` applies the sibling already chosen on the same condition row (sensor NAMES within a class, WAN members within a health-check, state-probe ROWS within their probe) so the list can't offer a value that matches nothing. Bounded for interactive use: 3h window + 250-asset deterministic sample, widened once to 48h/100 assets ONLY when the recent window is empty so a slow cadence can't read as "this hardware has no sensors". A source may declare **`candidateWhere`** (an indexed Asset where naming which devices can REPORT the dimension — firewalls for the SD-WAN dims, non-empty pin arrays for interfaces/tunnels/mounts, monitored for sensors/probes), applied before the cap whenever the scope exceeds it: a blind 250-of-14,500 sample almost never contains the few gates that report SD-WAN, so the picker answered "no health checks" about a fleet that has them (prod 2026-08-21). When the narrowed set fits under the cap the answer is exhaustive and `sampledAssets` reports the full scope, keeping the wizard's partial-list disclosure silent. `dimensionPickerMeta()` is merged into GET /automations/schema as `dimensionPickers`.
│   │   ├── notificationCadenceService.ts # How often the devices a draft automation covers take the reading it watches — backs `POST /automations/poll-cadence`. The wizard counts its hold + window fields in POLLS (2026-08-28), so it needs a cadence to convert to the seconds that are still what gets STORED, and to say which cadence it converted at. `streamForMetric` maps each metric / asset_state field to the collector that produces it (memory → cpuMemory, an interface counter → systemInfo, packet loss and monitorStatus → the probe), `resolveScopeCadence(scope, metric)` resolves the monitored scope through `notificationEngine.loadScopeAssetIds` and each asset through `monitoringService.resolveMonitorSettings` (memoized per (integrationId, assetType), so the reads are per CLASS, not per asset), and `summarizeIntervals` (pure) reports mode + min + max so the caption can name the number it used AND the spread behind it. A fleet-wide answer is a RANGE, never one invented number; an unresolvable asset contributes nothing rather than a guess. The Polaris host's own metrics skip it entirely — hostMetricsCollector is a fixed 30s tick.
│   │   ├── notificationEngine.ts     # The rule evaluator (run by the evaluateNotificationRules job). **One trigger gate, shared by every path** (`assetCanTrigger`): an automation fires only about a device that is `monitored` AND not suppressed (maintenance window / dependency-suppressed — business rule 16). The monitored half is applied in SQL for the threshold + composite + metric-preview loads (`scopeWhere(scope, monitoredOnly)`) and per-row in the event/change tail off the `assetDetail` row; the four lifecycle statuses that cannot carry monitoring at all (decommissioned / disabled / storage / quarantined) fold into it rather than being retested. It closes a specific hole: `monitorStatus` is NOT cleared when monitoring is turned off, so a `monitorStatus == down` automation kept an alert firing forever about a device nobody had polled since it was shelved — un-monitoring now clears the live alert through `clearVanishedStates` (`notification.out_of_scope`) the way leaving the scope does. Event and change triggers were the deliberate exception to the monitored half until 2026-08 and no longer are; a null `assetDetail` (the asset row is GONE, e.g. an `asset.deleted` event) still fires, and system-scoped events carry no assetId at all. Threshold/state path: batch-loads in-scope assets + latest sample readings (per-metric resolvers over the sample tables; rate metrics via two-sample counter delta; `probeLossPct` = failed-probe ratio over the window via one grouped aggregate on `asset_monitor_samples`, the same computation as the dashboard Packet Loss widget — works for ANY monitored asset, not just SD-WAN — and gated to devices that are currently ANSWERING (`assetIsAnsweringProbes`: monitorStatus up/warning only, filtered inside the resolver so the composite path + preview inherit it), with a live loss alert on an asset that stopped answering CLEARED as a handoff to asset-down (`system:device-down`) rather than frozen; its `windowSec` is used EXACTLY (5-min floor, 15-min default via PROBE_LOSS_MIN/DEFAULT_WINDOW_SEC) instead of `max(windowSec, DEFAULT_LOOKBACK)`, because for a windowed ratio the window IS the measurement — the wizard calls it History — business rule 29), compares, drives the NotificationRuleState machine (clear→pending→firing) with forDurationSec + cooldown + per-rule v2 `reset` semantics (normalizeRuleToV2): manual re-arm, timed afterSec sweep, auto with optional hysteresis clearThreshold (recovery requires crossing the CLEAR line — the band between clear and fire thresholds holds the alert firing so it can't flap; a BANDED alert held in the dead band eases to its base severity instead of parking at the last band) + clear-sustain sustainSec (recovery must hold that long, tracked on NotificationRuleState.recoveredSince — transition-only writes, cancelled on re-meet/dead-band), and `condition` — a custom AND/OR reset tree that is the SOLE recovery authority while firing, so the trigger going false doesn't clear the alert and the trigger re-meeting doesn't cancel the tree's sustain timer. It runs in a dedicated pass AFTER the readings loop (the tree's leaves need not be the trigger's metric, so an alert whose trigger stopped reporting must still be able to clear, where the auto path freezes) and RE-READS the firing rows from the DB rather than the pre-loop snapshot the carve-out / device-down / vanished sweeps have since invalidated; suppressed assets stay frozen. Leaf truths resolve DIMENSION-FIRST with a per-asset fallback (`resolveResetTruths` + `leafTruthByAssetDim`): a reset leaf on the firing row's own dimension space clears that alert alone, one on a device-wide metric falls through to the ANY-dimension fold and clears every alert on the device — see business rule 32. Kind coherence (device vs Polaris-host leaves) is enforced at save for single triggers as well as composites. ifOperStatus/ifAdminStatus readings are restricted to PINNED interfaces (`Asset.monitoredInterfaces`, the Down Interfaces widget's join) and ifOperStatus additionally requires admin-up — unpinned/unplugged and deliberately-disabled ports never alert. A vanished-state sweep (`clearVanishedStates`, both evaluators) clears firing/pending rows whose asset left the scope or whose dimension stopped being reported (`system:out-of-scope` / Event `notification.out_of_scope`); in-scope assets with no readings at all stay frozen, and suppressed assets are left alone HERE because `notificationService.clearSuppressedAlerts` owns them — it runs ahead of every tick (and on the maintenance entering edge) and RETIRES their alerts rather than freezing them, under their own reason (business rule 16). Event-tail path: consumes new Event rows since a stored cursor, matches event/change rules (glob over action + level + detailsMatch), enforces cooldownSec against recent Notification rows keyed (rule, assetId-or-resourceName) with in-batch self-dedupe, inserts notifications; a companion per-tick pass (`runEventRuleTimedClear`) clears timed-reset event/change notifications after afterSec — they have no state rows, so the regular timed sweeps never see them. State writes only on transition (capacityWatch-style). All templating (messageTemplate + email composition) renders through src/utils/notificationTemplate.ts; on fire, rules with emailComposition/escalation (or {asset.*} tokens) fetch asset detail via the per-tick `assetDetail` cache (SCOPE_SELECT stays tight), snapshot the token context onto Notification.templateCtx, and `buildComposedEmail(comp, ctx)` (exported; also used by the escalation sweep + preview) renders the outbound email passed to expandDeliveries. `previewRule(input)` dry-runs a draft (builder Test, no writes; scope-only drafts list matched devices; hysteresis drafts get per-match wouldClear/inDeadBand; returns `emailPreview` when the draft has emailComposition). Pure helpers `compareNum`/`compareValue`/`globToRegExp`/`readingMeets`/`recoveredMeets` unit-tested.
│   │   ├── notificationChangeEvents.ts # Bridge from the current-state persist* functions (LLDP/processes/SD-WAN/MCLAG) to the engine's event path. `maybeEmitChangeEvents(action, assetId, name, items)` writes one audit Event per diffed change IF a change rule subscribes (via isChangeActionSubscribed) — zero cost otherwise. The engine's event-tail then turns matching events into notifications.
│   │   ├── regionScopeService.ts     # Shared effective-region/other-tag resolver — union(role, user, group). `resolveTagScopesForUser(u)` (used by GET /auth/me) + `getEffectiveRegionTags(userId)` (used by the notifications region-scoped list). Group-derived tags re-resolved live from ssoGroups.
│   │   ├── notificationPreferenceService.ts # Per-user notification preference (business rule 39). Owns `NOTIFICATION_PREFERENCES` (`email` | `push` | `any`) + `NOTIFICATION_PREFERENCE_LABELS` (the vocabulary both clients render), pure `normalizeNotificationPreference(v)` (anything unknown → `email`, never “nobody” — this is read on the alerting hot path from a plain TEXT column) and pure `preferenceAllowsTransport(pref, transport)` (`email`/`web_push` only; every fixed-destination transport is always allowed and never asked about), plus `getNotificationPreference` / `setNotificationPreference` — the setter bumps `bumpRecipientIndex()` (the 30s user index carries the preference) and writes a `user.notification_preference.changed` Event, because “I never got paged” has to be answerable from the Events tab.
│   │   ├── notificationRecipientService.ts # Delivery routing: `resolveRecipientUsers(tags)` / `resolveRecipientUsersByIds(ids)` (individual-account recipients) / `resolveEmailRecipients({recipientUserIds?, addresses?})` (cc/bcc + escalation-tier address resolution) / `listRecipientUsers()` (rule-builder picker) / `scopeRegionTagsOf(scope)` / pure `dedupeEmailRecipients(to, cc, bcc)` (To wins over Cc; Bcc drops anything visible) + `expandDeliveries(notificationId, targets, opts {scopeRegionTags?, assetRegionTags?, composedEmail?, escalation?})` (resolves each target's NotificationChannel, fans out into concrete NotificationDelivery rows — for email/web_push the recipients = chosen user accounts ∪ device-region users (recipientDeviceRegion × the TRIGGERING asset's stripped region snapshot: `regionSnapshot(reading.tags)` from the engine, `Notification.regionTags` from the sweep) ∪ scope-region users ∪ legacy-tag users, plus custom email addresses; with a ComposedEmail, each email target gets ONE row whose meta snapshots {composed, to, cc, bcc, subject, text, html?} — or TWO when a recipient's role cannot acknowledge: `ackCapabilityByAddress()` (address → the role's `alerts` level; absent = no account = keeps the button) feeds pure `splitAckVariants(to, cc, bcc, capable)`, which splits the lists into an ack copy and a button-less copy (`fillComposedAckUrl(body, null)`), promoting Cc into an emptied To and sending a Bcc-only variant one message per address; the uncomposed per-address path and web_push instead stamp `meta.noAck` on the row, which `notificationDeliveryService` reads to drop `appendAckLine` / the payload's `ackUrl`; slack/teams/pushbullet get one fixed-destination row — snapshotted at fire time).
