With `opts.enforceUserPreference` (set by the CALLER — automationActionService, which alone can see the action GROUP) a target carrying `respectUserPreference` additionally drops USER recipients whose `notificationPreference` refuses that transport; typed addresses and address-book contacts are never filtered, having expressed no preference. Pure `preferenceWithholds(pref, transport, {hasPushDevice, hasEmail})` keeps anyone whose PREFERRED channel cannot reach them, so the filter routes an alert rather than deleting it; `pushDeviceCounts()` (one lazy memoized `groupBy`) supplies the device half. The two broadcast modes (`recipientAllUsers` / `recipientAllRegions`) are now applied on `transport === "web_push"` ONLY, so a mixed-channel action can't mail the whole roster off a push-block control. Short-TTL user-tag index cache (which carries `notificationPreference` alongside each user's tag scope). Also home of `buildComposedEmail(comp, ctx)` (moved from the engine so the action layer can compose without a circular import; the engine re-exports it).
│   │   ├── alertBrandService.ts   # The install's letterhead in the top-right corner of an alert email — logo, application name, subtitle. `buildAlertBrandBlock()` is the whole delivery-time step: read branding once, load the mark, render both bodies + the inline attachment; memoized 60s because every email in a drain wants the identical block. `{brand.header}` is a DEFERRED token like `{chart.*}` (the logo rides as an inline CID attachment — no remote images, and Gmail/Outlook drop data: URIs — which one context string cannot carry, and deferring also means an escalation sent at T+90min carries the CURRENT branding rather than a fire-time snapshot). Artwork follows business rule 27 rather than picking a file: the email card is white, so the LIGHT-inked `polaris-horiz-light.png` wordmark is the shipped choice, and because that art already spells the product name the app name is NOT printed beside it (rule 27's showName=false); an operator's own logo gets the name as its caption plus the `renderAccentedLogo("light")` composite when they enabled an accent. The subtitle renders either way — it is the operator's own copy, not a caption for the mark. Pure pieces the tests drive: `renderBrandBlock(parts,{html})`, `fitLogo(size)` (aspect-preserving fit into 150×46, never enlarging — an unconstrained 900px banner would squeeze the headline into a two-word column), `brandTokensIn`, `substituteBrandTokens`. Every failure rung drops the logo, then the block, and the email still sends: letterhead must never be the reason an alert does not arrive.
│   │   ├── alertChartService.ts   # The last-hour hardware-sensor / CPU / memory / response-time charts embedded in an alert email. `buildAlertCharts(assetId, tokens, {now?, thresholds?, lossWindowMs?})` reads the window from AssetTelemetrySample (cpuPct; memPct else memUsedBytes/memTotalBytes) + AssetMonitorSample (responseTimeMs, SUCCESSFUL probes only — plotting a failed probe as 0 would draw a fast device instead of an unreachable one; where those failures WERE is not lost, `failSpansFrom` (pure) merges consecutive failed PRIMARY polls into spans the CPU / memory / response-time charts shade red and break their line over, so a flat stretch reads as missing data rather than a steady reading, and the summary line carries the failed count for image-blocked readers), renders via utils/sparklineSvg, and rasterizes to PNG with @resvg/resvg-js (lazy import, already a dependency via appIconService). `chartTokensIn(...)` finds which {chart.*} tokens a body references; `substituteChartTokens(body, charts, {html})` swaps them for an inline `<img src="cid:…">` (HTML) or the now/avg/peak sentence (text); `attachmentsFor` returns only the images the final body cites. Built at DELIVERY time, not fire time — the drain is off the engine hot path, and an escalation at T+90min then charts the last hour as of sending rather than re-rendering a frozen snapshot. Every failure path (no samples, unreadable asset, missing native binding) degrades to the text summary: an alert must never fail to send because a chart did not draw. Packet loss is the one DERIVED series: `probeLossSeriesFrom` (pure, unit-tested) buckets the probe success/failure rows and plots the failure ratio, skipping empty buckets rather than plotting a polling gap as perfect health. It returns TWO ratios and both are used: the per-bucket values are the line's shape, while `ratioPct` — failed/total over the whole window, weighing every probe equally — is what the caption prints via sparklineSvg's `avgOverride`, because the mean of per-bucket ratios treats a 10-probe bucket and a 1-probe bucket as equals and so drifted from the reading the automation fired on (prod 2026-08-20 mailed `18.3 %` over a chart captioned `avg 6.7 %`; uneven bucket counts come from polling gaps, the anchor trimming a partial bucket, a suppressed asset's 2x interval, or the ICMP sampler oversampling failures). It also applies the ratio's ANCHOR (drop samples before the window's first success, matching probeLossQuery) so the picture and the caption describe the same probes, except with no success at all in the window, where every row is kept and the chart reads 100 % — the widget's `includeFullyDown` semantics, since an asset-down alert embeds this chart too — and it is the one chart whose WINDOW follows the automation rather than the hour (2026-08-20): `lossWindowMs` (resolved by the delivery drain from the rule's trigger via the engine-shared `probeLossWindowSec`) makes the graph span exactly the History the alert's ratio was measured over, with `lossBucketMs` scaling the 2-minute buckets up so ~30 points cover any span and the sparkline axis + summary line stating the real window (`timeAxisLabel`); CPU / memory / response time stay last-hour context. `chartTokenForMetric` maps the fired metric to the chart that explains it and answers for the asset_state fields too (`monitorStatus` / `consecutiveFailures` → the response-time chart, since a down device's story is the climb before it stopped answering). `isPortScopedAlert(metric)` / `PORT_SCOPED_METRICS` is the OPPOSITE decision: an alert on `ifOperStatus` / `ifAdminStatus` / `poeStatus` gets NO charts at all (empty map, zero queries), because a switch with a dead port is answering probes — that is how Polaris knows the port is down — so all four device series are flat and healthy and burying the finding. Only the interface STATE trio, deliberately: an `ifInErrorRate` / `ifOutBps` alert plausibly correlates with device load and keeps its graphs. What replaces them is alertInterfaceService's LLDP block.
│   │   ├── alertInterfaceService.ts # The per-INTERFACE facts an alert email carries when the thing that broke is one port — what the charts are replaced by (see alertChartService's `isPortScopedAlert`). `buildInterfaceLldpBlocks(assetId, metric, dimension)` is the whole delivery-time step: it returns `{html:"", text:""}` without querying unless the metric is interface-dimensioned (`INTERFACE_DIMENSION_METRICS` — the state trio plus the four counter rates, all keyed on ifName by their engine resolvers), then reads `AssetLldpNeighbor` for the port ONCE and renders both bodies from it. Two things make it work: (a) `persistLldpNeighbors` holds a vanished neighbour for a 48-hour STICKY window before deleting it, so a dead port's neighbour is still in the table at delivery — which is also why every entry prints "Last advertised", since the row predates the outage by definition and how stale it is IS the finding; (b) the port lookup is widened through `fortiapInterfaceAliases`, because a FortiAP's rows are normalized to whichever of lan1/eth0 its interface inventory reports (a switch port's alias set is just itself). `renderInterfaceLldp` emits a COMPLETE `<tr>` with its own heading or the empty string, so nothing needs a pruning pass of its own; the text form deliberately uses NO colons, because `pruneEmptyTextLines` deletes any "Label:" line with nothing after it and "LLDP neighbor on port2:" matches that shape exactly. Neighbour name falls back matched-asset hostname → LLDP systemName → chassisId; systemDescription is flattened + truncated to 100 chars (a firmware banner otherwise); capped at 4 neighbours with an "and N more" line. A failed read logs and yields nothing — an alert must never fail to send because the LLDP lookup did.
│   │   ├── automationTestService.ts # Backs the wizard's Summary-step "Test delivery" buttons (`POST /automations/test-delivery`). `runTestDelivery({rule, path, target, assetId?, actorUserId, actorUsername})` creates a REAL alert and dispatches ONE action of the draft — saved or unsaved — through the normal delivery path, then reports the outcomes + whether the message could carry a working acknowledge link. Pure `selectTestActions(rule, path, callerUserId)` resolves the addressed action out of `allRuleActionRefs`' walk. Three safety properties, each load-bearing: (1) the test Notification ALWAYS carries `ruleId: null` + `testRun: true` even for a saved rule, because notificationEscalationService sweeps `{cleared:false, ruleId: IN enabled}` and a test alert with a real ruleId would enter the escalation ladder and start paging on the next 60s tick (and no NotificationRuleState row is written, so the engine doesn't think the asset is firing); (2) only `notify` actions execute (plus the audit Event in event mode) — a test button that runs a registry script is RCE-by-button, and an api_call would open a real PagerDuty/ServiceNow ticket, so both are filtered server-side and reported as `skipped`; (3) it ONLY EVER reaches the caller, via a recipient REWRITE (`recipientUserIds: [caller]`, every other recipient field and emailComposition cc/bcc dropped), so the path is structurally incapable of reaching anyone else. The old `mode: "self" | "recipients"` choice was REMOVED in 2026-08 rather than defaulted off — a test answers "does this channel work, and what does the message look like", and answering it by paging the on-call is a cost nobody asked for; the field is gone from the route schema, which is a non-strict `z.object`, so a stale browser tab still posting `"recipients"` has it stripped and reaches only the sender. A destination with no private form (a Slack/Teams/Pushbullet webhook posts to one channel) is therefore not testable here at all — the wizard disables its button and points at the Delivery tab's own per-channel Test. Dispatch goes through `drainPendingDeliveries({notificationId})` — extending the drain rather than cloning it — under a 20s budget so a dead SMTP host can't pin an HTTP worker.
│   │   ├── automationActionService.ts # The single fan-out point between a fired alert and its automation's `actions[]` (engine fire + event tail + escalation sweep). Per action: notify → expandDeliveries with the ACTION's emailComposition ?? rule-level fallback (byte-identical to the legacy targets path for converted rules) + the scope-region AND device-region recipient tag sets (`ActionExecContext.scopeRegionTags`/`assetRegionTags`); api_call → one NotificationDelivery row {transport: "api_call", channelId: NULL, meta: {method, url, headers (UNMASKED — no secrets), body rendered at fire time, timeoutSec, escalation?}}; script → an AutomationScriptRun via automationScriptService.requestScriptRun (args rendered at fire time, single argv — NEVER executed inline; the runAutomationScripts job / agent queue drains it). Best-effort PER ACTION — each failure writes an `automation.action_error` warning Event and later actions still run. Also home of `actionsCarryBothMethods(actions)`: does THIS action group (the `actions[]` list being executed — rule actions, one band's, the reset list, one escalation tier's) reach recipients by BOTH email and web push? It is business rule 39's whole gate — resolved at most once per group, lazily, and only when some action set `respectUserPreference`, then passed to expandDeliveries as `enforceUserPreference`. A multi-channel action counts on its own.
│   │   ├── automationScriptService.ts # AutomationScript registry CRUD + run lifecycle. RCE-equivalent surface (gated automationScripts): create + every BODY change stamp a warning Event with old/new sha256; sha256 recomputed on every save (agents verify before executing); delete refused (409) while any automation's actions/escalation tiers reference the script (scan via normalizeRuleToV2). requestScriptRun validates exists+enabled+runTarget-compatible and creates the pending AutomationScriptRun (agent runs refused until the agent phase); listRuns + pruneOldRuns (90d retention, called from the runner's idle sweep). Interpreter vocabulary lives in notificationTypes.SCRIPT_INTERPRETERS.
│   │   ├── automationScriptRunner.ts # Server-side executor for pending runs (runOn="server"), driven by the runAutomationScripts job — script execution NEVER happens inline in the engine/drain. Claim pending→running via updateMany on a bounded id set (restart-safe) + stuck-running sweep (timeout+60s grace → status "timeout"); execute via execFile — body written to a 0600 temp file under STATE_DIR/data/automation-scripts-tmp, interpreter argv per platform (powershell/cmd on Windows), args as a SINGLE argv entry (never shell-interpolated), alert context in POLARIS_ALERT_ID/POLARIS_RULE/POLARIS_ASSET env vars, SIGKILL on timeout, 64 KB output caps (maxBuffer kill classified as failure, not timeout), temp file always deleted; record exitCode/status/stdout/stderr + one automation.script.run Event per run (warning on failure/timeout). Concurrency 2.
│   │   ├── notificationDeliveryService.ts # `drainPendingDeliveries()` — pulls pending NotificationDelivery rows (attempts<3), resolves each row's channel + config, dispatches by channel type with bounded concurrency (email rows with meta.composed send one to/cc/bcc message from the snapshot; rows without take the legacy per-address titleFor+message path), marks sent/failed (≤3 retries; missing channel = permanent fail — EXCEPT transport "api_call" rows, whose NULL channelId is legitimate: the whole request spec rides meta and failures take the normal retry path via apiCallChannel.sendApiCall), prunes dead push subscriptions (HTTP 410/404) and re-routes them: `enqueuePushFallbacks` queues an EMAIL for any recipient whose every push row on that alert has stopped being in play, using the action's own email channel from the push row's `meta.fallback` and cloning a sibling row's composed body — guarded by pure `pushStillInPlay` (per RECIPIENT, not per row; `sent` counts as reached and `pending` as still trying) and `alreadyEmailedOnChannel` (a SUBSTRING test, since a composed send is one row carrying the whole joined To list). Worth one alert per dead endpoint: the 410 also prunes, so later alerts fall back at FIRE time instead. Writes one summary audit Event (its details carry `emailedInsteadOfPush`). Driven by the deliverNotifications job. Modeled on eventArchiveService. Composed email rows get three delivery-time fills in one pass: the charts (alertChartService), the port's LLDP block (alertInterfaceService) and the letterhead (alertBrandService) — each appending its inline attachment only when the substituted HTML actually cites the cid.
│   │   ├── notificationEscalationService.ts # `runEscalationSweep()` (escalateNotifications job, 60s): for uncleared notifications of rules with ANY escalation chain (rule-level, per-action, band-level, or band-per-action — `allEscalationsOf`), iterates the chains active at the alert's current severity (`escalationChainsForSeverity` in notificationTypes: the rule/band LEVEL chain — bare numeric tier state keys, unchanged from pre-feature rows — plus one chain per effective action, state keys `a<i>:t<j>`; per-chain stopOn, so an ack stops "acknowledge" chains while "clear" chains keep going) and runs each due tier's ACTIONS through automationActionService.executeActions with escalation provenance + the Notification.regionTags device-region snapshot (rendered from the fire-time Notification.templateCtx + live {escalation.tier}/{escalation.elapsed} tokens), tracks per-tier progress on Notification.escalationState (firstSentAt/lastSentAt/count, bumped only when ≥1 action executed; repeats per repeatEveryMin up to maxRepeats, default 5; band timers restart from escalationState.bandSince), batched writes. ALSO drives REPEATS (`NotificationRule.repeat`): the same pass re-sends an alert's own notify actions while it stays unhandled, keyed `REPEAT_STATE_KEY` in escalationState.tiers, gated by its own pure `repeatIsDue()` (NOT tierIsDue, which resolves `maxRepeats ?? 5` and would cap the uncapped behaviour), filtered to `REPEATABLE_ACTION_TYPES`, and audited as `notification.repeated`. Two structural notes: the per-notification loop checks SUPPRESSION FIRST and no longer early-`continue`s on "no escalation chains" (a repeat-only automation has none, and that one early return would have disabled the feature), and the due-cutoff folds repeat intervals into the tier delays with an empty-array guard — `Math.min()` of nothing is Infinity, which makes the Prisma `triggeredAt` filter an Invalid Date. Pure `tierIsDue()` + `repeatIsDue()` unit-tested (notificationRepeat.test.ts).
│   │   ├── maintenanceScheduleService.ts # Maintenance schedules: CRUD (audited; every mutation runs the reconcile inline so ad-hoc windows apply before the response returns), target resolution (union of tagAssignmentService criteria matches + explicit assetIds, ∩ monitored=true; `previewTargets` = capped device-list dry-run), per-asset reads (`listAssetWindows` for chart bands, `getAssetMaintenanceInfo` for the edit modal / slide-over), `operatorReleaseAsset` (assets PUT route calls it BEFORE an operator status write off "maintenance" — closes open windows endReason="operator", clears maintenanceReturnStatus, does NOT write status so the operator's value wins), `releaseAssetsForDecommission` (the discovery Phase 2a/2b decommission sweeps call it for stale ids — deletion-at-source outranks the window: closes windows endReason="decommissioned", clears the parked status, and writes status="decommissioned" in ONE transaction so the reconcile can't re-enter or self-heal-reflip; also deletes the spent ad-hoc schedule), and `reconcileMaintenance()` — the serialized+coalesced core tick: diff desired (asset, schedule) pairs (schedule active per maintenanceRecurrence.isInWindow) against open AssetMaintenanceWindow rows; EXITS close rows (reason schedule/disabled/deleted/criteria) and restore the parked status via grouped updateMany when the asset's last window closes (status left as-is if something already moved it off "maintenance"); ENTERS skip pairs whose current occurrence the operator released, park the current status into maintenanceReturnStatus (a manual "maintenance" parks verbatim — no restore loop), flip to "maintenance" (statusChangedBy "system:maintenance"), createMany window rows; SELF-HEAL re-flips in-maintenance assets a system writer clobbered, absorbing the clobbered value into maintenanceReturnStatus; prunes closed rows >400 days. Events maintenance.entered/.exited via logEventsBatch. Scale: findMany + grouped updateMany/createMany, no per-row awaits outside transition events.
│   │   ├── directorySearchService.ts # Live GAL lookup for the address book: fans one typeahead query across every `entraid`/`activedirectory` integration carrying the opt-in `config.enableDirectorySearch`, merges + dedupes by address (a hybrid-joined person is in both), caps per source, and caches identical queries 60s so keystrokes don't hammer the tenant. **Nothing is persisted** — results live for one request; only an address an operator picks becomes a rule recipient or a saved Contact, which is the whole reason this isn't a bulk sync (a sync would land the entire employee roster in Polaris with its own retention/backup/audit surface). Failures DEGRADE: `Promise.allSettled`, so a revoked Graph grant or an unreachable DC yields the other backend's results rather than a 500. Query strings are never logged or written to Events — `Event.details` is readable by anyone with events access and is shipped off-host by the archivers. Min query length 2. Opt-in because both backends need permissions device discovery never required (Graph `User.Read.All` + `Group.Read.All` + `OrgContact.Read.All`, or `Directory.Read.All`; an AD bind that can read user objects).
│   │   ├── directorySyncService.ts  # SCHEDULED sync of the GAL into the address book (business rule 35) — the sibling that STORES, where directorySearchService only reads. Opt-in per integration (`config.enableDirectorySync`, default off, deliberately separate from `enableDirectorySearch`: same grants, different decision, because one reads and one stores). Runs as a post-sync pass of the owning AD/Entra discovery run, never as its own scheduler job. Owns two PURE decisions plus the pass itself. **`directoryExclusionReason(entry, filter)`** answers why an entry should NOT become a contact and returns a CATEGORY, never a name — it ends up in an Event, and Events must not carry directory PII; include-wins-over-exclude for OU and domain, matching `filterDevices`' existing semantics; a shared/room/equipment mailbox is excluded only on a POSITIVE identification, since `"unknown"` is what Graph forces (it exposes no mailbox type on /users — only `mailboxSettings.userPurpose`, a per-user call needing MailboxSettings.Read.All) and treating unknown as shared would silently drop an entire tenant. **`projectContactFromSources(sources)`** derives the contact's directory-owned fields from the full source set, highest-priority non-empty value per field (entra > ad) — projected rather than last-writer-wins because two directories that disagree about a job title would otherwise flip the row on every cycle, writing once per contact per run and never settling; a group in ANY source is a group, since that distinction changes who an operator thinks they are mailing. **PII posture** (see the file header): every non-excluded entry lands in Postgres and in every pg_dump, so the run Event carries COUNTS ONLY and warnings name integrations rather than people — the one exception being contactService's `contact.adopted`, which names the address because a single human act is audited by name while bulk machine activity is anonymous.
│   │   ├── deviceFilterService.ts  # Resolving a device-filter CONDITION TREE against inventory — the shared half of "which devices?", so the surfaces that ask it can't drift. Three of them store the same tree over `DEVICE_FILTER_FIELD_OPS`: an automation's `scope.condition` (resolved inside the engine, where the tree rides a scope carrying flat dimensions too), a `Contact.assetCondition`, and a `Tag.assetCondition`. The latter two want the plain answer — the SET of asset ids the tree covers — which lived privately in contactService until tags needed the identical thing. `resolveDeviceFilterAssetIds(cond, {where?})` is that answer; `deviceFilterSelect(conds, {needsInterfaces?})` is the select both it and the SINGLE-asset paths share. **Deliberately no SQL prefilter for the tree itself**: an `or`/`none`/`notAll` group makes any narrowing WHERE unsound, and unlike the flat criteria (always ANDed, which is what lets `buildPrefilterWhere` exist) there is no safe superset to ask for — so it is one findMany of scalar columns, operator- or reconcile-triggered rather than per tick. Both relation-backed fields stay conditional, which is why the select is a function: `fortigate` joins the sighting relation (the expensive half at 2000 assets) only when a rule asks about the gate, and `interfaceName` is resolved to per-asset verdicts in SQL by `scopeInterfaceIndex` rather than joined at all — no interface leaf, no query. The optional `where` is ANDed OUTSIDE the tree for a caller-owned eligibility rule (today only tag auto-assignment's decommissioned exclusion), never for narrowing derived from the tree.
│   │   ├── contactService.ts      # The address book. CRUD (audited `contact.created/.updated/.deleted`; `normalizeContactEmail` trims + lower-cases so the unique index is case-insensitive and the value matches resolveEmailRecipients' normalized set), `previewContactAssets` (device-filter dry-run — union of criteria matches + explicit pins, capped sample + total; NOT ∩ monitored, unlike maintenance), `searchAddressBook` (Polaris users ∪ contacts, deduped by lower-cased email with the USER winning — a user id survives an address change, a stored contact string doesn't — then prefix-first ranked; the shape directorySearchService extends with entra/ad rows), and `resolveContactsForAsset` — the FIRE-TIME path. That one is deliberately shaped to avoid a fleet scan: contacts ride a 30s TTL cache (invalidated by `bumpContactCache` on every write), a pin match is a plain id comparison needing NO asset load at all, and criteria are evaluated against the ONE triggering asset via tagAssignmentService's pure `assetMatchesCriteria` + a single `cidrsContainingIp` round-trip across every contact's CIDRs combined (skipped entirely when no contact filters by subnet). Cost scales with contact count, never with fleet size. Mirrors `reconcileTagsForAsset`.
│   │   ├── pushSubscriptionService.ts # Per-user Web Push subscription store (PushSubscription writes for the /push-subscriptions routes: upsert-by-endpoint with re-own on shared machines, owner-scoped delete). Readers stay elsewhere: notificationRecipientService fan-out + the web_push channel's 410/404 prune.
│   │   ├── notificationChannelService.ts # CRUD for the NotificationChannel registry (Delivery tab). Secrets (per the type's field defs) masked on read / preserved on write (credentialService discipline). `listChannels`/`listChannelsForBuilder`/`getChannel`/`getChannelRaw` (secrets, for senders)/`createChannel`/`updateChannel`/`deleteChannel`/`generateWebPushKeys`/`getWebPushChannel`. Enforces the web_push singleton.
│   │   ├── notificationChannels/        # Config-parameterized per-channel senders (take explicit config, no global reads): emailChannel.ts (sendSmtpEmail via nodemailer + sendM365Email via Graph; EmailMessage carries to: string|string[] + cc/bcc arrays; pure `buildGraphMessage()` maps to Graph to/cc/bccRecipients — Graph carries ONE body, HTML wins when both set, SMTP sends multipart), webhookChannel.ts (slack/teams/generic body shapes + netGuard SSRF guard), apiCallChannel.ts (the api_call action's HTTP dispatch — spec from delivery meta, not a channel row; netGuard SSRF re-check at send, default JSON content-type when a body is present, ≤60s timeout, non-2xx throws for the retry path; response bodies never stored), pushbulletChannel.ts (Pushbullet note API), webPushChannel.ts (web-push VAPID send + generateVapidKeys; throws gone=true on 410/404 so the drain prunes the subscription).
│   │   ├── roleService.ts           # Dynamic-role RBAC: Role CRUD, 30-key permission matrix, session-snapshot version cache (bumpRoleVersion), last-admin-equivalent invariant.
│   │   ├── userDashboardService.ts  # Per-user dashboard layout (widget instances + positions) CRUD backing /me/dashboard.
│   │   ├── tableTabsService.ts      # Per-user list-page TABS (`UserTableTabs`, one row per (user, scope)): `getTabsForUser` (EMPTY_LAYOUT when absent), `saveTabsForUser` (whole-blob replace — the client owns order + active tab), and the pure, unit-tested `sanitizeTabs` (≤20 tabs, unique ids, trimmed control-char-free names ≤40, per-tab `state` delegated to savedFilterService.sanitizeFilterState so a tab can never smuggle in a filter shape a preset couldn't; a stale `activeId` falls back to the first tab rather than 400-ing the whole layout). userDashboardService pattern — no Events, cascades with the user.
│   │   ├── savedFilterService.ts    # Saved table-filter presets (`SavedTableFilter`): `listSavedFilters(scope, viewerId)` (own ∪ public), `createSavedFilter` (same-(scope,owner,name) POST UPDATES rather than duplicating — the UI's overwrite flow), `updateSavedFilter`, `deleteSavedFilter`, `getSavedFilter` (for the route's ownership check), plus the pure, unit-tested validators `normalizeName` + `sanitizeFilterState` (the stored blob is another operator's browser input replayed into yours, so only the shapes table-sf.js emits are accepted: string / string[] / {op,q} / {op:empty|notempty} / {type:"date",from,to}, bounded at 60 columns × 200 values × 300 chars, 100 presets per user per scope) and `SAVED_FILTER_SCOPES` (scope → existing RBAC function key; `assets` → `assets`, so no new key/role migration). Writes `saved_filter.*` Events. userDashboardService pattern, but shareable rather than strictly per-caller.
│   │   ├── topologyGraphService.ts  # Device Map topology graph builder: `buildSiteTopology(siteId)` constructs the full GET /map/sites/:id/topology payload — FortiGate root + sibling FortiSwitch/FortiAP nodes (endpoints, wireless stations, subnets) and every edge class (controller-data FortiLink, interface-name-inferred, LLDP + ghost nodes, wireless-bridge, MCLAG ICL, per-edge interface details, HA-standby suppression) plus the savedLayouts embed. map.ts's topology GET delegates here (extracted verbatim from the route handler, 2026-08 audit); also exports monitorStatusToHealth + fetchRecentSampleStats, shared with map.ts's GET /sites pin-health payload. Read-only — no writer responsibilities.
│   │   ├── topologyLayoutService.ts # Shared Device Map topology layouts (TopologyLayout rows, one per (siteId, view)): getLayoutsForSite (the topology GET's savedLayouts embed), saveLayout (full-replace upsert, 404 unless the site is a firewall asset), deleteLayout (idempotent), plus the pure validators isValidViewKey ("flat" | "b|…" | "f|…") and sanitizePositions (finite coords, |coord| ≤ 1e7, ≤3000 nodes → AppError 400). userDashboardService pattern, per-resource + shared instead of per-user.
│   │   ├── applicationMapService.ts # Application Map graph builder + per-asset connection reads + the shared page layout. `buildApplicationMapGraph()` (GET /application-map): loads assets with non-empty mappedProcesses + their AssetProcessConnection rows (bounded lastSeen ≥ now−7d), bulk-resolves remote IPs (`resolveIpsToAssets` — Asset.ipAddress then AssetAssociatedIp.ip in two findMany-in queries — then `resolveIpsViaHistory` for the leftovers: a TIME-SCOPED AssetIpHistory fallback where the pure `pickHistoryHolder` chooses, per IP, the history row whose seen-interval best covers the newest connection observation, so an IP several assets held at different times attributes to the plausible holder rather than a rotated-off former one; every resolution query excludes `status="decommissioned"` — retired hardware must never soak up live traffic as an edge target). IPs that resolve to NO asset then get a LABEL-ONLY name: `resolveIpsToNameHints` (active `Reservation` rows with a non-empty hostname) first, then `resolvePtrNames` for PUBLIC IPs (reverse DNS with an in-process 6h/30m positive/negative cache, ≤25 uncached lookups per build each bounded to 1.5s; `isPublicIp` excludes RFC1918/CGN/ULA/noise): the grey unknown-ip node renders that name over the address and carries `ipHostname` + `ipNameSource` (`"reservation"` | `"dns"`), but stays an unknown-ip node — there is no asset record to open, so promoting it would be a lie. Active-only because a released/expired reservation is history, not current truth; hostname-only because `owner` is display metadata and `description` is free text, so neither is a reliable name, then runs the PURE `buildGraphFromRows` (unit-tested, no prisma): noise-IP filter (loopback/link-local/multicast/unspecified) → per-asset mapped-listener index → outbound rows land process→process (dest has a mapped listener on that proto/port) / process→asset / process→unknown-ip; inbound rows fill the reverse direction deduped against outbound observations (outbound wins — it knows the source process); same-process self-loops dropped, intra-asset proc→proc kept; ONE merged edge per (source,target) carrying a per-port breakdown (cap 16 + portOverflow, kind strongest-wins process>asset>external; each port also carries `ips` — ≤6 distinct observed addresses, outbound = the dialed remote IP / inbound = the local address it landed on — rendered as the edge rail's "Via IP" column and as a `via <ip>` label line on same-asset sibling edges). Unknown-IP hygiene: /24 (v6 /64) group nodes when >5 unknowns share the subnet, hard cap 100 after grouping + one overflow node, stats.truncated reported. Deterministic node ids (asset:<id>, proc:<assetId>:<b64url(name)>, ip:<ip>, ipgroup:<cidr>) so ApplicationMapLayout blobs survive refresh. Asset nodes carry deviceIconService iconUrls. Also `getAssetProcessConnections(assetId, name?, unit?)` (the process + service detail panels' listening/outbound/inbound DTO, filtered by process name or by owning unit, remote endpoints hydrated with matched asset id+hostname, 500/section) and the ApplicationMapLayout CRUD (get/save/deleteAppMapLayout — reuses topologyLayoutService.sanitizePositions).
│   │   ├── appMapDiscoveryService.ts # Service & process DISCOVERY RULES (list UI on Integrations → Polaris Agent; formerly the Application Map's "Discovery" modal) + the scope-driven process/service aggregate behind the wizard. `Setting("appMapAutoMap")` = `{version:2, rules:[{id, name, enabled, mode, source, scope, assetIds, processes:{names,patterns,regex}, services:{…}}]}`. `mode`: "map" pins the Application Map surfaces AND the monitor surfaces (mapping implies monitoring); "monitor" pins ONLY monitoredProcesses/monitoredServices (pre-mode rules normalize to "map"). `source`: "manual" (wizard-authored) vs "auto" — auto rules are minted/consolidated by `recordOperatorPinChanges` (the assets-PUT pin-diff hook): one single-item rule per (item, kind, mode) with `scope:null` + explicit `assetIds` (union semantics with scope; null scope + assetIds = JUST those assets — MaintenanceSchedule precedent); the same item pinned on another asset joins the existing auto rule, un-ticking removes the asset, and an auto rule losing its LAST asset is DELETED (must never decay into a null-scope match-everything rule). Manual rules are never consolidated or trimmed by the hook; the wizard flips an edited auto rule to manual. The hook is serialized through an in-process promise chain (Setting read-modify-write isn't atomic; browser PUTs all land on the web role), never throws into the asset save, inline-applies just the touched rules, and is audited `application_map.autorule.synced`. The pure `applyPinChangesToConfig` is the unit-tested core; `resolveRuleAssetLabels` resolves every rule's assetIds to hostnames for the GET's `assetLabels`. MANY rules on purpose: a single fleet-wide selection could only express "every asset reporting this program", which over-pins — mapping `truckscale.service` for three truckscale hosts also hit every other host running it. Each rule carries its own asset scope (a `tagAssignmentService` `TagCriteria`; null = every monitored asset), so the same unit can be mapped in one part of the fleet and left alone in another; when several rules match one asset their pins UNION. `normalizeConfig` folds the PRE-RULES single-selection shape forward into one "Imported selection" rule at read time (no migration job — same trick as the flat retention default), and enforces unique rule names (case-insensitive) + ids, ≤200 rules (raised from 50 when single-item auto rules landed); `normalizeRule` enforces the 64-entry-per-array cap matching the assets PUT, case-insensitive dedup keeping the FIRST spelling (pins match inventory case-sensitively; assetIds dedup case-SENSITIVELY, cap 1000), and compiles patterns at save so a bad regex is a 400 not a silent no-match. `getInventoryAggregate(scope)` is what makes the picker granular — bounded GROUP BYs over `asset_processes`/`asset_services` joined to `assets` on `monitored=true`, narrowed to the scope's asset ids (LIMIT 2000), plus `unnest(mappedProcesses|mappedServices)` GROUP BYs for the fleet-wide already-pinned count; never load per-asset rows to count them (~400k at 2000 hosts). `PROCESS_CAPABLE_ASSET_TYPES` (`workstation`, `server` — `server` covers vCenter VMs; ESXi `hypervisor` excluded, no agent runs there) bounds EVERY candidate query (inventory aggregate, `previewScope`, apply): inventory only comes from the agent / agentless SSH+WinRM, so counting firewalls, switches, APs and printers made the device count promise pins that could never land. Deliberately NOT applied to `pinnedCounts`, which must surface a hand-applied pin wherever it lives so Unmap-everywhere means everywhere. Widening that one constant is the switch for "processes on network hardware" later. The aggregates use `COUNT(*)` not `COUNT(DISTINCT assetId)` — both tables are unique on `(assetId, name|unit)` so they're equivalent, and the DISTINCT cost a sort/hash per group over the whole table; no index on name/unit is added because both are delete-replaced per asset per scrape, so it would tax every write fleet-wide to speed one wizard step. `previewScope(scope, assetIds)` backs the wizard's device step (same union semantics as apply). `resolveBlockPins` is the PURE resolver (exact names ∪ wildcard/regex patterns). **Mapping implies monitoring, one-way:** `computePending` keeps per-surface want-sets — map wants from "map"-mode rules only, monitor wants from EVERY rule — so a map rule also pins `monitoredProcesses` / `monitoredServices` (an operator who puts a service on the map wants its telemetry), computed against the full want-set so an already-mapped-but-unmonitored item catches up; the reverse never holds, so no monitor pin ever produces a map pin, and a "monitor"-mode rule never touches a map pin. Reported as `monitorPins` on the preview + apply results. `applyRules` is STRICTLY ADDITIVE — resolves each rule's target set (scope ∪ assetIds) once, loads the inventory for the UNION of in-scope assets a single time, evaluates every rule in memory, then writes pins = union(existing, computed) in chunked Promise.allSettled batches of 50, skipping assets with nothing fresh so a repeat tick is silent; removing an item or disabling a rule stops FUTURE pinning and never retroactively unpins, because the pin arrays are operator-owned. `unmapEverywhere(kind,name)` is the separate subtractive path (strips the pin fleet-wide, deletes matching AssetProcessConnection rows, removes the name from every MAP-mode rule so the reconciler can't re-add it — monitor-only rules keep theirs — and prunes auto rules the removal emptied). `reconcileAutoMap` is the entry point for the 30-min `reconcileAppMapAutoMap` job — the "and future assets" mechanism.
│   │   ├── settingsStore.ts         # createSettingStore<T>({key, ttlMs, parse}) — TTL-cached JSON-blob Setting accessor (get / peek / save / invalidate) collapsing the hand-rolled findUnique→parse→upsert+module-cache ceremony. Per-process cache (cross-role propagation bounded by ttlMs). Adopters: azureAuthService (sso), entraProxyAuthService (entraProxy), dashSettingsService (dashConfig); remaining hand-rolled sites migrate as touched.
│   │   ├── assetSourcePriorityService.ts # Operator-settable priority for the assets table's **Sources** column: `assetSourcePriority` Setting `{order[], integrationPrefix}` over createSettingStore (30s TTL). The value feeds `Asset.learnedLocation` through the projection, NOT just rendering — the column, its text filter, its sort, "behind FortiGate X" tag/maintenance criteria and the Device Map's per-site narrowing all read learnedLocation, so picking the winner at render time would make the column disagree with everything that filters on it. Propagation is PULL-based because the projection runs in the discovery process: `refreshProjectionPriority()` installs the order into `assetProjection`'s process-wide state at boot (every role, from app.ts) and at the start of every `runDiscovery` — which is also the next moment learnedLocation is written, so an edit is never observably stale. Reordering is not retroactive on its own. `saveSourceLocationPriority` REJECTS unknown/duplicate kinds (unlike the self-healing read path) and audits with the previous order (`asset.source_priority.updated`). `getSourcePrioritySettings` returns the order plus the catalogue entries so the UI renders labels/hints server-driven.
│   │   ├── dashSettingsService.ts   # Dash wallboard operator config: `dashConfig` Setting row `{enabled(default false), ipScope("rfc1918"|"all"|"custom", default rfc1918), allowedCidrs(canonical IPv4 CIDRs for custom)}` with a 10s TTL cache — the cache TTL is the cross-process propagation delay for the Server Settings → Web Server toggle (the web process writes; the dash process reads). Migrates a legacy `rfc1918Only` boolean on read; validates/normalizes custom CIDRs (rejects an enabled-but-empty custom list). proxyConfigService pattern.
│   │   ├── loginAccessService.ts   # Local-login source-IP restriction: `loginAccessConfig` Setting row `{enabled(default false), ipScope("rfc1918"|"all"|"custom", default rfc1918), allowedCidrs}` with a 10s TTL cache (dashSettingsService pattern, POLARITY INVERTED — `enabled` false means NO restriction, so an upgrade never starts refusing logins). Backs the gate in `src/app.ts` over `/login.html` + `POST /auth/login` + `/auth/login/totp`; `isLoginSourceAllowed` FAILS OPEN on a settings read error, because a DB blip must not become the lockout the feature exists to prevent. Scope decision delegated to `utils/ipScope.ts`, shared with the dash gate.
│   │   ├── apiDocsAccessService.ts # API-docs page source-IP scope: `apiDocsConfig` Setting row `{enabled(default TRUE), ipScope("loopback"|"rfc1918"|"custom", default rfc1918 — deliberately NO "all"), allowedCidrs}` with a 10s TTL cache (loginAccessService pattern). Backs the gate in `src/app.ts` over `/api` + `/api/` + `/api.html` (the unauthenticated developer-docs page): `docsSourceAllowed` is the pure decision (loopback ALWAYS allowed while enabled; disabled denies everyone, loopback included), `isApiDocsSourceAllowed` FAILS CLOSED on a settings read error — the opposite posture from loginAccessService, because this fronts an unauthenticated disclosure surface rather than a lockout-recovery path. Custom entries must sit inside RFC1918 (`isRfc1918Cidr`) — refused at save AND re-filtered on read so a hand-edited row can't smuggle a public CIDR. `deriveApiDocsNginxAllow` maps the posture to the allow-lines the nginx renderer's `{{API_DOCS_ALLOW_BLOCK}}` emits (defense in depth on managed proxy installs; the app gate stays authoritative everywhere).
│   │   ├── dashRoleSnapshotService.ts # Supplies the Dash wallboard's permission identity: the seeded `readonly` Role materialized via snapshotFromRole (60s TTL) so dashServer stamps req.roleSnapshot and every existing requirePermission/hasPermission gate resolves as a readonly caller. AppError 500 when the seeded row is missing.
│   │   ├── weatherProxyService.ts   # Status Map weather proxy backing /weather (main router + Dash listener): RainViewer frame index (5 min TTL, in-flight dedupe, serve-stale ≤30 min on upstream failure), radar tile proxy (frame id is a content hash → tiles are immutable → size-bounded FIFO cache ~48 MB / 4000 entries, no TTL; tile requests validate against the last TWO index generations so an animation started just before a rotation keeps resolving — and the endpoint can't be used as an open proxy), and Open-Meteo current temperature (cached per the same 1.5° grid the widget rounds to, 20 min TTL; negative results cached, transport failures throw 502 and never poison the cache — geocoderService precedent). Deduplicates every viewer's radar downloads into one upstream fetch per tile and lets egress-restricted wallboard kiosks show weather when only the Polaris server has internet. The widget is proxy-first with direct-CDN fallback (siteMap.js), so failures here degrade, never break.
│   │   ├── peerInferredLldpService.ts # Read-time supplementation of `AssetLldpNeighbor` from `Asset.fortinetTopology`. `buildInferredNeighborsForAsset(assetId)` synthesizes neighbor rows the persisted table can't see — FortiSwitch ports facing managed FortiAPs (via the AP's `parentSwitch`/`parentPort`), FortiGate FortiLink-side interfaces facing managed switches (via the switch's `controllerFortigate`/`uplinkInterface`), and the FortiAP-side reverse of (a). The FortiAP branch additionally normalizes the synthesized `localIfName` via `fortiapInterfaceAlias.normalizeFortiapInterfaceName` against the AP's `AssetInterface` (current-state) ifNames — this needs the FULL interface set, since the `eth0` being normalized TO is typically unpinned, which is why it can't read the pinned-only sample table — discovery stamps `uplinkInterface` from the FortiGate's managed_ap response in FortiAP-CLI naming (`lan1`/`lan2`) but the AP's own SNMP IF-MIB exposes the same port as `eth0`/`eth1`. Without normalization the inferred row would never line up with any row in the System tab's interface table. Prefers the eth* form, falls back to lan*, falls back to the raw value when neither alias exists. Returns `InferredLldpNeighbor[]` shaped like the real Prisma rows minus DB-only fields, stamped with `source: "peer-inferred"` and a pre-resolved `matchedAsset`. `dedupeInferredNeighbors(real, inferred, aggregateParentByMember?)` drops any inferred row where a real LLDP row exists on `(localIfName, matchedAssetId)`; real LLDP wins. With the optional membership map (built by `aggregateMembershipMap(interfaces)` from `ifType`/`ifParent`), a real row on an aggregate's *member* port also suppresses the inferred row synthesized on the *aggregate* — the FortiLink case (uplink inferred on `fortilink`, real LLDP learned on member `a`). Consumed by `GET /assets/:id/system-info` (merges into the response) and `GET /assets/:id/interface-history` (filters to the requested ifName; fetches the asset's full real-LLDP set + latest interface snapshot so member-vs-aggregate dedupe works). Read-only — never writes the table. `/map/sites/:id/topology` is unaffected since it consumes `fortinetTopology` directly.
│   │   ├── interfaceInventoryService.ts # CURRENT-STATE interface inventory writer (`AssetInterface`). `persistInterfaces(assetId, InterfaceSample[], now?)` maps the collector shape onto the table's 22 columns and delegates to `persistInterfaceRows(assetId, rows, now?)`, which is the core: dedupe-by-ifName (keeping the first occurrence — `(assetId, ifName)` is UNIQUE, so a device reporting a name twice would otherwise abort the whole scrape) + a 2000-row cap, both WARNED not silent, then delete-then-createMany in ONE `$transaction` so a concurrent reader sees the old set or the new set but never an empty intermediate (this table backs the System tab; an empty read renders as "no interfaces"). `firstSeen` is carried forward for a name still present and resets when one disappears and returns. `persistInterfaceRows` is exported so the agent push can reuse the rows it already built for the sample write instead of re-mapping 22 fields a second time. `dedupeAndCapInterfaces` + `INTERFACE_ROW_CAP` are exported pure for unit testing. **Callers must not invoke this from the fast pinned re-walk** — see the AssetInterface domain-model entry.
│   │   ├── interfaceTopologyService.ts # Inter-Fortinet topology inference from interface naming conventions. inferInterfaceTopology(seedAssetIds) reads the seed set's interfaces from the CURRENT-STATE `AssetInterface` table (one row per (assetId, ifName) by construction — a plain indexed read), bounded by a 1-hour `lastSeen` staleness filter so interfaces that stopped reporting don't draw edges. This replaced a DISTINCT ON over asset_interface_samples whose 1-hour timestamp window existed purely to keep it off the hypertable bulk — without the bound it scanned the entire active chunk and was observed at 13.5 min / 90M rows / 9 GB I/O on a fleet of ~600 infra assets. The cutover also FIXED a silent correctness bug: the fast pinned re-walk writes ifType/ifParent as NULL and DISTINCT ON took the newest row, so on a pinned aggregate the physical-member map saw nulls and lost it; the current-state table is written only by the full pass, which always populates them. It parses each ifName through fortinetSerialPattern, and resolves matches against the in-memory Fortinet asset inventory by serial-fragment endsWith (FortiOS-auto peer aggregates) or hostname exact/prefix-with-separator (operator-named MCLAG aggregates). Skips ambiguous (>1 hit) and self-loop matches. Returned edge ifNames prefer the underlying physical member when the matched aggregate has exactly one physical child (ifType="physical" + ifParent=aggregate) — operators trace cables by physical port, not by the FortiOS-stamped peer-named aggregate label; multi-member aggregates keep the aggregate name as the safe fallback (no single "the physical port" exists, and a comma-joined list would lie about the strict one-port-per-physical-link model). The aggregate name is still the inference SIGNAL (peer identity is encoded in it) — only the display ifName on the returned edge is normalized. Returns sibling edges plus a remoteAssets map for cross-site peers. Read-only — uses data the monitoring pipeline already collected, no new device queries. Wired into GET /map/sites/:id/topology AND `dependencyTreeService.recomputeDependencyTree` (Phase 12 of FMG/FortiGate sync) — the 1-hour window keeps that recompute under a second instead of blocking discovery for ~20 minutes.
│   │   ├── dependencyTreeService.ts # Dependency-aware monitoring suppression. recomputeDependencyTree(integrationId?) walks fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate / parentSwitch + interfaceTopologyService edges + AssetLldpNeighbor.matchedAssetId (filtered by `filterFreshLldpRows` — the table's 48h stickiness is a DISPLAY grace so the Neighbor column doesn't flap, but an edge that suppresses alerts needs the same freshness discipline interfaceTopologyService applies to its own inputs; a row is kept only if refreshed within 6h OR carrying the newest lastSeen for its (asset, source), the second arm keeping slow-cadence installs whole since lldpIntervalSeconds is settable to 24h) into a parent→child DAG, prunes via **physical-first** BFS layer assignment from each FortiGate (layer 1) outward — interface + LLDP edges form the primary adjacency, controller edges are a fallback for assets the physical pass didn't reach, with simple-path detection so a 3+ switch daisy chain that's only LLDP-visible between siblings (not back to the FortiGate) still chains correctly instead of collapsing every switch into a same-layer sibling of the FortiGate. MCLAG pairs and any branching / cycled controller-only component still attach as siblings. Wireless attachments override the controller signal: a **mesh-leaf AP** (seen as a station on its root AP, from `AssetWirelessStation`, or classified `meshUplink="mesh"` on its own `fortinetTopology`) depends on the root AP, and a **FortiLink switch bridged behind a FortiAP** (an AP↔switch `AssetLldpNeighbor` adjacency where the switch is not the AP's controller parent — or where the AP is a mesh leaf, whose wired LLDP adjacency is always bridged-behind) depends on that AP — in both cases the leaf's backwards controller edge is suppressed and a `mesh`/LLDP edge takes its place. **Retired assets leave the graph but stay in scope**: `decommissioned` / `disabled` infra assets (`EXCLUDED_LIFECYCLE_STATUSES`, as the endpoint half already did) are excluded from `depAssets` / the parent index / the interface + LLDP reads, so they parent nothing — rule 10 forces `monitored=false` and `evaluateSuppression` treats an unmonitored parent as transparent, returning ok when it finds no grandparents, which makes a layer-1 retired gate a permanent suppression veto its children can never escape. They remain in `inScope` so the transaction deletes their own computed rows and nulls their layer; filtering the read instead would strand a retired switch's rows forever. `storage` / `quarantined` stay in the graph on purpose (present devices, reversible). **Controller MEMBERSHIP bounds the graph**: every cycle asks each gate for its own managed inventory and stamps the answer on the GATE as `fortinetTopology.managedSwitchSerials` / `managedApSerials` — FMG from the native `/pm/config/device/<dev>/.../switch-controller/managed-switch` + `.../wireless-controller/wtp` reads (which answer for an OFFLINE gate, being FortiManager's own device DB), standalone from the gate's `/api/v2/cmdb/...` equivalents. A switch or AP absent from gate G's list cannot sit under G, so `violatesMembership` drops a contradicting interface / LLDP adjacency in BOTH directions (assignLayers builds undirected adjacency, so one direction would leave the layering intact) and also drops a child↔child edge whose ends belong to different gates — the cross-site link a child-side veto cannot express. **Tri-state**: an ABSENT field is unknown (unreadable roster / pre-feature row) and constrains nothing; `[]` is the real answer "manages none"; a populated list constrains to those serials. Discovery therefore stamps the field only when the roster read ANSWERED (`DiscoveryResult.managedMembership.switchDevices` / `apDevices`), so a failure can never masquerade as "manages nothing". Matched on SERIAL throughout; HA needs no carve-out because the stamp is written per cluster member. Deliberately independent of `cmdbSwitchSerials` / `cmdbApSerials`, which exist to PROTECT assets from the decommission sweep — membership informs the dependency graph ONLY and can never authorize a sweep. Supersedes the retired child-side `contradictsController` veto, which required the child's own `controllerSerial` and could only reject a direct child↔firewall pair. Kept edges prefer the most-physical `detectedVia` (mesh > interface > lldp > controller) for the audit-trail row, persists the resulting source="computed" rows in AssetDependencyParent and Asset.dependencyLayer per scope. Operator overrides (source="override") take precedence per asset; computed rows survive alongside for audit. reconcileDependencySuppression() is the 60s reconciler — source of truth for Asset.dependencySuppressed; "all-down" multi-parent semantics (a switch with redundant uplinks suppresses only when EVERY effective parent is down or itself suppressed). Unmonitored parents are transparent — the walk continues to their grandparents. propagateAfterStatusChange(assetId) is the latency-optimization hook fired from recordProbeResult on the confirmed up/down edge only (the monitor.status_changed Event also covers the →warning edge, but propagate does not). **The ENDPOINT half (2026-08)**: `syncEndpointDependencyEdges(infra, layers)` hangs every asset whose type is NOT firewall/switch/access_point off that infra tree as a leaf, with `source="endpoint"` and at most ONE parent, resolved most-specific-first by `buildEndpointDependencyEdges` — `Asset.lastSeenSwitch` (`detectedVia="switch-port"`) → `Asset.lastSeenAp` (`"wireless"`) → the freshest `AssetFortigateSighting.fortigateDevice` that resolves to a firewall (`"sighting"`). It exists because the tree was infra-only and "no parents" means "never suppressed": a camera-station server behind a dead FortiGate alerted as plain Down while every switch and AP behind that same gate correctly read "Dep. Down". One parent rather than a union of everything that resolves, because all-down semantics model REDUNDANT parents while a switch and its gate are in SERIES — listing both would let a dead access switch under a healthy gate satisfy "some parent is ok" and keep the endpoint alerting; the series behavior instead comes from the switch itself being suppressed by its gate, and an unmonitored intermediate stays transparent so gate state still decides. Assets already carrying a `source="vcenter"` row are skipped (the hypervisor placement is the more specific truth, and unioning would break vMotion-safe cluster suppression). The pass is fleet-wide and deliberately NOT narrowed by `integrationId` — most endpoints belong to an AD/Entra/vCenter integration that never calls the recompute — and DIFFS its writes (insert missing / delete gone / retype a changed detectedVia / stamp `dependencyLayer` = parent + 1 only where it differs) instead of delete-replacing, so a steady fleet writes zero rows per discovery finalize and two integrations finalizing at once can't churn each other. Its failures are caught and logged: the endpoint half can never fail the infra recompute. Pure helpers (buildDependencyEdgesFromInputs, assignLayers, evaluateSuppression, switchNameFromLastSeenSwitch, resolveEndpointParent, buildEndpointDependencyEdges) are exported for unit testing.
│   │   ├── downDetectionService.ts # WHO DECIDES A DEVICE IS DOWN. Down used to be a Monitor Settings value (`failureThreshold` resolved through the (integration, assetType) tier hierarchy); it is now owned by the `monitorStatus == down` AUTOMATION covering each asset, via its `missedPolls` count. Which automation wins when several match is business rule 18's EXISTING `scopeRank` ladder — deliberately not a second precedence system, so one rule decides both whose count governs an asset and which automation alerts on it (all down automations share one `triggerSignature`, keyed by compared value and NOT by device filter, precisely so they land in one carve-out group). `resolveDownDetection(assetId)` answers `{threshold, recoverySustainSec}` or **null = PASSIVE** (no automation covers it: still polled, still charted, no verdict rendered — the sixth `monitorStatus` value); `resolveDownThreshold` is the count-only wrapper. **The same automation owns the way BACK** (2026-08-29): its `reset.sustainSec` — the wizard's "must stay cleared for N polls", stored as seconds — rides the same lookup and `recoveryPollsFor(verdict, intervalSec)` converts it back to polls at the asset's own cadence, so the probe loop holds the asset in `recovering` until that many probes have ANSWERED. Both directions from ONE `Map.get` deliberately: a second lookup could resolve the halves onto different rules. The drain is the FLOOR (`max(threshold, polls)`, business rule 30's bucket still owes one answer per miss) and only an `auto` reset counts, a `condition` tree being its own recovery authority. HOT PATH: called once per probe per asset at 2000 assets / 60s, so it is ONE `Map.get` over a snapshot rebuilt at most once per `DOWN_DETECTION_TTL_MS` (60s) plus once per rule write; `createTtlCache`'s in-flight-counts-as-fresh rule means a cold start under 2000 concurrent probes performs exactly ONE build (2 queries), which is the property `tests/unit/downDetectionCache.test.ts` pins. The build is 2 queries — enabled rules + `monitored: true` assets on a tight 11-column select (deliberately NOT the engine's `SCOPE_SELECT`, which drags `monitored*` array columns this resolver never reads). Staleness: rule edits invalidate explicitly (unconditionally, from all three notificationRuleService CRUD sites — an edit can turn a rule INTO or OUT OF a down rule); ASSET scope drift rides the TTL alone (instrumenting every asset writer is not viable), and the one case where staleness could produce a WRONG rather than stale verdict — a brand-new asset — is exact, because `fallback` answers from the all-assets rule, which covers any asset by definition. Degradation: a failed rebuild serves `lastGoodIndex`; with no snapshot at all everything reads passive, because refusing to render a verdict is strictly safer than inventing one and it self-heals next probe (a rejection is never cached). `pickDownWinner` is pure + unit-tested: most-specific wins, and on a same-rank TIE the SMALLER count wins (matching `getMetricSeverityTiers`' existing more-sensitive-wins convention, and the safe direction for a monitoring product — both tied automations still fire, so taking the smaller means neither ever fires later than its own config promised), then older `createdAt`, then lower `id` for a stable diagnostic identity. Conflicts are summarized per distinct rule PAIR (not per asset) in one warn per rebuild and surfaced per-asset by `describeDownDetectionFor`. Also fires a one-shot `monitor.down_detection_absent` warning Event on the TRANSITION into a zero-rule fleet — the state where nothing is judged and the thing that would normally alert about it is exactly what was deleted. Metrics: `polaris_down_detection_build_seconds` / `_assets{coverage}` / `_unavailable_total`
│   │   ├── mapRegionService.ts      # Device Map regions: operator-drawn polygons stored as a JSON blob in Setting under key `mapRegions` (allocationTemplateService pattern). Each region carries a unique name; firewalls whose lat/lng falls inside the polygon — and FortiSwitches / FortiAPs whose `fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate` matches one of those firewalls — get tagged with `region:<name>`. **`Subnet` rows carry the tag too**: a subnet whose `fortigateDevice` matches an enclosed gate (same `controllerIdentityKeys` set) inherits the region, which is what gives the IPAM Networks list (Sources column = `fortigateDevice`) a region to filter on. `computeMembership` returns `{assetIds, subnetIds}` and the tag primitives come in pairs (`addTagToAssets`/`addTagToSubnets`, `removeTagFromAllAssets`/`removeTagFromAllSubnets`); `ReconcileSummary` counts the two populations separately (`added`/`removed`/`assetsTouched` vs `subnetsAdded`/`subnetsRemoved`/`subnetsTouched`). The reconciler **re-evaluates membership in both directions, bounded by provenance**: every add records a `RegionTagAssignment` row (one per (region, target) pair the service itself tagged — the `TagAutoAssignment` pattern, keyed by region id so a rename doesn't disturb it, with a `targetType` because subnets are targets too), and the strip half removes the tag only from recorded pairs that have drifted out of membership (`diffRegionMembership`, pure). A device that moves — a re-pinned gate, a switch repointed to another controller, a subnet re-served by a different gate — loses the tag on the next reconcile; a hand-applied tag (no provenance row, which also covers tags predating provenance) is never touched. Manually *removing* a tag from an in-polygon asset will be re-added on the next reconcile. Rename/delete keep their wholesale strips (`removeTagFromAllAssets`/`removeTagFromAllSubnets`); delete also clears the region's provenance. Region creation upserts a `Tag` registry row at `region:<name>` under category "Map Regions" so it shows up in the asset edit modal's tag picker; rename rotates the registry row; delete removes it. Fired from CRUD endpoints (await), end-of-FMG/FortiGate `syncDhcpSubnets` Phase 13, and a 6h periodic safety-net job. Membership is computed by `pointInPolygon` from `src/utils/geo.ts`; only firewalls have lat/lng so endpoints are never auto-tagged. **Blob writes serialize (2026-08-25):** every create / update / delete goes through `withRegionBlobLock`, which takes a `pg_advisory_xact_lock` (classid `0x504c5255` "PLRU") as the first statement of a transaction wrapping the read AND the write. Without it the read-modify-write on the single `mapRegions` Setting value lost updates whenever two writers overlapped — which the map's edit mode did on every multi-polygon Save (`Promise.all`), persisting one edit out of N while every PUT returned 200. `loadAll` / `persistAll` therefore take an optional client so the locked transaction can own both halves; the tag-registry mirroring stays OUTSIDE the lock (different table, swallows its own failures, and holding the blob lock across a Tag upsert would serialize every region write behind it). **Derived nesting levels (2026-08):** `getRegionHierarchy()` builds the containment forest via `utils/regionHierarchy.buildRegionHierarchy` and caches it keyed on the `mapRegions` `Setting.updatedAt` — a free, exact version stamp, so a stale entry is unreachable even before the 5-minute TTL fires (the TTL is only a memory bound). Reading that version costs one indexed `findUnique` per call and is DELIBERATE: Polaris runs split-role, so a region edited in the web process must not leave a monitor process serving stale levels; only the geometry build is memoized. `invalidateRegionHierarchy()` is called from inside `persistAll` rather than at the three CRUD call sites, so a future write path cannot forget it — and levels are global, so any write invalidates everything. `listRegionsWithLevels()` is the decorated read projection (`MapRegionWithLevel` = MapRegion + `level`/`depth`/`parentId`/`childIds`/`ancestorIds`, still name-sorted); **`listRegions()` deliberately stays UNdecorated** because `reconcileMapRegions` and `notificationRuleService.listScopeOptions` both call it, and a decorated object round-tripped back through `persistAll` would write derived fields into the blob — the exact failure deriving-on-read exists to prevent (pinned by a test asserting the persisted keys after a decorated read followed by a write). `diffRegionLevels(before, after)` is pure and backs the audit trail, because editing ONE polygon can re-level an entire ancestor chain and change who gets paged for regions the operator never touched.
│   │   ├── regionHierarchyService.ts # The ALERT-ROUTING view of region nesting: `deviceRegionsAtLevels(assetRegionNames, levels, index)` (pure) answers which regions sit at each **asset-relative** level for a triggering device — 1 = the device's own innermost region, 2 = the division containing it, walked outward along the containment edges. **Asset-relative, not global, and that is the whole point:** global levels count outward from the leaves and have GAPS on an uneven tree, so filtering a snapshot on `level === 2` reaches NOBODY for a device whose branch skips it while reaching a mid-chain region for a device in a deeper branch — the same automation paging a division manager for one alert and a local tech for the next. Level 1 is resolved as the innermost region(s) the asset carries (those that are not an ancestor of another region it also carries — a reconciled asset carries its leaf AND every container), then each higher level is one step out. The outward walk deliberately does NOT require the parent's tag to be in the snapshot, because `computeMembership` tags each region independently and a division's tag can be one reconcile behind — an escalation must not fall silent for that. `regionLevelIndex()` builds the name→{parentName, level} map from `mapRegionService.getRegionHierarchy` and is deliberately NOT given a second TTL cache (that read is already memoized per blob version; the remaining indexed `findUnique` is what makes a region edit visible immediately in the monitor process, and callers on a fan-out path memoize the RESULT per notification instead). Imports `stripRegionPrefix` from `utils/tagNormalize`, NOT from `notificationService` — the latter imports `notificationRuleService`, which imports this module, so that path would close a runtime cycle.
│   │   ├── assetGhostMergeService.ts # Ghost merging, two flavors. (1) Endpoint-ghost merge: collapses a duplicate "fortigate-endpoint" placeholder Asset (created when a managed device's mgmt interface pulled a DHCP lease and the gate's DHCP/device-inventory pathway learned its MAC independently — hostname = the device serial) into its canonical infrastructure asset. `isMergeableGhostSourceKinds` / `isMergeableEndpointGhost` gate eligibility (fortigate-endpoint provenance required, ANY authoritative source — fortiswitch/fortiap/fortigate-firewall/ad/entra/intune/polaris-agent — disqualifies; the empty "manual" row an operator edit stamps doesn't). `mergeEndpointGhostIntoAsset(canonicalId, ghostId)` transfers AssetMacAddress/AssetAssociatedIp/AssetIpHistory/AssetFortigateSighting rows (delete-on-conflict), drops the ghost's AssetSource rows, stamps the ghost's MAC when the canonical has none, carries `monitored=true` over (+ recomputeMonitorOverrideForAssets) when the ghost was operator-monitored, and deletes the ghost (sample hypertables have no Asset FK — orphaned rows age out via drop_chunks). Callers: the inline ghost sweep in `syncDhcpSubnets`'s FortiSwitch/FortiAP loops (`sweepEndpointGhostsInto` — candidates by base-MAC and hostname==serial only, never bare IP) and the one-shot `mergeFortiswitchEndpointGhosts` startup job. (2) The duplicate-hostname policy + executor behind mergeDuplicateHostnameAssets (moved from the job 2026-08 so they are unit-testable): decideDuplicateHostnameGroup (pure canonical pick — source-kind tiers, lastSeen/updatedAt tiebreak, same-tier conflicting-MAC skip) + mergeDuplicateHostnameGhost (per-ghost transaction: side-table transfer, null-fill scalar absorption + tag union, bumpLastSeen-gated lastSeen adoption, ghost cascade-delete).
│   │   ├── tagAssignmentService.ts  # Filter-based tag auto-assignment ("managed sync"). A tag carrying a device filter auto-applies / removes itself on matching assets. **Two shapes, one live per row.** CURRENT is `Tag.assetCondition` — the SAME nested AND/OR condition tree the automations device filter and the address book store, validated against `DEVICE_FILTER_FIELD_OPS` and evaluated by the same `evaluateScopeCondition`, resolved fleet-wide through the shared `deviceFilterService.resolveDeviceFilterAssetIds`. LEGACY is the flat `Tag.criteria` blob (`{version, match:"all", rules:[...]}`, rules ANDed, values ORed) over manufacturer / model / os / osVersion / hostname / department / location (exact|contains|pattern) + assetType / status (exact) + subnet (inCidr) + the relation-backed `integration` / `fortigate`; it is still READ so a pre-cutover row keeps matching, and folds forward through the pure `criteriaToCondition` (persisted by the `migrateTagFilterShape` one-shot). Every reader normalizes through **`tagFilterOf`**, `tagIsManaged` is the managed-tag allowlist, and **`tagFilterView`** is the editor projection (stored tree + `assetConditionEffective` fold + `assetFilterUnconvertible`) so a legacy tag opens in the builder instead of rendering as unfiltered — without which the operator's next save would silently clear a live filter. Two decisions the tree path has to state that the flat one got for free: **an EMPTY tree is NO filter, never "all devices"** (`normalizeTagCondition` collapses it — `and([])` is true for every asset, and a tag has no All-devices control, so the only way to reach it is a half-built form, which would tag the whole fleet on save), and **a decommissioned asset is ineligible unless the filter mentions status** (`tagEligibilityWhere` / `tagAssetIsEligible`, ANDed OUTSIDE the tree so it stays sound under `or`/`none`/`notAll` — carried over from `buildPrefilterWhere`, where it was implicit). The LEGACY three-stage resolver survives for flat rows: `buildPrefilterWhere` (a Prisma where-clause that is a strict SUPERSET of the predicate so narrow criteria don't load the whole fleet — subnet rules + prefixless patterns are predicate-only), then `cidrContainmentMap` (one inet `>>=` round-trip, family-aware v4/v6) for subnet membership, then the in-memory `buildMatcher` predicate (wildcards compiled once via `compileWildcard`). Diff-based reconcile (`reconcileTag` / `reconcileAllTags` / per-asset `reconcileTagsForAsset`) keyed off the `TagAutoAssignment` provenance table: adds to newly matching assets + records provenance; removes the tag ONLY where a provenance row exists, so a hand-applied copy of the same name on a non-matching asset is preserved. `reconcileTagsForAsset` handles both shapes off ONE asset read and joins the interface inventory only when some filter asks about it. `previewTagFilter({condition|criteria}, tagId?)` is a write-free dry-run (match count + sample + `+add/-remove` diff) taking either shape. Fired inline on Tag create/edit (and strip-on-clear / delete), end-of-discovery (integrations Phase 13.65), asset create/update hooks, and a 6h safety-net job (`reconcileTagAssignments.ts`).

Write-time enforcement lives in the db.ts extension (`clampMonitoredForStatus` for writes that stage a status, `enforceMonitorableStatus` for writes that stage `monitored: true` with none); this covers what those can't reach — rows that predate the widened status set, raw-SQL writers, and any row the best-effort guard skipped on a failed read. │   │   ├── clampFailureBucket.ts   # Startup sweep for the missed-poll bucket's CEILING (business rule 30): clamps any `Asset.consecutiveFailures` above `MAX_MISSED_POLL_BUCKET` (100) and retires the dormant `awaitingRecoveryConfirm` bit. The bucket was UNBOUNDED before 2026-09-01, so a device dark overnight at a 60 s cadence reached ~480 and then owed 480 answered polls before it could read `up` — eight hours of its down alert repeating and escalating after it came back. Does NOT resolve each asset's own cap: `nextFailureBucket` clamps before it moves the level in either direction, so the next probe of either outcome pulls an over-cap row to that asset's exact number; this exists for the surfaces that read the column BEFORE that probe (the strip's tooltip, `runsHeavyCadences`, `consecutiveFailures` as an automatable field). Two idempotent single UPDATEs, deliberately NOT marker-guarded.
│   │   ├── enforceSubnetUniqueIndex.ts # Self-healing startup job: creates the `subnets_block_cidr_key` UNIQUE index on (blockId, cidr) when missing. Migration 20260806000000 SKIPS creation (with a WARNING) on an install that already carries duplicate rows from the pre-lock race, because failing the migration there would block the whole upgrade over historical data. Deliberately NOT marker-guarded — it retries every boot, so the index appears on its own once an operator merges/deletes the duplicates. Steady state is two cheap catalog queries. Stamps a warning Event (`subnet.unique_index_blocked`) per boot while duplicates remain, and `subnet.unique_index_created` when it succeeds.
│   │   ├── auditPollingCapability.ts # Read-only startup sweep naming stored polling methods with no collector behind them — the ones reporting a healthy tick forever while gathering nothing. Walks per-asset overrides, class overrides and each integration's baseline through `collectorCapability`, logs one warning per finding and writes ONE `monitor.polling_capability_gap` Event (count + a bounded sample) so the finding ships out through the syslog / SFTP archivers. Changes NOTHING — an operator may have set a method in anticipation of the collector landing, and silently rewriting their intent would be worse than the gap. Not marker-guarded: the answer changes as collectors land and as settings are edited.
│   │   ├── backfillSecretEncryption.ts # Seals previously-PLAINTEXT secrets in Credential.config / Integration.config / NotificationChannel.config / Setting.value. The db.ts extension seals every new write, but an existing install has years of plaintext credentials in those columns — which is the actual exposure (any `pg_dump` contains them). Reads through `prismaBase` (the UNEXTENDED client, so it sees the RAW stored value and can tell sealed from unsealed) and writes through the extended client (which seals). NOT marker-guarded: `POLARIS_SECRET_KEY` may be configured LATER than the upgrade that ships this code, and it is naturally idempotent (`sealValue` no-ops on already-sealed input). Exits immediately when no key is configured.
│   │   ├── scheduledBackup.ts       # Periodic scheduler (5-min tick, scheduler role only so a split-role install takes ONE backup, not one per monitor replica): takes an automatic backup when `isScheduledBackupDue`, copies it off-host when configured, and prunes old SCHEDULED copies to `retainCount` (never touches manual or pre-update backups). A failed run writes `server.backup.scheduled_failed` (error) + `backupSchedule.lastError`; a failed off-host copy writes `server.backup.offhost_copy_failed` (warning) without failing the run. Default-off, so the tick is a cheap due-check until an operator enables it.
│   │   ├── decommissionStaleAssets.ts # Every 24h: decommission assets not seen in N months
│   │   ├── monitorAssets.ts          # Two ticking loops with independent `running` guards. Light loop (probe + fastFiltered) ticks every 5s; heavy loop (telemetry + systemInfo) ticks every 30s and calls `runRetentionPrune` (fleet-coordinated single-flight via persisted `Setting("lastRetentionPruneAt")` + a Postgres advisory lock — replaced the old in-memory `lastPruneAt=0` trigger that fired on every boot and caused the 2026-06-17 prune pile-up). A wedged systemInfo on dead hosts blocks ONLY future heavy ticks — light loop keeps firing on its own clock so per-minute probe polling stays close to its configured cadence regardless. Default concurrency is CPU-aware (`cpus().length * 2` for light, `cpus().length` for heavy), env-overridable via POLARIS_PROBE_CONCURRENCY / POLARIS_HEAVY_CONCURRENCY.
