│   │   ├── seedManufacturerProfiles.ts # One-shot startup (Slice 6a): converts the hardcoded `VENDOR_TELEMETRY_PROFILES` constant into `ManufacturerProfile` + `ManufacturerProfileMetric` + `ManufacturerProfileMetricOverride` rows. Idempotent (marker `Setting.seedManufacturerProfilesSeededAt`). One profile per distinct canonical manufacturer (Cisco / Juniper / Mikrotik / Fortinet / HP / Dell); the Fortinet sub-family entries (FortiSwitch / FortiAP) become `modelPattern`-keyed overrides under the umbrella Fortinet profile. Vendor memory queries with the bytes form (Cisco used+free; FortiSwitch used+total) are translated via `memoryQueryToDoubleScalar()` and seeded as `type="double_scalar"` with the matching `CombinerKind` (`a_over_a_plus_b_as_percent` / `a_over_b_as_percent`); percent-only vendors (Juniper, generic Fortinet, FortiAP) seed as plain `scalar`. Disk is always seeded as `double_scalar` with `a_over_b_as_percent` since the hardcoded profile carries `usedBytesSymbol + totalBytesSymbol`. Calls `refreshProfileCache()` after seeding so the in-memory cache is warm for downstream code. The constant stays runtime-authoritative — this job only owns persistence. Best-effort: failures log and never block boot.
│   │   ├── seedBaselineAutomations.ts # One-shot startup: seeds the baseline automations (NotificationRule rows) in three independently-markered sets. Set 1 (~11 rules, marker `Setting.seedBaselineAutomationsSeededAt`) mirrors the alertable dashboard widgets — asset down, interface/IPsec-tunnel down, high CPU/memory/temperature/disk, slow response, packet loss (probeLossPct), storage-fills-soon, recent reboot. Set 2 (12 rules, marker `Setting.seedBaselineAutomationsV2SeededAt` — its own key so pre-v2 installs pick it up without duplicating set 1) covers the notable system-generated Event families with event-trigger automations: discovery failed/aborted, quarantine + reservation push failures (queued + permanent), agent disconnected / upgrade failed, capacity escalations (detailsMatch direction=escalated), ip-override conflicts, auto-decommissions, HA standby down, login lockouts — all enabled, in-app only, storm-proofed with a `cooldownSec` plus a real reset — a timer, or (where Polaris writes the counterpart event) `reset.mode="event"` on it: agent disconnected clears on `agent.connected`, discovery failed on `integration.discover.completed`, agent upgrade failed on `agent.upgrade_succeeded` (relies on the engine's event-tail cooldown + timed-clear + counterpart-reset passes); glob-vs-writer pinning in seedBaselineAutomations.test.ts. SEED-ONCE per set, NOT self-heal: once a marker is stamped that set never re-runs, so a rule the operator edits/DELETES stays gone. Built through `ruleInputSchema` + `createRule` (canonical v2 shape); numeric rules auto-clear with hysteresis at the widget's warning level. Delete a set's marker + restart to force a re-seed (resurrects that whole set). **V3 (down detection)** is a THIRD marker (`seedBaselineAutomationsV3SeededAt`) and differs in kind: it is COMPUTED from live data, not a static array. Down stopped being a monitor-settings value (business rule 36), so V3 resolves each monitored asset's effective pre-cutover `failureThreshold` and mirrors it into automations — one all-assets rule at the dominant value plus one `assetTypes:[t]` rule per class that differed (rank 1, so it wins for that class) — then retires the pre-cutover "Asset down" row via `deleteRule` (the SERVICE, so its active notifications are soft-cleared) ONLY when `updatedAt === createdAt`. An edited row is kept + flagged (`automation.seed.v3_retained`): it still governs at `DEFAULT_MISSED_POLLS`, and the operator must be told the count is theirs now. Order is CREATE-then-retire (the reverse leaves a window with zero down automations = a momentarily blind fleet), and it refuses to retire if the replacement failed to save. Known gap, logged rather than hidden: `scopeRank` doesn't rank `integrationIds`, so one class with different thresholds across two integrations collapses to the more-sensitive value + an `automation.seed.threshold_conflict` warning Event.. **V5** (`migrateLossCeilingV5`, marker `seedBaselineAutomationsV5LossCeilingSeededAt`) retrofits `ignoreAtOrAbove: 90` onto existing installs' packet-loss automations — the seed marker means they never re-seed, and with the loss anchor removed (rule 29) an all-assets loss rule with no ceiling trails a second alert behind every outage. Bounded like V3's retire step: only probeLossPct triggers stating NO ceiling, and only rules never edited (updatedAt === createdAt); an edited one is left alone and NAMED in a warning Event, because narrowing someone's tuned alert silently is worse than leaving it noisy

│   │   ├── mergeFortiswitchEndpointGhosts.ts # One-shot startup cleanup. Idempotent — re-runs find zero candidates once convergent.
│   │   ├── mergeDuplicateHostnameAssets.ts  # Periodic safety-net cleanup — runs once at boot AND every 30 min (discovery re-creates duplicate-hostname rows continuously, so a boot-only pass let them accumulate between restarts on long-lived prod). Broader sibling of `mergeFortiswitchEndpointGhosts` — handles every shape of accumulated duplicate-hostname Asset row (workstation ghosts where the FortiGate created one `fortigate-endpoint` per MAC sighting, Phase-1 backfill `manual`-only placeholders that didn't get swept, FortiSwitch/FortiAP ghosts the narrower job's NULL-MAC filter misses post-baseMac, etc.). Groups every Asset row by `lower(hostname)`, walks groups with ≥2 rows, picks a canonical by source-kind priority (`entra`/`intune`/`ad`/`polaris-agent` (1) > `fortiswitch` (2) > `fortiap` (3) > `fortigate-firewall` (4) > `fortigate-endpoint` (5) > `manual` (6) > no sources (7); tiebreak by most-recent `lastSeen` then `updatedAt`), and merges every sibling into the canonical inside a single `$transaction`. The pick policy + merge transaction live in assetGhostMergeService (decideDuplicateHostnameGroup / mergeDuplicateHostnameGhost) — the job owns the schedule, group query, dry-run, and logging. Side-table transfer with delete-on-conflict on `AssetMacAddress` / `AssetAssociatedIp` / `AssetIpHistory` / `AssetFortigateSighting`; cascade-delete handles `AssetSource` / LLDP / wireless / `AssetInterfaceOverride` / pending `Conflict` rows pointing at the ghost / `AssetDependencyParent` rows on either side (the 60s `dependencyReconciler` tick recomputes from authoritative topology). The ghost's sample/rollup time-series + `AssetCustomWidgetSample` are NOT cascaded (no FK since migration `20260615000000`) — they orphan and age out via `drop_chunks`, since a cascade delete would decompress their TimescaleDB chunks into bloat (prod incident 2026-06-08). `AssetCustomWidgetSample` is now a standalone managed hypertable (migration `20260621000000`) pruned on the system-info umbrella window, so its orphaned rows age out the same way. Scalar-field absorption fills empty canonical fields from the ghost (macAddress, ipAddress, serialNumber, manufacturer, model, os, osVersion, assignedTo, notes, learnedLocation, acquiredAt) and keeps the more-recent `lastSeen`; tags union-merge. Tie-safety: groups where two rows are tied at the same tier AND have non-null disagreeing primary MACs are skipped as "genuinely two devices" and logged at warn with the asset ids for operator review. Dry-run mode via `POLARIS_GHOST_MERGE_DRY_RUN=1` env var — logs every decision (canonical id + ghost ids + source kinds + tiers) without writing; use on first deploy to review choices, then unset and let the next cycle actually merge. Writes one `asset.duplicate_merged` Event per merged group for the UI audit trail. Idempotent — re-runs without the env var find zero candidates once convergent. No marker; the query itself is the converge check.
│   │   ├── detectDuplicateIpAssets.ts  # Duplicate-address sweep — first run 45s after boot, then every 10 min; scheduler role only (`runsSchedulers`), so a split-role install runs one grouped scan for the fleet rather than one per monitor replica. Thin wrapper over `reconcileDuplicateIpConflicts()` in services/duplicateIpConflictService.ts (business rule 40). A sweep rather than a write-time hook because an asset’s IP is staged by ~17 projection write sites and a duplicate is a property of the FLEET, not of the write that made it; one query answers it for every address at once and a clean fleet issues zero writes. │       ├── cidr.ts                  # CIDR parsing, contains(), overlap(); isPrivateIpv4 + isLoopbackIp + isPrivateOrLoopbackIp (RFC1918/loopback source-IP tests, v6-mapped-v4 aware) + isRfc1918Cidr (is a CIDR fully inside private space — the API-docs allow-list rule) + normalizeAllowlistCidr (canonical IPv4 CIDR / bare-IP→/32, IPv6 rejected) + ipMatchesAnyCidr (source-IP ∈ any CIDR) backing the Dash custom source-IP scope
│       ├── dashConfig.ts            # Dash wallboard listener config: resolveDashPort() (POLARIS_DASH_PORT, default 3001) + resolveDashBind() (forced 127.0.0.1 in proxy mode; POLARIS_DASH_BIND otherwise). Consumed by dashServer + the nginx renderer callers ({{DASH_PORT}}).
│       ├── ipScope.ts              # The shared source-IP scope resolver — ipInScope / isIpScope / describeIpScope over "all" | "custom" (allow-list CIDRs) | "rfc1918" (private + loopback) | "loopback" (this host only). ONE copy behind the Dash wallboard gate (dashServer.isSourceAllowed), the local-login gate (loginAccessService) AND the API-docs gate (apiDocsAccessService), because the subtleties must not drift: ::ffff: v4-mapped sources unwrap, a real IPv6 source never matches a v4 entry, an EMPTY custom list fails CLOSED. Each surface narrows the vocabulary at its own edge (dash/login Zod enums exclude "loopback"; the docs scope excludes "all"). Only as trustworthy as req.ip — i.e. as the deployment's trust-proxy hop count.
│       ├── securityHeaders.ts       # buildHelmetOptions() — the shared helmet CSP/HSTS/referrer options used by BOTH src/app.ts and src/dash/dashServer.ts (extracted so the map-tile img hosts + weather/fonts connect-src can never drift between the two surfaces).
│       ├── safeRedirect.ts          # `safeNextPath(raw)` — reduces an untrusted post-login `?next=` to a same-origin relative path. REBUILDS the path from parsed URL components (pathname+search+hash against a fixed opaque base) rather than returning the caller's own string after a prefix blocklist, so no smuggled authority (`//evil`, `/\evil`, an absolute URL) can survive whatever the input was; falls back to `/` for anything off-origin and for `/login.html` (which would read to the operator as a failed login). Sole consumer: auth.ts `GET /entra-proxy/login`. Pinned by tests/unit/safeRedirect.test.ts.
│       ├── geo.ts                   # Pure (no I/O) `pointInPolygon(point, polygon)` ray-cast test on [lat,lng] pairs. Used by `mapRegionService` to compute which firewalls fall inside an operator-drawn polygon.
│       ├── geoPolygon.ts            # Pure polygon-VS-polygon geometry — the sibling `geo.ts` deliberately does NOT grow into (that file is a 112-line leaf on the discovery hot path). `polygonContainsPolygon(outer, inner)` answers `contains | overlaps | disjoint | equal-area | approximate`, and is what makes map-region LEVELS derivable from nesting. Three tests in order, all three needed: a bbox prefilter (rejects nearly every real pair in O(1)); every vertex of `inner` inside-or-on `outer`, early-exiting on the first outside vertex (that early exit is why a rejected candidate costs ONE point test rather than V_inner of them); and no edge of `inner` PROPERLY crossing an edge of `outer` — because all-vertices-inside is wrong for a CONCAVE outer, where a child can have every vertex inside a C-shaped parent while its body cuts straight across the notch. `pointRingPosition` supplies the `"boundary"` answer `pointInPolygon` documents as unspecified, and containment counts boundary as inside, so a child drawn with a vertex snapped onto its parent's edge is still a child; `segmentsProperlyCross` returns FALSE for a shared endpoint and for collinear overlap for the same reason (a child sharing an edge with its parent is nesting, not overlap). `equal-area` (within `AREA_EPS_REL`) is what makes containment a STRICT partial order and therefore acyclic — no pair can each contain the other, so levels can never cycle. A shared accumulating `WorkBudget` bounds one hierarchy build (200 regions at the 1000-vertex schema cap is ~10⁸ primitive ops); on exhaustion containment degrades to the bounding-box answer marked `approximate` rather than stalling a request, and deterministically so as long as the caller iterates candidate pairs in a stable order. Areas are square DEGREES — comparison-only, never surfaced to an operator. Antimeridian crossing is out of scope, the same documented limitation `geo.ts` carries.
│       ├── regionHierarchy.ts       # Pure derivation of the map-region containment FOREST and a level per region from polygon nesting alone (`buildRegionHierarchy({id, polygon}[])` → `{byId, rootIds, maxLevel, warnings, truncated}`). Input is ids + polygons ONLY — no names, no colors — so it stays testable and can't drift into a service. **Carries BOTH `depth` and `level`, and they are not interchangeable:** `depth` counts inward from the outermost ring (0 = top-level) and is always gap-free, while `level` counts outward from the leaves (1 = contains nothing) and CAN have gaps — a parent holding one bare leaf and one 3-deep chain is L4 with children at L1 and L3 and no L2 beneath it. `level` is the operator's mental model and what the region tree displays; `depth`/`ancestorIds` is what code routes on, so **never compute a routing target with `level + 1` arithmetic**. Two swappable `LevelRule`s: `levelByDepth` (the default — ANY container is strictly above its children, the only reading where level implies containment rank, which is what "operators get the leaf, managers get the container" needs) and `levelByBranchingCount` (the literal "more than one child" wording, kept and tested but NOT default because it puts a single-child wrapper at the same level as its child, so level can no longer tell a front-line region from its manager wrapper). Immediate parent = the SMALLEST container; each unordered pair is tested exactly once with the larger ring as the candidate container (a strictly-contained ring always has strictly smaller area), which is also what makes a budget-degraded result deterministic. Warnings are `overlap | duplicate | degenerate | self-intersecting | ambiguous-parent | approximate | cap-exceeded` — and two of them need real geometry rather than the raw relation: `equal-area` alone cannot tell a genuine duplicate from two same-sized regions in different states (which must warn about NOTHING) or from two same-sized regions that partly overlap, and `overlaps` alone fires on a child sitting in a concave parent's notch, which never touches it. A real edge crossing is the only signal reported as overlap. Above `MAX_HIERARCHY_REGIONS` (500) the forest is not computed at all and every region comes back flat with `truncated: true`.
│       ├── entraClientCredentials.ts # `buildClientCredentialsTokenRequest()` — the Entra ID client-credentials token REQUEST shape (URL + form body), shared by the Graph token fetch (entraIdService) and the Azure Resource Manager token fetch (azureArcService). The two transport policies (caching, error surfaces, secret scrubbing) deliberately stay in their services. Agent code signing was a third consumer until it moved to an internal-CA PKCS#12 keystore, which mints no token at all.
│       ├── bearerToken.ts           # Shared bearer-token mint format: `TOKEN_PREFIX` ("polaris_") + `generateRawToken()` (32 base64url chars) + `TOKEN_INDEX_PREFIX_LEN` — one contract for both token stores (apiTokenService + agentTokenService, which carried byte-identical private copies).
│       ├── loginRedirect.ts        # "Send me back where I was going" across a login. `rememberLoginTarget(req,res,target)` drops a 10-minute, NON-HttpOnly `polaris_next` cookie (sanitized through safeNextPath first, and skipped for "/") when app.ts bounces an unauthenticated request off a protected page; `takeLoginTarget(req,res)` reads it back and ALWAYS clears it, falling back to "/". A cookie rather than a `?next=` parameter because three of the five login paths (SAML, OIDC, Entra App Proxy) return on a URL Polaris does not control AND call `req.session.regenerate()`, which drops anything stashed in the session. Not HttpOnly because login.js reads it after a local/TOTP login — safe because safeNextPath reduces it to a same-origin PATH and refuses /login.html. `readCookie(header, name)` is the one-value cookie lookup (Polaris runs no cookie-parser). Consumed by auth.ts's SAML/OIDC/entra-proxy callbacks and by public/js/login.js. Business rule 25.
│       ├── alertEmailTemplate.ts   # The DEFAULT alert email, expressed as a `{token}` TEMPLATE rather than server-side string building: `DEFAULT_ALERT_SUBJECT` / `DEFAULT_ALERT_TEXT` / `DEFAULT_ALERT_HTML` + `defaultAlertEmailTemplate()`. The same strings are (a) what `buildComposedEmail` falls back to for any piece an operator left blank and (b) what the automation wizard prefills into a new Notify action (schema.defaultEmailTemplate) — so the email in the inbox is the text on the screen. HTML is table-based with inline styles and no remote assets (Outlook renders through Word; images are blocked by default). `pruneEmptyRows` / `pruneEmptyDivs` / `pruneEmptyTextLines` / `pruneDeadLinks` run on the RENDERED body (the first three at compose time, `pruneEmptyChartSection` at DELIVERY time in notificationDeliveryService, after `substituteChartTokens` has decided which charts had data): every {asset.*} token renders "" when unset, so a device Polaris knows little about would otherwise mail a table of blank cells, an empty headline, an `<a href="">` button that reloads the reader's page, and a "LAST HOUR" heading over nothing. **`pruneEmptyRows` must never match across a nested `<table>` or a second `<tr>`** — its pattern is anchored so the match FAILS at a container row rather than matching-and-skipping it (skipping consumed the first fact row with it): a container `<tr><td>` plus the first fact row's empty value cell reads as a two-cell label/value pair, and dropping that span took the facts table's opening `<table>` tag with it, reparenting the surviving rows onto the 600px card and closing the card early at the now-unmatched `</table>` — "Last hour" and the buttons rendered OUTSIDE the box on every alert whose first fact row was empty, i.e. every alert about Polaris itself. Facts rows are built by one local `fact(label, value)` helper with a FIXED 140px label column (auto layout sized the columns from content, so a body down to "Automation"/"Raised" gave the labels most of the width and wrapped the values into a gutter) and print `{time.local}`, not `{time}`. The header is TWO COLUMNS — the severity line / subject / trigger sentence on the left, `{brand.header}` (alertBrandService's letterhead) right-aligned opposite it. That makes the header a two-cell row, i.e. exactly the label/value shape `pruneEmptyRows` deletes, and on an install with no letterhead the second cell is empty; the one-cell `<table>` wrapped around `{brand.header}` is what fails that pattern at the row (a span containing a `<table>` never matches, and a one-cell row is never a candidate), so the headline can't be deleted along with the empty letterhead. Keep it there.
│       ├── alertSubject.ts        # What an alert is ABOUT, as a label (pure): `POLARIS_SELF_LABEL` ("Polaris server") + `eventSubjectLabel(resourceType, resourceName)`. Most alerts are about a device and the subject is its hostname; an EVENT-triggered alert fires on whatever the audit Event happened to, and the seeded system automations (capacity, backups, updates) fire on `resourceType: "system"` Events that carry NO resourceName — the resource IS this install. Those alerts had no subject at all: a blank headline, a subject line reading "[WARNING]  — Capacity severity escalated", and nothing saying the alert was about the Polaris server rather than somebody's switch. Named here rather than at the call site because three fields must agree on it — the `{asset}` token, the stored `Notification.assetHostname` the in-app/mobile lists render, and the event-path cooldown key (which dedupes on assetId-or-hostname and would stop matching across ticks if the stored row and the in-batch key disagreed). An unnamed resource of any other type stays "" — the row prunes rather than inventing a subject. "server" and not `triggerSubject`'s "Polaris host": that phrase reads naturally as a possessive mid-sentence, but as a standalone inbox subject it invites reading as a monitored machine named Polaris.
│       ├── sparklineSvg.ts         # Pure SVG line charts for the alert email (`sparklineSvg(points, opts)`, `seriesStats`, `formatReading`). Percentage metrics pin the axis to 0–100 so two messages are comparable; open-ended metrics get 10% headroom; a flat line still gets a band, a single sample renders as a dot, and an empty window says "no data in this window" instead of drawing a blank box a reader mistakes for a blocked image. The x-axis spans the WINDOW, not the samples. `alarmSpans` shades where a sensor raised its own alarm bit; `failSpans` shades where polls FAILED and additionally splits the series into runs — each gap bridged by a `<linearGradient>` stroke that fades out and back in, so an outage never renders as a straight interpolated line through the minutes nothing answered, and the fill closes at each run's own extent rather than under the gap. No text measurement and no external fonts — resvg has neither.
│       ├── triggerSummary.ts       # "What fired, and what the reading was", in the wizard's own words: `triggerSummary({trigger, value, dimensionLabel?, sensorUnit?})` → "Response time (median over 5 minutes) is 760 ms", plus `triggerSubject` and `humanDuration`. Deliberately mirrors `triggerSentence` / `AGG_PHRASE` / `humanDuration` / `CMP_PHRASE` in public/js/automations-wizard.js and `comparatorPhrases` in buildSchemaCatalog — an operator who reads "median over 5 minutes" while building the automation must read the same phrase in the email it sends. Three behaviours worth knowing: a hardware sensor states its OWN unit (the METRIC_META "(sensor unit)" placeholder is never printed), `hwSensorAlarm` reads as a STATE ("is in ALARM" / "is OK") because "is 1" means nothing to a reader, and a reading that isn't available falls back to the CONDITION ("is above 60") rather than a bare subject, which reads as a broken template. It speaks for every trigger type, not just metrics: a device-state trigger reads through the builder's `FIELD_META` label ("Monitor status is down", never the `monitorStatus` column name — that sentence heads the most-sent alert in the product), and an event/change trigger names what ACTUALLY happened over what was configured ("integration.discover.error on FMG-Ashfield" rather than "an audit event matching integration.discover.* occurred"), taking `eventAction` / `eventResource` from the engine's event tail. Pure; fills the `{trigger.summary}` token.
│       ├── alertSeverity.ts        # How ALERT severities COMPARE (the colour counterpart is severityStyle.ts below): `ALERT_SEVERITY_RANK`, `alertSeverityRank(sev)` (0 for absent/unrecognized — an unknown severity must not out-rank a critical nor crash a list render), `higherAlertSeverity(a, b)` (ties keep `a`). Pure, and a util rather than a service because three consumers need it — the NOC feeds' severity-first sort, `activeAlertSummaryByAsset` behind the Assets list's alert indicator, and the asset slide-over's Alerts tab. nocDashboardService re-exports `ALERT_SEVERITY_RANK` under its old name (it was exported from there first). Mirrored browser-side by `_alertSevRank` in public/js/assets.js, pinned by tests/unit/assetAlertIndicator.test.ts.
│       ├── severityStyle.ts        # Severity → colour for every surface that paints an alert OUTSIDE the browser: `severityHex(sev)` (no "#", the shape Teams MessageCard themeColor wants) + `severityCss(sev)`. Shared by webhookChannel, the alert email builder and the public /ack page; in-browser surfaces keep using the `.badge-level-*` / `.sev-*` classes in styles.css. Also carries the SEPARATE **down-state palette** — `downSeverityHex(sev)` / `downSeverityCss(sev)`, the colour a `down` monitor state is drawn in per severity (business rule 36): Down is not inherently red, red is what `critical` looks like. Deliberately not the alert-wide `SEVERITY_HEX` above, which colours a whole alert where nothing competes; these land on a response-time chart already spending amber on a below-threshold miss, blue on a recovering probe and grey on a dependency-explained one, so each value is pulled deeper than the neighbour it sits beside. `critical` stays `#d32f2f` so a default install is unchanged; an absent or unrecognized severity falls back to it. Mirrored browser-side by `DOWN_SEV_COLOR` in public/js/chart-severity.js and pinned to it by tests/unit/downSeverityColor.test.ts.
│       ├── prismaTextFilter.ts      # `buildPrismaTextFilter(field, value, op, {nullable})` — the TableSF text-column operator contract (contains/not_contains/empty/is_not_empty) → Prisma where-level fragment; nullable columns get a null arm. Shared by events.ts + assets.ts (previously two near-identical builders).
│       ├── sleep.ts                 # THE promise-setTimeout `sleep(ms)` — replaced four byte-identical private copies (arpPrimeService, winrm, queueService, reclaimBloatedChunks) + the dbRetry inline. `sleepWithAbort` (fortimanagerService) and `sleepSync` (certInfo) are deliberately separate.
│       ├── text.ts                  # Tiny shared string/param helpers: `truncate(s, max=200)` (display ellipsis — was three private copies) + `csvParam(raw)` (comma-separated query param → trimmed array | undefined — was five route-local implementations).
│       ├── assetSourceTags.ts       # Asset-tag identity prefixes (`entra:` / `ad:` / `ad-guid:` / `sid:`) — cross-file protocol values written by the discovery sync (discoveryEngine.ts) and parsed back by conflict resolution (conflictResolutionService.ts); were duplicate const sets in both files.
│       ├── tlsDispatcher.ts         # `insecureTlsDispatcher()` — lazily-created singleton undici Agent with `connect.rejectUnauthorized:false`, passed as the fetch `dispatcher` by fgRequest (fortigateService) and rpcAttempt (fortimanagerService) when the integration's `verifySsl === false`. Scopes the TLS relaxation to exactly the opted-in connections — replaced the process-global NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED flip, which raced parallel query chains and could disable verification for unrelated in-flight TLS in the same process.
│       ├── chassisIdentity.ts       # Pure "is this still the same FortiGate?" decision behind business rule 41. `classifyChassis(stored, discovered, clusterSerials)` → unknown / learn / same / replaced, and `verdictWritesSerial` says which of those may write `Subnet.fortigateSerial`. TRI-STATE both ways: an absent stored serial LEARNS (a first sighting is not a swap, which is why no migration backfills the column) and an unreadable DISCOVERED serial is UNKNOWN and constrains nothing (one failed CMDB read would otherwise declare the whole fleet replaced). The comparison is membership in the reporting device's own chassis SET, not equality with one value, or every HA failover would report a replacement — and that set is per DEVICE, since a chassis re-registered under another FMG device entry is genuinely a replacement for this subnet.
│       ├── chunk.ts                 # chunkArray(items, size) — the array batching behind every chunked $transaction / paced Promise.all fan-out (replaced 15 hand-rolled slice(i, i+N) loops, 2026-08 audit). Error semantics stay with the caller.
│       ├── concurrency.ts           # mapWithConcurrency / mapSettledWithConcurrency -- the bounded-concurrency mapper (2026-08 dedup of four hand-rolled pools). NOT for producer-fed pools: fortimanagerService discovery dispatch semaphore stays custom (two concurrent producers, no items list).
│       ├── fortinetDetectedDevice.ts # Shared post-fetch processing of two FortiOS monitor tables the FMG-proxied and direct-REST discovery paths fetch over different transports: processDetectedDeviceRows (switch-controller/detected-device → switch MAC table + AP→switch-port uplink pairing + FortiSwitch base-MAC stamping) and processArpRows (network/arp → discovery ARP table, all-zero/broadcast MACs skipped). Type-only imports from fortimanagerService.
│       ├── fortinetParentKey.ts     # THE resolution order for "which Asset is this FortiSwitch/FortiAP's parent?". `fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate` holds FortiManager's DEVICE NAME, which is NOT the gate's configured hostname (what Asset.hostname is projected from) — every consumer used to compare the two, so on installs where they diverge switches/APs resolved to NO parent (prod 2026-08-12: dependency suppression never fired, so a FortiGate in a maintenance window left its switches reading "Down" not "Dep. Down"; the Device Map drew the gate with no children; region membership + subnet propagation + interface auto-monitor all skipped them). Order: `controllerSerial` (definitive, stamped by discovery from 2026-08) → the gate's OWN `fortinetTopology.deviceName` (FMG's name for it, correct on pre-fix data so no re-discovery needed) → hostname (the historical match, kept for gates whose deviceName stamp predates the field) → the name as a serial (a FortiSwitch switch-id IS its serial, which is what an AP's LLDP table reports as parentSwitch). Exports the pure resolver (buildInfraParentIndex / resolveInfraParentAsset), the stamp readers (readControllerStamp / readParentSwitchStamp / readFirewallDeviceName), and the query-builders the Prisma consumers share (controllerStampWhereOr / topologyStampWhereOr / parentAssetWhereOr / controllerIdentityKeys). Consumers: dependencyTreeService, topologyGraphService, routes/map.ts, peerInferredLldpService, autoMonitorInterfacesService, mapRegionService, connectionPathService. NOT for the second class of `controllerFortigate` consumer — anything ADDRESSING an FMG/FortiOS API (monitoringService parent-FortiGate polling, the discovery decommission sweeps, infraDhcpBinding, descriptionSyncService's transport grouping, the Sources column) must keep using the device NAME.
│       ├── fortinetRestCredential.ts # A per-asset `restapi` Credential, mapped onto the auth half of a FortiOS REST call. Exists because every FortiOS collector assembles its request through `buildFortinetConfig()`, which read the INTEGRATION's token and nothing else — fleet-wide by construction ("must be the same across all managed FortiGates"), so a fleet where each gate carries its own api-user could not be polled over REST at all, while the asset modal had been offering a REST API credential picker on every `rest_api` stream the whole time. `pickRestApiCredential(...chain)` takes the first `restapi`-typed row out of `asset.<stream>Credential ?? asset.monitorCredential` (type-filtered: the asset default is usually an SNMP community, and authenticating a REST call with it fails in a way that reads as a broken token); the class-override tier is deliberately not consulted, a credential shared by a whole asset class being the fleet-wide token this exists to escape. `restApiCredentialAuth(config)` maps it to `{apiUser, apiToken, verifySsl, port?}` — **auth plus port and TLS verification only, never the host**: the `baseUrl` is required by `validateRestApiConfig` and is what the credential's own Test button dials, but honouring it here would let one credential mistakenly selected on twenty gates poll ONE device and file its CPU under all twenty. A wrong port is a connection error an operator can read; a wrong host is a mis-attribution that looks exactly like real data. `verifyTls` (credential) → `verifySsl` (FortiGateConfig), both defaulting to NOT verifying, as both sides always have
│       ├── object.ts                # asObject(v) — shallow-copy a non-null object, {} otherwise (the masked-config merge helper shared by agentSigningService + notificationChannelService).
│       ├── secretMask.ts            # THE secret-mask sentinel: `SECRET_MASK` ("••••••••") + `isMaskedSecret()` (bullet-run detector) shared by every secret-bearing surface (credentials, integrations, delivery channels, agent signing, LDAP/OIDC auth settings, event-archive settings) for the mask-on-read / preserve-on-masked-echo round-trip. `LEGACY_ASTERISK_MASK` ("********") is accepted ONLY by the LDAP/OIDC merge paths (pre-consolidation glyph) — never extend asterisk recognition to other surfaces.
│       ├── errors.ts                # AppError class with httpStatus
│       ├── logger.ts                # Structured logging (pino)
│       ├── assetInvariants.ts       # Write-time Asset invariants: clampAcquiredToLastSeen (acquiredAt ≤ lastSeen) + bumpLastSeen — the write path for Asset.lastSeen/lastSeenSource (no-regress advance + provenance stamp; every discovery/merge/conflict/presence writer routes through it). For monitored assets, bumpLastSeen refuses discovery-origin sources (discovery/device-inventory/dhcp-lease) — the monitor probe is the presence authority, stamping "probe" via the probePatchBuffer hot path
│       ├── icmpPing.ts              # pingHost(host, timeoutMs) — single-echo ICMP via the system `ping` binary. Shared by monitoringService's probeIcmp and presenceVerificationService's ping fallback
│       ├── burstPing.ts             # BATCHED ICMP BURST measurement — `burstPing(targets[])` returns per-target {sent, received, avgRttMs} so packet loss is a real ratio of PACKETS rather than a ratio of status-poll outcomes (which can only read in steps of 1/N over the window's N polls, and shares its evidence with down detection). Two backends behind one signature: **fping** when it is on PATH — one process per BURST_CHUNK (500) targets, bounded by BURST_COUNT x BURST_PERIOD_MS rather than by host count, so a 2000-asset sweep costs 4 spawns instead of 2000 — and a bounded fan-out of per-host `burstPingHost` (icmpPing.ts) when it is not. fping is OPTIONAL because two supported install targets cannot have it: RHEL ships it only via EPEL and Windows Server has no build, so deploy/setup-*.sh install it best-effort and the fallback keeps loss correct (just slower — measured at ~3.3s per host on Windows, whose `ping` paces at a fixed ~1s per echo with no interval flag, vs ~1s on POSIX). `suggestedSweepIntervalSec(count, hasFping)` is what the sweep scheduler reads for its floor rather than assuming 60s — fping is ~constant-time in fleet size, the fallback is linear over FALLBACK_CONCURRENCY. `detectFping()` probes once per process and caches BOTH answers. A target ABSENT from the returned map was never successfully attempted (unresolvable name, no `ping` binary) and must NOT be counted as loss — only "asked and heard nothing" is. `parseFpingOutput` / `parsePingSummary` are exported and pinned by tests/unit/burstPing.test.ts: their failure mode is silent and INVERTED (a parser that stops matching reports zero rows, and a fleet with no parseable loss data reads as a fleet with no packet loss). Decides nothing about an asset — ICMP does not authenticate the device it reaches, so a burst informs a ratio and never moves monitorStatus. **`pingTargets` is the STATUS-PROBE shape**, as distinct from the uniform loss sweep: it takes per-target timeouts and runs one fping per DISTINCT `probeTimeoutMs` (`bucketByTimeout`, fastest bucket first so a 30s outlier cannot hold up the fleet's verdict). `count` defaults to 1 and that default is load-bearing — down is defined in missed POLLS (rule 30), so extra echoes here would redefine what a missed poll means. A duplicate target inside one bucket collapses; the SAME target in two different buckets is kept, because those assets are entitled to different timeouts. A nonsense timeout falls back to the default rather than dropping the host, since silently not probing an asset is the worst failure available
│       ├── httpCheck.ts             # THE decision core of the `http` polling method — an operator-defined HTTP GET health check (`normalizeHttpPath` / `defaultHttpPort` / `resolveHttpTarget` / `statusAccepted` / `bodyMatches` / `evaluateHttpCheck` / `MAX_BODY_BYTES`). Pure, so the verdict is unit-testable without a socket; `probeHttp` in monitoringService owns only the transport. The check DEFINITION lives on an `http`-typed Credential (scheme / port / path / expected status / expected body / match mode / auth), which is what lets one "GET /healthz expect OK" row cover a fleet and stay selectable at the asset, class-override and integration tiers; `Asset.httpCheckPath` overrides just the path for the one device whose endpoint sits elsewhere — and a BLANK override means "no override", NOT "/", so clearing the asset field returns the device to the credential rather than silently repointing it at the web root. Four decisions carry the feature. **The body match is the load-bearing half**: a web server that has lost its backend still completes the handshake and still returns 200 with an error page, which is exactly what ICMP and an SNMP `sysUpTime` GET cannot see — so a non-matching 200 FAILS with the missing content named. The `failOnMismatch` toggle that used to let a mismatch pass is gone (stripped on save): a widget records an outcome and an automation decides what "down" means, so a mismatch stored as a pass would make `expectBody` decorative. A laxer rule = leave `expectBody` empty. **Status is judged before content**, because a 401 is a broken credential rather than missing content and blaming the body sends the operator to the wrong field. **Redirects are never followed** — a 302 to a login page is the single most common way an HTTP health check reports "up" about a device serving nothing; an operator who wants the 3xx sets `expectStatus` to it. **The body is capped** at MAX_BODY_BYTES (64 KB) and the request torn down at the cap, which bounds both a device streaming a log file at the check path and the text an operator-authored `regex` runs against — that pattern is not analyzed for backtracking (nothing static can be), so the cap is what keeps a pathological one from wedging a monitor worker; `contains` is the default for the same reason, and a truncated miss says so, since "not found in the first 64 KB" is a different finding from "not found". The regex is COMPILED at credential save (`validateHttpConfig`), because an invalid pattern otherwise fails once per asset per interval forever with the operator finding out from a probe error column. Also holds the **Test Connection diagnostics** shape (`HttpProbeDiagnostics` / `bodyExcerpt` / `describeHttpTarget` / `MAX_EXCERPT_CHARS` = 4 KB): the request line as dialed, status, content-type, bytes read, cap flag, match verdict and a body excerpt, so an operator can pick their expected string out of what the device actually returns. Filled by `probeHttp` ONLY when handed an out-param (the `probeAsset(assetId, out?)` precedent), so the monitor hot path allocates none of it; surfaced as `httpDiagnostics` on `POST /credentials/test`. Response headers beyond `content-type` are deliberately NOT returned — a full dump would put a live `Set-Cookie` into the modal — and the body never reaches the audit Event
│       ├── probeTarget.ts           # Validation for an operator-TYPED credential-test target (`normalizeProbeTarget` / `isValidHostname`) — the "enter an IP or hostname" half of Test Connection, as opposed to picking an asset and borrowing its address. Pure, and separate from cidr.ts because it is not IP math: it accepts hostnames too, and only the IP branch defers to `isValidIpAddress` so that math stays in one place. **It REFUSES rather than salvages**, which is the whole design: operators paste `https://10.1.2.3:8443/healthz` out of a browser bar, and trimming it down to the host would silently drop exactly the parts configured ELSEWHERE — scheme and port come from the `http` credential's `useHttps`/`port` (or the transport default: 161 SNMP, 22 SSH, 5985/5986 WinRM) and the path from the credential — so the test would dial something other than what is on screen and then attribute the result to the credential. A URL, an embedded port, a path, embedded `user@`, or a query string each get a message naming which field already owns that value. IPv6 is the one legal use of a colon, so `looksLikeIpv6` (bracketed, or 2+ colons) gates the port check — a malformed v6 literal still falls through to "not a valid IP address or hostname" rather than being mis-reported as carrying a port. Never throws; the caller renders the reason inline like a probe failure
│       ├── digestAuth.ts            # HTTP Digest Access Authentication (RFC 7616) for the HTTP check — `parseDigestChallenge` / `buildDigestAuthorization` / `authSchemesOffered` / `newCnonce`. Pure except `newCnonce` (the cnonce and nc are INJECTED), so the hash arithmetic is unit-testable against the published RFC 2617 §3.5 and RFC 7616 §3.9.1 vectors — which is the point of testing it at all: a digest client that computes a self-consistent but wrong hash authenticates against nothing, and a test asserting its own output would pass just as happily. Exists because nothing in the dependency set speaks Digest (undici included) while the devices that need it are exactly the ones the HTTP Check was built for — a camera, a PDU, an older BMC; Axis OS answers VAPIX with `WWW-Authenticate: Digest` and 11+ disables Basic by default, so a Bearer/Basic-only client fails to authenticate against a device it can otherwise reach perfectly. Three decisions. **Digest is a HANDSHAKE, not a header** — the response hash is keyed on a server-issued nonce, so the request cannot be pre-authenticated: `probeHttp` fires bare, reads the 401 challenge, and re-fires ONCE, never a loop, because a server that rejects a correctly-computed response will reject it again and retrying past that turns a wrong password into a request amplifier aimed at the device. The second request inherits what REMAINS of the probe timeout rather than a fresh one, so a slow device can't hold a monitor worker for twice the configured window. **The nonce is deliberately NOT cached**: a cache keyed by (host, realm) would cut the steady state back to one request, but it has to carry a strictly-increasing `nc` per nonce, and a stale or raced counter reads to the server as a REPLAY — i.e. it trades a cheap doubling of a cheap request for an auth failure that only appears under concurrency. **`qop=auth-int` and unknown algorithms THROW rather than guess**, so the operator reads "auth-int is not supported" instead of a second opaque 401; MD5 / MD5-sess / SHA-256 / SHA-256-sess / SHA-512-256 are computed, and an absent `algorithm` means MD5 per the RFC. `authSchemesOffered` exists for the diagnostic that makes a 401 actionable — a device asking for Digest while the credential is set to Basic is otherwise indistinguishable from a wrong password
│       ├── lossSweep.ts             # WHO gets burst-pinged and HOW OFTEN — the pure decision layer for the ICMP loss sweep (the measurement itself is burstPing.ts). REPLACES the retired lossSampler.ts, and the difference IS the feature: the old sampler ran only while an asset was `warning` or `recovering`, and that window was itself the sampling bias that got it disabled a day after shipping (business rule 29d — it sampled precisely when probes were already failing, so failure periods were oversampled and the alert's reading diverged visibly from the wall-clock average its own chart drew). The sweep is UNIFORM instead: every eligible asset, every cycle, the same burst, whatever state it is in — affordable only because the pinger is batched. `lossSweepIncludes(asset, eff)` excludes exactly three things: not `monitored` (which covers rule 10's four unmonitorable statuses), `maintenance` (the one status that KEEPS monitored true while polling stops, rule 16), and `responseTimePolling === "disabled"` (rule 30 already reads that as "do not reach out to this device"). It deliberately KEEPS two things the sampler excluded: `down` assets (the old corroboration argument — an ICMP reply from a squatter dragging a dead device's loss down — was load-bearing only while loss shared a stream with down detection; the sweep never calls recordProbeResult and the engine's answering gate already blocks a down device from alerting — note the bursts fired during an outage are still SAMPLED, so the strip and the charts keep their resolution, but they are stamped `AssetMonitorSample.assetDown` and their whole failure run is excluded from the loss RATIO, business rule 29h) and dependency-suppressed assets (the old exclusion was a COST argument that batching retired; their failures are still marked explained via AssetMonitorSample.dependencyDown, rule 38b). `lossSweepTarget` picks ipAddress, else dnsName, else hostname. `lossSweepIsDue` is the cadence half; `resolveSweepIntervalSec` floors the operator's interval at what the installed pinger can actually finish, because publishing sweeps faster than they drain grows the queue without bound. `chunkForSweep` preserves order so a chunk INDEX is stable for a stable fleet — that is what lets publishMonitorSweepJob use it as a pg-boss singleton key, so a backed-up sweep COALESCES instead of piling on. LOSS_SWEEP_ENABLED ships TRUE, unlike the sampler it replaces: loss is measurably wrong without it, and a fix that ships switched off is a fix nobody gets
│       ├── monitorStatus.ts        # The monitor state vocabulary + the pure predicates that read it. `MonitorStatus` is the six-state union (up / warning / recovering / down / unknown / **passive**) plus `MONITOR_STATUS_LABELS` / `monitorStatusLabel()`, the ONE operator-facing name per state (`warning` renders as **Missed**, `unknown` as **Pending**), mirrored browser-side by `POLARIS_MONITOR_STATUS_LABELS` in `public/js/api.js` — it lives here because the union used to be spelled out in three places, which is how a sixth state gets added to two of them. `runsHeavyCadences(asset)` is the heavy-cadence gate shared by the two documented-lockstep due-set builders (`monitoringService.loadMonitorPassCandidates` and the pg-boss publisher in `jobs/monitorAssets`): `up` ⇒ true, plus `passive` whose `consecutiveFailures === 0`. That passive arm is load-bearing — a passive asset is never "up", so a bare `=== "up"` gate would stop telemetry / systemInfo / interfaces / storage / LLDP / processes for it and every chart on a passive device would silently go flat with nothing erroring. `isConfigStatusEdge(prev, next)` marks a transition into or out of `passive` as a CONFIGURATION edge rather than a device edge, which is what stops one rule save that rescopes 2000 assets from bursting 2000 `monitor.status_changed` Events and 2000 concurrent dependency propagations **The state machine itself lives here as of 2026-09-01**, as two pure functions the probe path CALLS rather than reimplements inline: `nextFailureBucket(cf, success, threshold, recoveryPolls)` — the leaky bucket of business rule 30, now with a CEILING, locking at `bucketCapFor(threshold, recoveryPolls)` (the larger of the missed-poll count and the automation's reset count, bounded by `MAX_MISSED_POLL_BUCKET` = 100) the moment a miss declares the outage — and `monitorStatusFor(cf, success, threshold)`, which reads `cf == 0` as up, an ANSWERED probe as recovering whatever the level, and a MISS as down at or above the threshold else warning. Two bugs closed together: unbounded, an overnight outage left `cf` around 480 and the asset owed 480 answered polls (eight hours of a down alert repeating and escalating after recovery); and with the answered branch below the threshold test, an answered probe during a deep outage read `down`, which no chart can paint on an `ok` point, so it came out the plain series green and an outage drew red then green then blue then green. Both are mirrored — not imported — by `replayProbeStates` in services/probeOutageService.ts and `replay` in public/js/monitor-states.js, pinned by tests/unit/monitorStatusStateMachine.test.ts (which now IMPORTS them rather than hand-copying, the copy having silently pinned a retired machine once already) and tests/unit/assetIntermittencyBar.test.ts. `owesRecoveryConfirmation` was REMOVED here in the same change: the cap serves the reset count through the drain, so the `Asset.awaitingRecoveryConfirm` bit it read is dormant.
│       ├── probeLossAnchor.ts      # The two halves of the packet-loss RECOVERY anchor (business rule 29b), pure. `stampsRecoveryAnchor(previousStatus, success)` is the WRITER's predicate — true only for a success out of `down`/`unknown`, the states a device leaves without having been answering, which covers both the usual recovery into `recovering` and the `failureThreshold === 1` jump straight to `up`; deliberately FALSE out of `warning`, because a lossy device sits in warning between failures and stamping there would restart the loss window every few probes and report ~0% forever. `effectiveLossAnchorMs(firstOkMs, recoveryMs)` is the READER's arithmetic — the later of the window's first success and the last outage's end, null when nothing answered — the JS mirror of probeLossQuery's `GREATEST("firstOk", "recoveredAt")` (Postgres GREATEST ignores NULLs; so does this), used by alertChartService's loss chart — for its CAPTION, the line being drawn over the whole window — so the emailed number and the reading that fired agree. Extracted because each is a one-liner whose failure mode is silent
│       ├── wildcard.ts             # `compileWildcard(pattern)` (shell-style `*`/`?` → an ANCHORED regex, regex metacharacters escaped) + `compilePattern(pattern, regex)` + `MAX_PATTERN_LENGTH`. Lived in autoMonitorInterfacesService until the contact device filter needed the same `matches` semantics — notificationTypes evaluates that tree and must not pull `db.js` in behind a pattern compile, so the pure half moved to a util and the service re-exports it for its existing importers (tag criteria, app-map discovery rules, storage auto-monitor, the integrations route) and their tests. The length cap bounds what one stored pattern can cost; on the raw-regex path that's a mitigation, not a cure — see the header for why that's a deliberate call.
│       ├── criteriaToCondition.ts  # Folds a flat `TagCriteria` blob forward into a nested condition tree (`criteriaToCondition(raw)` → `{condition, unconvertible[]}`), so a device filter written before the cutover opens in the shared builder with its rules intact — the `normalizeRuleToV2` pattern. TWO surfaces fold through it: `Contact.assetCriteria` → `assetCondition` and `Tag.criteria` → `assetCondition`. Criteria rules are ANDed → root `and`; values WITHIN a rule are ORed → an `or` subgroup (a single value stays a bare leaf); `exact`/`contains`/`pattern` → `equals`/`contains`/`matches`; subnet `cidrs` → `inCidr` leaves. `unconvertible` names any field with no tree equivalent — today just `integration`, which only an API caller could have written — and a NON-EMPTY list is the caller's signal to keep the flat blob, since converting would widen the coverage and dropping the rule would narrow it. Pure and dependency-free (its own minimal input shape, no service import).
│       ├── hardwareSensors.ts       # Hardware Sensors classification: classifyHardwareSensor(name, restType?) → {sensorClass, unit} (REST type wins, else name heuristic for FortiGate fgHwSensorTable rows: temperature/fan/voltage/current/optical/power/disk/other — optical and current are tested BEFORE the generic power pattern, since "SFP1 RX Power" contains "power" and would otherwise store its dBm reading unlabelled) + the SENSOR_CLASS_UNITS class→display-unit map (°C/RPM/V/A/dBm/W; power+other unitless) + normalizeFgAlarmStatus / normalizeRestAlarmStatus. Plus the ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB (RFC 3433) trio: `entityTypeColumnTrusted(typeCodes)` (a table reporting ONE type code across every row is defaulting, not describing — FortiSwitchOS stamps celsius(8) on optical, fan and voltage rows alike — so names classify instead; ≤1 row is trusted since there is nothing to be uniform with), `classifyEntitySensor({typeCode, unitsDisplay, descr, typeColumnTrusted})` which weighs evidence in descending quality (entPhySensorUnitsDisplay saying dBm → the type enum has no optical member, so this is the only reliable optical signal; then the type code when trusted; then the descr name heuristic; then the type code anyway — that last fallback is what keeps a FortiSwitch's unnamed `sensor-18` celsius row a temperature row), and `entityOperStatusToAlarm(oper)` mapping nonoperational(3)→"alarm", ok(1)→"ok", and unavailable(2)→NULL (an empty SFP cage reports unavailable; alarming on it would fire on every unused port). Dependency-free; consumed by the hardware-sensor collectors in monitoringService and re-exported as `sensorClassUnits` in the automation-builder schema (notificationTypes.buildSchemaCatalog) so the wizard's hwSensorValue unit hint matches what the samples store. Plus `alarmStatusToFlag(alarmStatus) → 0 | 1 | null`, the pure mapping behind the **`hwSensorAlarm`** automation metric: `"ok"`→0, `"alarm"`→1, an unrecognized non-empty status →1 (a claim that something is off-nominal, not missing data), NULL/blank →null. That null is load-bearing and business rule 24 turns on it — the FortiAP-controller path publishes no alarm bit and leaves the column NULL, and mapping that absence to 0 would assert health nothing ever verified. The ENTITY-SENSOR-MIB path DOES populate it now, from entPhySensorOperStatus via `entityOperStatusToAlarm`, with the same discipline: unavailable(2) stays NULL rather than becoming an alarm.
│       ├── stateProbes.ts           # STATE PROBES — the pure 0/1 mapping behind the `customStateValue` automation metric. A Manufacturer Profile widget with `widgetType="state"` points at a status-shaped OID (alarm bit, PSU present, fan-tray OK) and DECLARES how a raw reading becomes true: `StateMap {mode, values[], trueLabel, falseLabel, trueIsProblem}` over modes `nonzero` (default — the plain alarm bit) / `zero` (inverted health register) / `equals` / `notEquals` (SNMPv2 TruthValue, where true(1) is the GOOD state) / `gte` / `lte`. Declared rather than assumed because vendors disagree on polarity and some agents answer strings, so a bare `value >= 1` is wrong about as often as it's right. `evaluateStateMap(raw, map) → 0|1|null` compares numerically when both sides parse as numbers and case-insensitively as strings otherwise; **null means "no reading" and is load-bearing** — an absent/unreadable/incomparable row must not become 0, because 0 is a positive claim of health that would clear a live alert (and on a `trueIsProblem=false` probe would raise one about hardware that isn't there). `joinStateRows(values, labels, map)` joins the value walk with the optional `labelSymbol` walk on the shared OID index suffix so a table probe's rows are nameable ("TMP1 External", not ".14" — the index differs per model), dropping null rows. Plus `normalizeStateMap` (never throws — degrades to nonzero, used on the read path), `validateStateMap` (authoring-time 400s: a comparison mode with no operand would evaluate every reading false and look healthy forever), `stateLabel` / `stateIsProblem` / `describeStateMap`. Dependency-free; the single source of truth shared by the collector, the profile editor's validation, and the automation builder's labels.
│       ├── stats.ts               # Small numeric reducers for the notification engine's aggregation paths — today just `median(values)` (returns null on an empty set, mirroring how an empty window means "no reading" rather than 0; averages the two middle values on an even-length set; sorts a copy so the caller's array is never mutated). Its own util rather than inline in the engine because the engine aggregates in two structurally different places — the per-dimension asset_metric groups in `reduceReadings` and the flat host_metric row set in `resolveHostMetricReading` — and a twice-written median is exactly the kind of thing that goes subtly wrong (off-by-one on the even midpoint, sorting the caller's array in place).
│       ├── loginLockout.ts          # Per-username login-failure counter + temporary lockout
│       ├── backupPassword.ts        # Pure (no I/O) strength floor for the optional encrypted-backup passphrase. `validateBackupPassword(raw)` returns null for empty/whitespace (unencrypted backup is a legitimate choice), throws `{code:"WEAK_BACKUP_PASSWORD"}` for supplied-but-too-weak (< `BACKUP_MIN_PASSWORD_LEN`=12 chars or < 4 distinct chars), else returns the passphrase unchanged (no trim — spaces are valid key material). Called by `POST /server-settings/database/backup`; restore stays unvalidated (must accept whatever encrypted an existing file). 2026-06-03 review, finding M5.
│       ├── secretBox.ts            # Envelope encryption for secrets stored in JSON columns. `sealValue` / `openValue` / `isSealed` / `generateSecretKey` / `secretEncryptionEnabled`. AES-256-GCM, fresh 12-byte IV per value, key from `POLARIS_SECRET_KEY` (64 hex chars, or base64, or any longer passphrase hashed to 32 bytes — believing you have encryption when you do not is the worst outcome, so a pasted passphrase works rather than silently no-opping). Self-describing token `psec:v1:<iv>:<tag>:<ct>` so plaintext and sealed values coexist during the backfill and forever on un-keyed installs. When the key is UNSET, sealing is a NO-OP and values store as plaintext — deliberately the pre-2026-08 behavior, so an in-app update can never leave an install unable to reach its own FortiManager because a new env var appeared; the absence surfaces as the `secrets_key_unset` capacity watch reason plus a boot warning. `openValue` NEVER throws: a wrong/missing key logs once and returns `""`, so a key mismatch degrades to "this credential stopped authenticating" instead of an exception on every monitor tick.
│       ├── configSecretFields.ts   # Which JSON keys hold secrets, and the recursive walk over them. `SECRET_CONFIG_KEYS` is a NAME UNION rather than per-type lists (the three services keep their own per-type lists for MASKING): importing those vocabularies into db.ts would invert the dependency direction, and a per-type list that MISSES a field stores a real secret in plaintext silently, whereas a union that includes a field which happens not to be secret for some type merely encrypts a harmless value. `transformSecretFields(value, fn)` returns a NEW structure (Prisma args + results are shared with callers), recurses to a depth cap, and touches only string leaves under a secret key — so `monitorOverrideService`'s raw `integrations.config #>> '{fortigateMonitor,addAsMonitored}'` read, which bypasses the extension entirely, is unaffected. `secretJsonFieldFor(model)` names the column (`Setting` → `value`, the other three → `config`).
│       ├── pgEnv.ts                # Connection URL → libpq PG* env vars (`pgEnvFromDatabaseUrl`, `pgChildEnv`, `redactDatabaseUrl`). Exists because `pg_dump`/`psql` used to take the connection string as an ARGV element, which put the DB password in `ps aux` for the duration of every backup — and, since the backup route built the command as an interpolated shell string, into Node's `Command failed: <command>` message, which was being concatenated into an AppError and returned in the HTTP response body. Handles percent-encoded credentials (a password containing `@`/`/`/`:`), the `postgres://` alias, `sslmode` → `PGSSLMODE`, and Prisma's `?schema=` → `PGOPTIONS=-c search_path=` (libpq has no PGSCHEMA). Overwrites any inherited PG* var: a stray `PGDATABASE` silently dumping the wrong database is exactly the failure this prevents.
│       ├── crashHandlers.ts        # Process-level last-resort `unhandledRejection` / `uncaughtException` handlers, installed from src/index.ts BEFORE any subsystem imports so every role inherits them. Node 20 defaults to `--unhandled-rejections=throw` and the units run a bare `node dist/index.js`, so any escaped rejection terminates the process — previously with only Node's raw stack trace on stderr: no pino line, no role label, no metric, and `Restart=on-failure` bringing it straight back so a repeating crash was invisible outside journald. Does NOT keep the process alive (continuing past an unhandled rejection means running with unknown invariants); it makes the crash LEGIBLE — one structured fatal log naming the role and origin, one `polaris_process_crash_total{role,kind}` increment, then `exit(CRASH_EXIT_CODE=70)`, distinct from the `1` the boot-time config guards use so exit-code history separates "misconfigured, never started" from "was running, then died".
│       ├── netGuard.ts              # Pure (no I/O) SSRF guard for operator-supplied outbound hosts. `isBlockedOutboundHost(host)` / `assertOutboundHostAllowed(host)` block loopback / link-local (incl. 169.254.169.254 cloud metadata) / unspecified / multicast literals (and the `localhost` hostname + IPv4-mapped-IPv6 forms) while leaving RFC1918/ULA LAN device addresses — the normal integration target — allowed. Wired into every integration config schema carrying a `host` (FortiManager / FortiGate / Windows Server / Active Directory) via `refineConfigHost` superRefine, plus an explicit re-check on the loose-record update path in `integrations.ts`. Literal-only; DNS-rebinding is a documented residual (2026-06-03 security review, finding M4).
│       ├── locationCodes.ts         # Pure (no I/O) physical-location code grammar for the Device Map: parseLocationCodes(raw) extracts `a:`(area)/`b:`(building)/`f:`(floor)/`r:`(room)/`jb:`(junction box) tokens from a FortiSwitch/FortiAP admin description (keys case-insensitive, matched at start/after whitespace so `hub:` isn't a token; value runs to the next known token; duplicate key → last non-empty wins); resolveEffectiveLocation({description, deviceDescription}) returns the description's codes when it carries ANY (exclusively — no per-key fall-through, so a removed code leaves the group immediately) and falls back to the device description wholesale otherwise (Asset.notes is deliberately not a source — notes are operator-only and never inform the map); locationGroupKey(value) (trim/collapse/lowercase grouping key). Consumed by topologyGraphService.ts (the map topology GET's payload `location` per node).
│       ├── cableMembers.ts        # Pure (no I/O) pairing decision behind the Device Map's inter-switch physical-member expansion: `pairCableMembers(aSide, bSide)` takes each side's resolved member ports (each stamped `physical` + `down`) and returns the cable `lines`, the `unpaired` surplus, and the members `droppedDown` by link state. Two rules, both from one prod symptom — a single cable between two FortiSwitches drawn as TWO parallel teal lines naming the SAME far-end port (2026-08-24). (1) A physical port terminates exactly ONE cable, so a lone PHYSICAL member is never repeated across parallel lines; the prior expansion padded the short side by reusing its only member across max(a,b) lines, which is how one cable rendered as two whenever the far switch's evidence claimed an extra member. A lone AGGREGATE name IS still repeated — it labels the whole bundle, and a side whose CMDB trunk membership wasn't scraped degrades to that name. Asymmetric counts therefore draw min(a,b) lines and the surplus comes back as `unpaired`, which topologyGraphService prints in the edge's operator-visible reason instead of drawing. (2) Link state is a TIEBREAK, not a filter: a member the device reports as anything but `up` loses to a live sibling, but a side holding exactly one member keeps it whatever its state (a genuinely down link must still render, greyed, rather than vanish), and a member with no reading is kept — unknown is not down. Sole consumer: topologyGraphService's memberCableEdges.
│       ├── maintenanceRecurrence.ts # Pure (no DB) recurrence math for MaintenanceSchedule.schedule JSON: `scheduleShapeSchema`/`validateScheduleShape` (Zod — oneshot {startAt,endAt} local-ISO no-timezone, or recurring daily/weekly(daysOfWeek)/monthly(dayOfMonth clamped to month length)/yearly(month+day) with optional startTime/endTime — endTime ≤ startTime spans midnight, matched on the START day — and optional activeFrom/activeUntil inclusive date bounds), `isInWindow(schedule, date)`, `currentWindow(schedule, date)` (the half-open [start,end) occurrence containing date — identifies the occurrence for the operator-release re-entry check), `nextWindow(schedule, date)` (UI summaries; two-year scan horizon). SERVER-LOCAL wall-clock throughout — the scheduler evaluates per tick, so DST shifts need no precomputed-next-fire invalidation. Fully unit-tested.
│       ├── tagNormalize.ts          # Shared normalize for the two operator-typed tag dimensions (region tags + free-form "other" tags) on Role / User / GroupMapping: normalizeTags(input, label) (trim/drop-empty/dedupe-case-insensitive/cap) + unionTags(...lists) (deduped, sorted union for the effective scope at /auth/me). Extracted from roleService.normalizeRegionTags.
│       ├── notificationTemplate.ts  # Shared notification template vocabulary + renderer (single-brace {token} — NOT {{ }}): TEMPLATE_VARIABLES catalog (surfaced to the builder via /notification-rules/schema.templateVariables), buildTemplateContext(parts) (flattens rule/reading/asset-detail/escalation into a token→string map; snapshotted onto Notification.templateCtx), renderNotificationTemplate(tpl, ctx, {html?}) (single regex pass — substituted values never re-interpolated; html mode escapes interpolated VALUES only), escapeHtml, templateNeedsAsset (does any template reference {asset.*}?), setRecoverySentence(ctx, sentence) (writes a recovery sentence to BOTH `{trigger.summary}` — the body's headline slot — and `{message}`; the default body prints no {message} line, so a resolved/reset email whose only text lived there said nothing about what happened, and the fire-time trigger sentence re-rendered against the recovered reading reads like a fresh alert. Called by the engine's fireResolved/fireReset and notificationService's operator-clear reset path), notificationsPageUrl ({link} token + email View footer), formatElapsed ({escalation.elapsed}), isDeferredToken (a token a LATER pass fills — `ack` per recipient, anything `chart.*` per delivery — which the renderer must preserve even under unknown:"blank"; matched by prefix rather than an enumerated list, because the enumerated one drifted and silently blanked {chart.trigger} before the pass that fills it ever ran). Used by notificationEngine, notificationEscalationService, and notificationDeliveryService.
│       ├── mac.ts                   # Pure (no I/O) MAC normalization — the single home for all four shapes: `normalizeMacOrNull(raw)` → colon-UPPERCASE or null for empty / non-12-hex / all-zero (Asset storage); `macColonUpperOrNull` (loose — all-zero kept; global search + AssetMacAddress side-table shape); `macHexKeyOrNull` (bare-hex UPPER match key, all-zero rejected so match indexes can't collide on 00:00:… — discovery byMac + duplicate-hostname merge grouping); `normalizeMacLowerColon` (FortiOS wire form, pass-through on unrecognizable input — re-exported as `normalizeMac` from reservationPushService for the FortiOS-facing services).
│       ├── arpTable.ts             # Pure (no I/O) shaping of one FortiGate's ARP table before it reaches asset_arp_entries. `prepareArpRows` normalizes the MAC to colon-uppercase, folds an empty interface to NULL (FortiOS answers "" for an entry it cannot attribute, and a port named "" would render as real), dedupes on (ip, mac, ifName) keeping the FRESHEST row — a known age beats an unknown one, then lower wins, since FortiOS reports one binding twice when an interface and its VLAN child both resolve it — orders interface-then-numeric-IP so the cap slices deterministically, and caps at ARP_ROWS_PER_ASSET_CAP (4000) reporting what it dropped. Two MACs claiming one IP are KEPT as two rows: that is a duplicate-address finding, not a dedupe. `arpRowKey` is the (ip, mac, ifName-or-"") business key the firstSeen carry-forward and the writer's own uniqueness both use; `groupArpRowsByDevice` buckets a run's flat rows by lowercased FMG device name. Consumed by services/arpTableService.ts
│       ├── arpNeighbors.ts         # Pure (no I/O) decoding of a device's IP neighbour cache out of IP-MIB SNMP walks — the SNMP half of the ARP Table tab. Two generations, preferred then fallback like the Q-BRIDGE→BRIDGE FDB pair: `ipNetToPhysicalTable` (RFC 4293, IPv4 ARP *and* IPv6 NDP) then the deprecated `ipNetToMediaTable` (RFC 1213, IPv4 only). The ADDRESS is decoded from the OID INDEX in both cases, which on the modern table is the only place it exists — its index objects are not-accessible, so walking them answers nothing — and `parsePhysicalIndex` therefore has to honour the RFC 4001 length prefix (`<ifIndex>.<addrType>.<len>.<bytes…>`); a decoder that assumes 4 bytes invents addresses on every IPv6 row rather than failing. `buildArpNeighbors` drops rows whose MAC or index does not decode, type `invalid(2)`, and state `invalid(5)`/`incomplete(7)` (an incomplete entry is a resolution attempt in flight, so storing it would claim a binding that never resolved), while KEEPING `stale(2)` and `local(5)`. An unresolved ifIndex yields `ifName: null` rather than dropping the row. `ageFromLastUpdated` turns `ipNetToPhysicalLastUpdated` (a sysUpTime STAMP, not an age) into seconds and returns null — never 0 — when either value is missing or the stamp is in the future, since 0 would read as "just refreshed". `arpNeighborsFromFortiosRest` maps the REST endpoint's rows onto the same shape so the writer never learns which transport produced them. Consumed by monitoringService (`collectArpNeighborsSnmp`) and services/arpTableService.ts
│       ├── oidCompare.ts            # Pure (no I/O) numeric OID comparison: compareOids(a, b) (component-wise numeric, prefix-before-extensions — SNMP lexicographic order) + makeOidMonotonicGuard() (stateful per-walk guard: advance(oid) returns false the moment an agent returns an equal-or-lower OID). Backs the walk-loop defense in both monitoringService walk paths (internal snmpWalk + operator snmpWalkRaw): net-snmp's subtree/walk re-anchors on the last varbind with NO non-increasing check (and its backwardsGetNexts strict mode passes EQUAL OIDs), so a broken agent that echoes the queried OID back on GETBULK (field case: ControlByWeb X-4xx) would otherwise loop forever — in the internal walk the echoed base OID never matches the `baseOid.` prefix filter, so not even the row cap would trip, and the walk would hold the per-host SNMP gate indefinitely. On trip: AppError 502 naming both OIDs + "try an SNMP v1 credential or firmware update" (surfaced verbatim by the SNMP Walk tab).
│       ├── manufacturerNormalize.ts # Pure (no DB) cache + sync normalizeManufacturer(); imported by db.ts Prisma extension to canonicalize every Asset/MibFile manufacturer write
│       ├── osNormalize.ts           # Pure (no DB) normalizeWindowsOs() / normalizeOsInData() / windowsBuildFrom(): corrects the Windows product name EVERY discovery source gets wrong (Microsoft froze the registry `ProductName` key at "Windows 10" when Windows 11 shipped, and AD's operatingSystem / Entra+Intune / gopsutil-in-the-agent all read it) and labels the build with its marketing release ("23H2 (10.0.22631.7219)"). Build number is the authority: FAMILY comes from a threshold (>= 22000 ⇒ Windows 11, never goes stale), the RELEASE LABEL from a table (an unlisted build keeps its raw osVersion rather than being guessed at). Windows Server is excluded entirely — its ProductName is already correct and build 26100 is BOTH Win11 24H2 and Server 2025. Idempotent, so re-running it over its own output (every discovery cycle) is a no-op. Called from projectAssetFromSources (so the projection's output, projectionDriftService's comparison and conflict proposals all agree — normalizing only on the way to the DB would report permanent drift) AND from the Asset write hooks in db.ts (the catch-all for the inline writers: discoveryEngine's fortigate-endpoint path, the agents system-info route, conflictResolutionService, the assets PUT route)
│       ├── snmpDescrIdentity.ts     # Pure (no I/O): reads a vendor's OWN documented sysDescr FORMAT — `descrReadDue(lastDescrAt)` + `DESCR_READ_INTERVAL_SEC` gate the probe-borne read; `parseVendorSysDescr(descr)` → `{manufacturer, model, osVersion, productType}`, plus `sameDescrObserved(prev, next)`, the monitor path's no-I/O gate. The narrow exception to snmpIdentity.ts's refusal to derive a model from free text: a vendor whose layout is DOCUMENTED is parsed, everything else yields undefined. Every parser anchors on the vendor token (AXIS field 1 is an operator-settable device name), claims a field only when it is shaped right, and yields nothing at all — never `{manufacturer}` alone — when the layout does not read. The reading becomes an `snmp-sysdescr` AssetSource row, so WHETHER it wins is `assetProjection.ts`'s priority call, not this file's; `decideDescrAdoption` was retired with that cutover (two places answering "may this overwrite that?" is how two writers end up trading values every cycle).
│       ├── snmpIdentity.ts          # Pure (no I/O): turns an SNMPv2-MIB **system group** walk into asset fields for a network Discovery (business rule 34) — `parseSnmpIdentity(rows)` over what `snmpWalkRaw(host, config, "1.3.6.1.2.1.1", n)` returns, plus `vendorFromSysObjectId` / `vendorFromSysDescr` / `enterpriseFromSysObjectId` / `SYS_OIDS`. Nothing did this before: every other system-group reader in the repo takes exactly ONE object (`sysUpTime` for the reachability probe, `sysLocation` over FortiOS REST), and the only sysDescr/sysName elsewhere are LLDP *remote*-neighbour columns describing someone else's device. Four decisions. (1) **The vendor table is small and explicit and an unknown arc yields NOTHING** — the enterprise registry has tens of thousands of entries, and a wrong manufacturer is a field an operator never re-checks while an empty one is a field they fill in; the seeded arcs mirror `oidRegistry.BUILT_IN_OIDS` so the two can't disagree about who 12356 is. (2) **sysObjectID outranks sysDescr, EXCEPT for the generic agent arc** — the arc is a registered assignment and a vendor word in the description can name the OS on someone else's hardware, but Net-SNMP's own arc (2021 / 8072) names the AGENT by definition, so a Linux-based PDU running net-snmp takes the description's vendor instead. (3) **Unconfigured-agent placeholders are dropped** ("Sitting on the Dock of the Bay", "Me <me@example.org>", unknown / not set / n/a): storing them puts a site that doesn't exist into an asset's Location — the placeholder-serial rejection in utils/hardwareIdentity.ts, same reasoning. (4) **A `model` comes from a FORMAT, never from a pattern** — the system group has no model object and a cross-vendor regex over sysDescr fails silently on the vendors it wasn't written for (the entPhysicalIndex==ifIndex equivalence, again), so `model` / `osVersion` / `productType` are filled in ONLY by `utils/snmpDescrIdentity.ts`, from the vendors whose delimited layout is documented; a device outside that table reads exactly as it did before those fields existed, and a vendor scalar via `vendorTelemetryProfiles`' `modelIdentity` is still the better source where one exists. Note the empty-string guard on sysUpTime: `Number("")` is 0, so an agent answering the OID with no value would otherwise report "just rebooted". Tests: tests/unit/snmpIdentity.test.ts
│       ├── ifMib.ts                 # Pure IF-MIB (RFC 2863) enum decoders — `ifStatusLabel` (ifAdminStatus / ifOperStatus) and `snmpIfTypeLabel` (ifType → the canonical physical/aggregate/vlan/loopback/tunnel vocabulary). EXTRACTED from monitoringService.ts (2026-08) so the network-Discovery scan can decode an interface list from a bare `snmpWalkRaw` without importing the monitor service — a util may not depend on a service, and the scan runner is a service importing both. Two consumers, one table: a second copy is how a scan would come to disagree with the collector about what ifType 161 is. Both return **null for an unrecognized value rather than a plausible default** — ifType has hundreds of registered values against a five-value pin vocabulary, so defaulting to "physical" would drop propVirtual into a byTypes pin set. Tests: tests/unit/snmpInventory.test.ts
│       ├── interfaceIdentity.ts      # Pure (no Prisma): which name IS an interface, and which merely DESCRIBES one. `buildInterfaceIdentity(rows)` turns an asset's current-state `asset_interfaces` rows into `{ names, labelToName }`; `canonicalInterfaceName` / `canonicalizeInterfaceRows` / `canonicalizeInterfacePins` map a label back onto the port that carries it. Exists because the SNMP collectors resolve a port's name as `ifName` with an `ifDescr` fallback and walk each column with its own `.catch()` — so a tick where the `ifName` walk failed named every port by its `ifDescr`, which on a FortiSwitch is the operator's port DESCRIPTION. `port9` was collected as `MORGAN-221E-1` (the AP plugged into it), that name became an IDENTITY in the inventory / pin list / sample table, and the alert read "Interface PoE status on MORGAN-221E-1 is fault" (prod 2026-08-25). Three rules, each a decision: a real `ifName` always wins (a FortiSwitch reports `ifAlias` = the port name, so a label that IS a port name is never a label); a label two ports claim resolves to NOTHING (the `poeIfNameByIndex` discipline — a reading on the wrong port is worse than one under an odd name); an UNKNOWN name passes through unchanged (a port that appeared since the last full scrape has no row yet, and dropping it would hide new hardware). Consumed by `recordSystemInfoResult` / `recordFastFilteredResult` / `persistLldpNeighbors` via `interfaceInventoryService.loadInterfaceIdentity`. Tests: tests/unit/interfaceIdentity.test.ts, tests/integration/interfaceIdentityReconcile.test.ts
│       ├── snmpInventory.ts          # Pure: decodes an interface list (`parseScanInterfaces`) and storage-mount list (`parseScanStorage`) out of raw IF-MIB / ifXTable / hrStorageTable walks, for a network Discovery. Exists because the wizard's monitoring step offers pins by NAME while the integration pickers are fed by `interface-aggregate` over assets that already exist and have been polled — at scan time neither is true, so without collecting during the authenticated identification pass the step could only offer a blank pattern box. Output shape IS the resolver's input shape (`ResolverInterface`), so the same pure `resolvePinnedInterfaces` / `resolvePinnedStorage` decide what a selection pins whether the names came from a scan or a polled asset; nothing here writes `AssetInterface` (the device is not an asset yet).
