Capped at 2000 rows/asset with a loud warn; not a retention entity and never pruned. **The switch-port VLAN columns come from SNMP first, the controller CMDB second.** Q-BRIDGE-MIB fills `nativeVlan`/`taggedVlans` on every switch-class asset (`collectPortVlansSnmp` → `utils/portVlans.ts`), and the parent FortiGate's managed-switch CMDB overlays on top where it can reach — it is config truth and the only source that can say `allowed-vlans all` (`trunksAllVlans`, which q-bridge cannot express). Two decisions carry that: `dot1qVlanStaticUntaggedPorts` is believed only when it is a STRICT SUBSET of the egress bitmap, because FortiSwitch publishes it as a verbatim copy and the RFC egress-minus-untagged subtraction against a copy reports every trunk as carrying nothing; and the CMDB overlay writes only where it has a value, so a port the controller is silent about keeps what SNMP found.

#### AssetInterfaceOverride

**AssetInterfaceOverride** — operator-typed Interface Comments override. Polaris-local by default; when the originating integration's `syncDescriptions` toggle is on it is description-synced to the device (FortiGate `system/interface` description / FortiSwitch port description, Polaris-primary) and carries per-row sync state (`syncStatus` ∈ synced/failed — `conflict` only on legacy rows from the retired newest-wins engine, `lastSyncAt`, `syncError`, `syncedValue` = last synced value). See business rule 14.

#### AssetMacTableEntry

**AssetMacTableEntry** — the switch's layer-2 forwarding database (CAM table), from Q-BRIDGE-MIB `dot1qTpFdbTable` (RFC 4363, VLAN-aware — preferred) with a BRIDGE-MIB `dot1dTpFdbTable` fallback (RFC 4188, no VLAN dimension, hence `vlanId` NULL rather than a guess). Current-state, delete-replaced per scrape by `persistMacTable` — an FDB entry ages out on the switch in minutes, so history would answer a question the switch itself can't. **Both source tables report a `dot1dBasePort`, NOT an ifIndex**: the join runs through `dot1dBasePortIfIndex` then the scrape's ifIndex→ifName map, and unlike the PoE correlation this join is defined by the MIB and reliable. **And the MAC is not always in the INDEX**: the RFCs index both tables by the address, but agents in the field don't all honour it — a FortiSwitch indexes `dot1dTpFdbTable` by a plain ROW NUMBER (`…17.4.3.1.3.1`, `.2`, `.3`) and publishes the MAC only in the `dot1dTpFdbAddress` COLUMN, so an index-only decode drops every row on the very devices this table exists for (prod 2026-08). `resolveFdbIdentity` therefore reads the address column FIRST and falls back to the index — which is also right for the conformant case, since Q-BRIDGE's `dot1qTpFdbAddress` is an index object and typically not-accessible, so that walk answers nothing and the index decode runs unchanged. The VLAN still comes from the index, the only place Q-BRIDGE carries it. `basePort` is stored alongside `ifName` so a row whose join failed stays identifiable instead of appearing to belong to no port — and the MAC Table tab — which groups INTERFACE-FIRST, one expandable row per port with its MACs nested under it and the per-port count on the header line — **hides those rows by default** behind a count + Show toggle, since a FortiSwitch trunk/LAG pseudo-port (base port 32768 and up) publishes no `dot1dBasePortIfIndex` row, so every MAC behind the trunk lands there unattributable and swamps the real per-port entries. Hidden, never dropped: they are legitimate sightings that just can't be placed on a port. `status` keeps the RFC distinction — only `learned` is a real endpoint sighting, `self` is the reporting bridge's OWN address — useful only to exclude it from endpoint counts, NOT a peer signal (a peer switch appears in this table as a `learned` entry on the port facing it) — and `invalid` (an aged-out entry the agent hasn't reaped) is dropped at collection. `matchedAssetId` resolves through the SAME cached MAC index LLDP matching uses, because a per-row lookup would dominate the write at a few thousand rows per switch. Capped at 4000 rows per asset with a **loud** truncation warning — a partial table makes the per-port MAC counts, and any uplink inference drawn from them, quietly wrong. Collected SNMP-only on the system-info (heavy) cadence and gated to `assetType="switch"`; `undefined` preserves stored rows, `[]` wipes — so a table that ANSWERED but decoded to zero rows returns `undefined` (a read failure is not an empty forwarding database) and warns with `undecodable`/`unusableStatus` counts, because that silence is exactly what made the index-shape mismatch above read as a switch with nothing plugged into it. Surfaced at `GET /assets/:id/mac-table` (`assets:read`, returns entries + per-port learned-MAC counts) and the asset-details **MAC Table** tab. Also feeds **MAC-derived topology inference**: `peerInferredLldpService` emits `source:"mac-inferred"` neighbours for ports with exactly ONE learned asset-matched MAC (`inferDirectAttachments`), merged read-time into the Device Map + interface slide-over alongside the existing `peer-inferred` rows — so inference is no longer LLDP-only. **Display-only by design: nothing writes `AssetLldpNeighbor` and nothing writes `AssetDependencyParent`**, because dependency edges drive all-down suppression and a wrong edge silences real alerts; edge-writing waits on bidirectional confirmation validated against a real fleet. A multi-MAC port infers nothing (an uplink's data says "a switch with a network behind it", not which device the port IS).

#### AssetArpEntry

**AssetArpEntry** — the FortiGate's layer-3 neighbour cache, one row per `(IP, MAC, interface)` binding. The **L3 sibling of `AssetMacTableEntry`**: that table answers "what is plugged into port 7" from a switch's forwarding database, this one answers "what is at 10.4.12.63" from the router's own resolution of the address. **Accumulate + age** (the `AssetProcessConnection` pattern), NOT delete-replace: a binding still present has its `lastSeen` bumped, `firstSeen` survives, and rows age out on the flat **`arpEntries`** retention window (Server Settings → Retention, default 30 days). That is what lets the tab's range selector — Current / 1h / 12h / 24h / 7d / 30d — answer "who was at this address last Tuesday" at ONE row per distinct binding instead of one per poll; a snapshot table would be ~52M rows/month across a 40-gate fleet at the 600 s cadence. History is therefore an **interval, not a timeline**: a MAC that flips away and back between two polls is invisible, and a binding recurring after a gap collapses into one row spanning it. Plain table with real FKs, not a hypertable. **`ifName` is `""`, never NULL**, for a row the device attributed to no interface — it is part of the business key, and Postgres treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index, so a nullable column would insert a fresh duplicate every poll for exactly those rows; the route maps `""` back to null on the way out. **TWO WRITERS, which accumulate makes safe** (a partial view bumps what it saw and touches nothing else — under delete-replace the pair would wipe each other): (1) the **monitor system-info pass** (`systemInfoIntervalSeconds`, 600 s default) for monitored firewalls, over **FortiOS REST** (`/api/v2/monitor/network/arp`, `includeArp`) or **IP-MIB SNMP** (`collectArpNeighborsSnmp`) per the resolved polling method — the SNMP half additionally carries **IPv6 NDP** entries and a real per-entry age from `ipNetToPhysicalLastUpdated`, neither of which the REST endpoint exposes; and (2) **discovery Phase 7.5b** (`pollInterval`, 12 h default for both Fortinet types), which covers gates that are unmonitored or have system info off and costs nothing extra, because those rows are already read for the Phase 7.6 `Reservation.lastSeenArp` presence stamp (business rule 17) and Phase 7.7 placeholder-MAC adoption (business rule 26). Neither writer can express "the cache is empty" — nothing is ever wiped by a poll, only aged out by retention — so discovery's delete-replace scoping (`arpQueriedDevices`, the per-device `didArpQuery` flag) now only decides which gates get *recorded*, not which get cleared. **The gate resolves name → serial → assetId** (the run's own `DiscoveredDevice` list, then the `fortigate-firewall` `AssetSource` row whose externalId IS the serial), never through the hostname — the mismatch `utils/fortinetParentKey.ts` exists to prevent. **`matchedAssetId` is MAC-only** and is filled in but never cleared (`COALESCE` in the upsert), since the monitor pass has no warm asset index while discovery does: joining on the IP as well would attribute the row to the very asset it disproves, an ARP entry asserting that address belongs to that MAC being exactly the evidence that an asset still carrying it under a different MAC is stale. Pure shaping in `utils/arpTable.ts` (normalize, fold an empty interface, dedupe on `(ip, mac, ifName)` keeping the **freshest** row, order interface-then-numeric-IP, cap 4000/asset with a **loud** warn); pure SNMP decoding in `utils/arpNeighbors.ts` (RFC 4001 length-prefixed index, `invalid`/`incomplete` rows dropped). Two MACs claiming one IP are deliberately kept as two rows — a duplicate-address finding, not a dedupe. Surfaced at `GET /assets/:id/arp-table?range=` and the asset-details **ARP Table** tab (firewall-class only), which states the device's actual cadence and warns that short-lived entries can be missing entirely.

#### AssetTrunkMember

**AssetTrunkMember** — FortiSwitch trunk → local physical port, from the `fsTrunkMember` OctetString at `1.3.6.1.4.1.12356.106.3.1.0` (a SCALAR, hence the trailing `.0`). The trunk name is built from the PEER's serial number, so this is the switch stating its own adjacencies over SNMP rather than leaving them to be inferred — and it covers exactly the FortiLink switch↔switch and switch↔FortiGate links LLDP does not republish in managed mode. Current-state, delete-replaced per scrape by `persistTrunkMembers` (the `AssetLldpNeighbor` / `AssetMclagPeer` pattern; shape deliberately close to MCLAG, both being "local port faces peer device, keyed by serial"). **The name is the peer serial left-truncated to 15 characters**, with `-0` on a switch trunk eating two of them — which is why a switch appears to lose three leading characters and a FortiGate only one. Matching is therefore a SUFFIX test (`matchTrunkPeer` in `utils/fortiswitchTrunkMap.ts`), never a reconstruction: rebuilding the serial would hard-code a cap a firmware release could change. An ambiguous tail (two serials sharing it) resolves to NULL rather than to a guess, and so does one that is not serial-SHAPED: only the trunks the switch auto-creates are named for a peer, while the operator's hand-configured LAGs ride the same scalar named for whatever is plugged into them (`Storage Node 2`, `APPHOST01`, `_FlInK1_ICL0_`), so `isPeerSerialTail` (alphanumeric, ≥10 chars) gates the lookup — those rows are still a real trunk/member edge, they just name no peer. The OID was read one level too deep (`…106.3.1.1.0`) until 2026-08-28, which answers noSuchObject: a scalar GET resolves an error varbind to null, and null is the same "device does not publish this" signal a non-Fortinet switch produces, so the whole trunk half of the scrape was silently absent on every switch. Feeds `peerInferredLldpService` as `source:"trunk-mapped"` — named for being device-STATED, not inferred, unlike its `peer-inferred` and `mac-inferred` siblings. Collected SNMP-only on the system-info cadence, gated to `assetType="switch"`; `undefined` preserves stored rows, `[]` wipes. **The same read is the only source of the trunk/member edge on a directly-polled switch**, so the scrape does not just persist these rows — it regroups them (`trunkMemberMap`) and runs the shared `overlayFortiswitchTrunkMembers` against the interface list, stamping `ifParent` on each member and `ifType="aggregate"` on the trunk. Without that the System tab listed a trunk and its member ports as unrelated flat rows on every switch outside the controller-CMDB overlay's reach (which needs a resolvable `controllerFortigate`), because IF-MIB itself publishes no aggregation.

#### AssetPhysicalEntity

**AssetPhysicalEntity** — field-replaceable hardware inventory from ENTITY-MIB (RFC 4133) `entPhysicalTable`: transceivers, PSUs and fan trays with the vendor / model / serial / hardware-rev an operator needs to raise an RMA or find the spare. Current-state, delete-replaced per scrape by `persistPhysicalEntities` (the `AssetLldpNeighbor` / `AssetMclagPeer` pattern), plain table with a real FK to Asset — the no-FK rule is hypertables-only, and this deliberately is not one: inventory changes on a maintenance window, not a cadence. Scoped by `entityPhysicalIsInventory` to rows the device flags `entPhysicalIsFRU`, else module/powerSupply/fan rows carrying a serial or model — a chassis publishes a row per container, port and sensor, hundreds of them naming nothing replaceable. Capped at 500 rows per asset with a **loud** truncation log. `firstSeen` survives a re-scrape for a module still in place (so "this SFP has been in this port since March" holds) and resets when the serial in that slot changes, i.e. on a swap. SNMP heavy cadence only; `undefined` from a transport that can't supply it preserves stored rows, `[]` wipes — the LLDP contract. `ifName` is present on the model but **deliberately never populated**: correlating a module to an interface by entPhysicalIndex == ifIndex is the same equivalence the FortiSwitch sensor annotation was reverted for (97e54fd2), right often enough to look correct and silently wrong the rest of the time. The honest chain is entPhysicalContainedIn → entAliasMappingIdentifier (RFC 4133), which needs a real switch to validate against; the column waits for it.

#### AssetProcessConnection

**AssetProcessConnection** — ACCUMULATE + AGE socket facts (listening ports / outbound connections / inbound peers) for MAPPED processes (`Asset.mappedProcesses`, the Processes-tab "Map" toggle — independent of `monitoredProcesses`). Plain table with a real FK to Asset (not a hypertable); rows upsert on the business key via `persistProcessConnections` (batched `INSERT … ON CONFLICT` bumping `lastSeen` behind a 5-minute churn gate, `firstSeen` kept; per-(process,kind) caps 200/500/200) and age out on the flat `appMapConnections` retention window (Server Settings → Retention; `POLARIS_PROCESS_CONN_RETENTION_DAYS` is now only its default seed). Collected per-minute for mapped processes ONLY (never full-host collect-then-filter): agent stream `processConnections` (gopsutil `net.Connections`, direction heuristic on-agent — local port ∈ own listen set ⇒ inbound, ephemeral ports never stored) or the agentless ssh/winrm `processes` cadence. Also carries `unit` (Phase 3, attribute-only, not in the business key, **backfill-only on conflict** — an empty stored value adopts the incoming unit, a non-empty one is never overwritten): the owning systemd unit / Windows service resolved from the PID's cgroup, so rows can be attributed to a UNIT — the agent additionally collects connections for PIDs whose unit is in `Asset.mappedServices` (Services-tab "Map"). Unmapping a process (by name) OR a unit deletes the matching rows immediately. Drives the **Application Map** page + the process detail panel's Ports & Connections section + the Services detail panel's (via `GET /assets/:id/process-connections?unit=`).

#### AssetMclagPeer

**AssetMclagPeer** — current-state MCLAG ICL peers (one row per local `mclag-icl-port` on a FortiSwitch), full-replaced per scrape by `persistMclagPeers` (delete-replace, plain table — same pattern as `AssetLldpNeighbor`/`AssetSdwanRule`). Parsed from the parent FortiGate's `switch-controller/managed-switch` CMDB; `peerSn` (the canonical pairing key) resolves to `matchedAssetId`. Drives the asset-detail "MCLAG Peer" General-tab row + the Device Map sibling ICL edge (`mclagEdges`). FortiManager + standalone FortiGate (shared `fetchFortiswitchControllerPortsCmdb`).

#### AssetStateSample

**AssetStateSample** — the **0/1 sibling** of the above: one row per (asset, **state probe**, table row) per scrape, written by the same `collectAndRecordCustomWidgets` pass. A `ManufacturerCustomWidget` with `widgetType="state"` is a *state probe* — a status-shaped OID (alarm bit, PSU present, fan-tray OK) whose reading is normalized to a boolean at scrape time by the probe's operator-DECLARED `stateMap` (`src/utils/stateProbes.ts`: modes `nonzero`/`zero`/`equals`/`notEquals`/`gte`/`lte` + `trueLabel`/`falseLabel`/`trueIsProblem`). Declared rather than inferred because vendors disagree on polarity — SNMPv2 TruthValue is `true(1)/false(2)`, plenty of enums use 2 for the bad state, some agents answer strings — so a bare `value >= 1` is wrong about as often as it's right; storing the boolean means the automation engine never has to know. Alertable per row via the `customStateValue` asset_metric (dimensions `stateProbeId` + `stateRowPattern`). Two invariants: **`value` is 0 or 1 and never null** (the collector DROPS an absent/unreadable/incomparable row, because 0 is a positive claim of health that would clear a live alert — and on a `trueIsProblem=false` probe would raise one about hardware that isn't there), and **`rowKey`** (the OID index suffix, `""` for a scalar probe) is the stable dimension identity while `rowLabel` (resolved from the probe's optional `labelSymbol` sibling walk, joined on that index) is what operators filter and read — so renaming a row keeps its alert. Its own table rather than another `kind` on AssetCustomWidgetSample because the alerting dimension is the ROW: real columns make the engine's read an indexed `(assetId, probeId, timestamp)` scan and the builder's row picker a plain GROUP BY, instead of unpacking a JSON array per sample every 60s. Standalone detail-only hypertable, **deliberately no rollups** (averaging a boolean gives a duty cycle, not a state), same no-FK rule and same `pruneSystemInfoSamples` umbrella window.

#### SshHostKey

**SshHostKey** — trust-on-first-use pins for SSH **server** host keys (one row per dialed `(host, port)`, plain table `ssh_host_keys`, no Asset FK — a host is often onboarded before it exists as an Asset). Written by `sshHostKeyService.verifyOrPin`: no pin → store + accept, match → accept, **differs → refuse** the connection + warn-level `ssh.host_key.mismatch`. Fingerprints are `SHA256:<unpadded base64>`, identical to `ssh-keygen -lf`. Gated per credential by `SshConfig.verifyHostKey` — **opt-in, default OFF** (default ON for new credentials), mirroring WinRM's `verifyTls`, because before this Polaris passed no `hostVerifier` to ssh2 and accepted ANY host key on every SSH path (agent install, agentless processes, the SSH probe). `buildHostVerifier` in `utils/remoteExec.ts` is shared by both `ssh2.connect` sites and fails closed. Operator list + Delete on Integrations → Polaris Agent → Windows SSH Deployment; deleting a pin is the audited recovery for a rebuilt host. See business rule 21.

#### Credential

**Credential** — named SNMP / WinRM / SSH / REST API / **HTTP** credentials for monitoring probes. The `http` type carries **authentication only** — `authMode` (`bearer` | `basic` | `digest`) plus its carrier — and deliberately has no "none" mode. It used to carry the whole health check as well; that half moved to a manufacturer custom widget in 2026-08 because a check varies by vendor AND model while a login varies by vendor or site, so sharing one row meant a second path needed a second copy of the same password. See business rule 33. The `ssh` type takes `password` OR `privateKey` (+ optional `passphrase` for an encrypted key — operator-supplied escrow keys only; a Polaris-generated deployment key is never exported so a passphrase would sit beside the key it protects), plus opt-in `verifyHostKey` (business rule 21). `publicKey` is present but deliberately NOT masked. Secret fields inside `config` are **encrypted at rest** by the Prisma extension in `src/db.ts` when `POLARIS_SECRET_KEY` is set (see business rule 20b); masked-on-read at the API layer as before. The same applies to `Integration.config`, `NotificationChannel.config` and the secret-bearing `Setting` rows.

#### ManufacturerProfile

**ManufacturerProfile** / **ManufacturerProfileMetric** / **ManufacturerProfileMetricOverride** / **ManufacturerCustomWidget** — operator-editable per-manufacturer telemetry profile + custom widget definitions. `ManufacturerCustomWidget.widgetType` is `gauge | line | table | state | http`. **`state`** is a state probe (nullable `stateMap` + `labelSymbol`, `listStateProbes()` flattens them for the automation builder) — see `AssetStateSample` above. **`http`** is an HTTP CHECK (migration `20260825000000`): `symbol`/`mibId` are NULL on it (it names a request, not an OID — required for every other type, enforced in the service since the rule is per-widgetType and a column cannot express it), the definition lives in `httpCheck Json?`, and `credentialId` points at an `http` Credential (`SetNull`; NULL = unauthenticated). Every widget type is gated by `modelPattern` — blank means every asset of that manufacturer. See business rule 33.

#### NotificationRule

**NotificationRule** — operator-defined alert definition. Flexible discriminated `trigger` (JSON union: `asset_metric` | `asset_state` | `host_metric` | `event` | `change` | `composite` — the last a nested AND/OR tree `{kind: asset|host, op, children}` of metric/state leaves, ≤3 deep / 2–10 leaves, and/or only; composite rules alert PER ASSET (ANY-dimension leaves, dimensionKey ""), while a 1-leaf composite collapses server-side to the legacy single trigger — `collapseCompositeTrigger` — keeping per-dimension alerting + hysteresis) + asset `scope`, per-rule `clearBehavior` (manual / auto-resolve / timed), `cooldownSec`, `messageTemplate`, `requireAckNote` (refuse an acknowledgement with no note — business rule 25), `channels` (default `["in_app"]`), and `targets` (JSON array of outbound deliveries: `{ channelId, recipientUserIds?, addresses?, recipientScopeRegion?, recipientTags?(legacy) }` referencing **NotificationChannel** rows — recipients combine individual user accounts, custom emails, and (when `recipientScopeRegion`) users matching the rule's scope `region:` tag(s); recipient routing only applies to email/web_push channels). Also carries optional `emailComposition` (rule-level outbound-email customization: `subjectTemplate` / `bodyTextTemplate` / `bodyHtmlTemplate` + `cc`/`bcc` recipient sets; templates use the single-brace `{token}` vocabulary in `src/utils/notificationTemplate.ts`, surfaced to the builder via `/schema.templateVariables`; when set, each email target sends ONE message with its full To list + Cc + Bcc instead of the default per-address fan-out; NULL = pre-feature behavior) and optional `escalation` (≤5 tiers, `stopOn: "acknowledge"|"clear"` — stored as posted in EITHER shape: legacy email tiers `{afterMin, channelId, to, cc?, bcc?, template overrides?, repeat*}` or **v2 tiers of actions** `{afterMin, actions[≤10 notify|api_call|script], repeat*}`; readers normalize via `normalizeEscalationToV2`, and the `escalateNotifications` sweep runs due tiers through `automationActionService.executeActions` — legacy tiers produce byte-identical emails: per-field tier→rule composition fallback + the `[ESCALATION n]` default-subject prefix; a tier's state bumps only when ≥1 action executed). Evaluated by `notificationEngine` on the `evaluateNotificationRules` job; in-app is always implicit, `targets` drive email/chat/push via `notificationRecipientService` → `NotificationDelivery` → the `deliverNotifications` job. CRUD gated by the `automationManagement` RBAC key (renamed from `notificationManagement` in the Automations cutover, migration `20260721000000`). The trigger/scope/target vocabulary + builder catalog live in `src/services/notificationTypes.ts`. `scope.condition` is a nested AND/OR/NONE/NOT-ALL rule tree (fields assetType/manufacturer/model/hostname/os/tag/subnet/interfaceName/status/assetId; ≤5 deep, ≤100 rules) evaluated by the pure `evaluateScopeCondition` — `interfaceName` ("Device interface") matches the device's current-state `AssetInterface` inventory rather than a column, resolved in SQL by `scopeInterfaceIndex` instead of joined, and contributing nothing to `scopeRank` — shared by the engine's post-SQL filter, the in-memory matcher, and `scopeRegionTagsOf` (which also mines positive `region:` tag rules from trees for recipientScopeRegion routing); flat scope dimensions remain valid and AND with a condition when both are present. User-facing name: an **Automation**; a fired instance is an **Alert**. **Repeat until handled (migration `20260825000000`):** nullable `repeat` Json (`{everyMin: 5..1440, stopOn: acknowledge|clear, stopAfterHours?}`) re-sends the alert's own notifications while it stays unhandled. Only escalation TIERS could repeat before — the engine's `fire()` sends the base actions once and never revisits them, so an alert nobody acknowledged went quiet after one email. Swept by the SAME `escalateNotifications` tick (it already owns unhandled-detection, the suppression pause, per-key state and templateCtx rendering), keyed `REPEAT_STATE_KEY` (`"repeat"`) in `Notification.escalationState.tiers` — collision-free against the level chain's bare numerics and the per-action chains' `a<i>:t<j>`. **Three deliberate asymmetries with escalation:** it re-runs `REPEATABLE_ACTION_TYPES` (notify) ONLY, because unbounded re-execution of a ticket-creating `api_call` or a registry `script` is not the same blast radius as an extra email (and `validateRuleV2` refuses a repeat on an automation with no notify action anywhere — a repeat that can never send is a dead setting that looks alive); it is UNBOUNDED unless the operator sets the optional `stopAfterHours`, which is why it needs its own `repeatIsDue` rather than `tierIsDue` (that resolves `maxRepeats ?? 5` and would silently cap the one behaviour that was asked to be uncapped); and it labels its email `[REMINDER n]` via the normal-fire composition path, never escalation's per-field tier→rule merge, with `meta.repeat` as a key separate from `meta.escalation`. A repeat and a due escalation tier in the same sweep BOTH send — skipping the reminder would drift its clock and make "every 15 minutes" a lie. `repeat` had to reach `DbRule` because `ruleWantsContext` gates the `templateCtx` snapshot: without it a repeat-only automation snapshots nothing and every reminder loses `{value}` / `{threshold}` / `{trigger.summary}` / every `{asset.*}`. Audited as its own `notification.repeated` Event, not `notification.escalated`. NULL = never repeats, which is every pre-feature automation, and it is deliberately NOT seeded into the baseline automations. **Reset actions (migration `20260812010000`):** nullable `resetActions` Json — actions that run when the alert **ENDS**, on every path that ends one: auto / hysteresis / custom-condition recovery, the timed sweep (including the event-tail timed clear, which now selects the alerts instead of bulk-updating a count), and an operator clearing by hand (`clearNotifications`). Plain `actionSchema`, never escalatable — an escalation chases an unhandled alert and there is nothing to chase about a recovery, the same reason `bandNotify.resolvedActions` stay bare. They run **before** the clear (mirroring `fireResolved`), so their delivery rows and acknowledge tokens attach to a live notification; the message names how it ended, and the context uses the `resolved` pseudo-severity. NULL = silent, which is what every stored automation keeps until it is edited — nothing retroactively starts emailing on recovery. The wizard’s **“When this resets”** list (Actions step) MIRRORS the trigger’s notify actions as they are created and detaches a row the moment it is edited or deleted, so telling the same people it came back costs nothing. On a NEW automation it also seeds the same default `event` action the fire list carries, so a recovery is audited the way the firing is (an ordinary removable row — the mirror leaves it removed). Emptying the list **unticks the toggle**: `collectStep5` saves an empty list as `null`, so a ticked box over no rows was a state the next open would contradict. `resetActions` is the **eighth** location in `allRuleActionRefs`. **Rule-shape v2 (migration `20260722000000`):** nullable `reset` Json (`{mode: manual|auto|timed|condition|event, clearThreshold?, sustainSec?, afterSec?, condition?, resetEvent?}` — hysteresis + clear-sustain for auto; `condition` = a custom AND/OR reset tree, allowed on ANY trigger with a continuous condition — `TRIGGER_TYPES_WITH_RESET_CONDITIONS`, i.e. everything but `event`/`change`, which fire on an instant and have nothing to recover — restricted to leaves of the trigger's own kind (device vs Polaris-host), mirrored to legacy as `clearBehavior:"auto"`. Those two get **`mode:"event"`** instead (`TRIGGER_TYPES_WITH_RESET_EVENT`, the exact complement): `resetEvent` names the counterpart audit Event that clears the alert (`agent.disconnected` → `agent.connected`), matched in the SAME event-tail pass as the triggers and scoped to the same subject the alert is filed under — `assetId` when the event names an asset, else the resource label — with a rule that matched an event as a TRIGGER dropping that event's reset hit so a wide glob can't clear the alert it just raised. Also mirrored to legacy as `clearBehavior:"auto"`. See business rule 32) supersedes `clearBehavior`/`clearAfterSec`, and nullable `actions` Json (unified outcome list: `notify` | `api_call` | `script` | **`event`**) supersedes `targets`. **`event` = write the `notification.triggered` audit Event** — present by default (migration `20260810120000_event_action` appended it to every stored rule, and both normalizers inject it when folding a legacy shape forward) and removable for a deliberately noisy automation; the engine writes that Event only when the action is present. It carries no config and takes no `escalation` (an instantaneous Event has nothing to chase), and it is deliberately NOT added to `event`/`change`-triggered rules, whose tail writes no Events by design. The in-app **Alert** is NOT optional: `NotificationDelivery` rows, the escalation sweep, acknowledge/clear and `NotificationRuleState` all key on `Notification.id`, so a notify/api_call action can't exist without one. Every reader normalizes via `normalizeRuleToV2`; the `migrateAutomationRuleShape` one-shot persists v2 onto old rows; CRUD keeps the legacy columns rewritten as a lossless mirror (`legacyMirrorOfV2`) so the pre-wizard UI and pre-upgrade backups stay coherent. Input accepts BOTH shapes (legacy bodies fold into v2). Script actions validate against the `AutomationScript` registry at save and require `automationScripts=fullwrite` on top of `automationManagement`; escalation input accepts both the legacy email-tier shape and v2 tiers-of-actions. **Severity bands (migration `20260726000000`):** nullable `severityBands` Json (numeric asset_metric/host_metric triggers only) stacks higher tiers on the base trigger threshold/severity (tier 0) — each band `{threshold, severity, operator?, forDurationSec?, actions[], escalation?}` carries its OWN actions + time-escalation + **sustained duration** (tiers share the trigger's sampling — aggregation/window/dimensionFilter — but may override the comparison `operator` and the hold time; omitted `forDurationSec` inherits the base trigger's, 0 = apply immediately); `severityForValue` resolves the most-severe satisfied tier instantaneously, and `resolveTierLadder`/`updateTierMetSince`/`sustainedSeverity` (all pure, in notificationTypes) layer the per-tier hold on top — backed by `NotificationRuleState.bandMetSince`. Nullable `bandNotify` Json `{onIncrease(def true), onDecrease(def false), onResolved(def true), resolvedMode: reuse|dedicated, resolvedActions?}` is the per-automation transition policy. One alert per asset climbs/eases severity in place (re-notifying with the entered band's actions per policy) and clears below tier 0. `validateSeverityBands` enforces a numeric ordered operator (base + any per-tier override) + **strictly-increasing severities** (thresholds need not be monotonic — most-severe-met wins); band/resolved/per-band-escalation actions get the same `automationScripts=fullwrite` gate + ref checks. **Precedence / carve-out:** when two automations watch the SAME thing (`triggerSignature` = metric/field + dimensionFilter; null for host/event/change/composite = exempt) a more-specific one (`scopeRank` ladder least→most: all assets < device type < OS < manufacturer < model < tag < region < subnet < hostname) carves the assets it covers out of the less-specific one — those assets drop their readings, any active alert clears (`notification.superseded`), pending debounce resets; same-rank ties both fire. `buildShadowIndex`/`isAssetShadowed` in the engine; `previewRule` surfaces it both authoring directions (`carveOut.carvedOut`/`carvesFrom` + per-match `excludedBy` + `specificity`). See business rules 18–19. `scope.condition`'s `assetId` field still validates + evaluates for saved rules but is no longer offered in the builder. **Actions redesign (2026-08):** (1) **Per-action escalation** — top-level and severity-band actions may carry their OWN `escalation` chain (`escalatableActionSchema`; escalation-tier actions and `bandNotify.resolvedActions` stay bare, so chains can't nest); the sweep iterates `escalationChainsForSeverity` — the rule/band LEVEL chain (state keys stay the bare numeric tier indexes) + one chain per effective action (state keys `a<i>:t<j>` via `escalationTierStateKey`), with per-chain `stopOn`. `allRuleActionRefs` is the canonical walk over all seven action locations — the `automationScripts` route gate, `assertActionRefs`, and `ruleWantsAssetDetail` all collect through it; `ruleWantsContext` uses `ruleHasAnyEscalation`. (2) **Device-region + address-book recipients** — notify actions/targets take `recipientRoles` (every user holding one of the named Roles — role IDS, so a rename can't reroute; resolves to users, so it works on email and push alike and in cc/bcc) and `recipientAssetContacts` (route to the address-book **Contact** rows whose device filter covers the TRIGGERING asset — ownership is stated once on the contact instead of per rule; email transports only, since a contact is an address with no push endpoint behind it; the addresses are resolved by `automationActionService` and handed to `expandDeliveries` as `assetContactEmails`, because `contactService` imports `notificationRecipientService` and the expander fetching them itself would close an import cycle) and `recipientDeviceRegion`: route email/push to users whose region tags match the TRIGGERING asset's `region:` tags (engine passes `regionSnapshot(reading.tags)`; the sweep reads `Notification.regionTags`); `recipientScopeRegion` (rule-scope region) still honored on old rules but no longer offered in the builder. (3) **Event-path hardening** — the event tail now enforces `cooldownSec` (against recent Notification rows keyed rule + assetId-or-resourceName, self-deduping within a batch) and `runEventRuleTimedClear` clears timed-reset event/change notifications after `afterSec` (they have no state rows, so the regular timed sweeps never saw them).

#### Notification

**Notification** — a triggered alert instance. UI surfaces: the dashboard's **Active Alerts** widget (Notification-backed since 2026-08 — it read audit Events before, so automation-less discovery/sync failures showed as permanent un-clearable "alerts" and `Event.level`'s critical/serious collapse rendered a `serious` automation as "error"; it now gates on `alerts:read`, carries the automation's own severity, and drops a row when the alert clears) + the asset-details Alerts tab (the dedicated page-level Alerts list was removed from /automations.html 2026-07; the `/alerts` API + acknowledge/clear flows and the `alerts` RBAC key are unchanged). /notifications.html remains a permanent redirect for delivered push deep links; both pages now gate on `automationManagement:read`. Carries snapshotted `regionTags` (stripped of the `region:` prefix → compares directly to a viewer's region tags) + `assetHostname` so it renders/scopes after the asset is deleted, plus (when the rule has emailComposition/escalation) `templateCtx` — the fire-time token→string context snapshot escalation emails render from — and `escalationState` (per-tier `{ firstSentAt, lastSentAt, count }` written by the escalation sweep, keyed per chain — bare numeric indexes for the rule/band-level chain, `a<i>:t<j>` for per-action chains). Soft-clear (`cleared`) preserves history. View gated `alerts:read`; acknowledge (note + by/at) gated `alerts:write` (readonly cannot); clear gated `alerts:fullwrite` (admin + assetsadmin). (`alerts` = the renamed `notifications` key.)

#### NotificationRuleState

**NotificationRuleState** — per-(rule, asset, dimension) firing state machine (`clear`→`pending`→`firing`) for sustained-duration + debounce + auto-clear. Writes only on transition (capacityWatch-style guard) so the engine hot path scales with *changes*, not fleet size. `assetId=""` for host/global rules. `firingSeverity` (severity-bands) tracks the band the active alert is currently in, so the engine detects increase/decrease/same crossings across ticks; `metRun` / `clearRun` / `lastReadingAt` carry POLL-COUNTED holds for the sources with no sample series to count — the Asset columns, the delete-replaced SD-WAN rule table, the windowed-ratio metrics recomputed per tick, and a composite tree's own outcome: the run advances only when that stream's poll anchor moved (`advanceRun`), so the engine's 60-second tick can't count five polls against a device polled every five minutes, and all three are zeroed whenever the row returns to `clear` (a stale `metRun` would let the next qualifying reading skip the hold outright). A series-backed trigger stores none of them — its run is the leading count of qualifying samples, computed per tick (`leadingRun`). `bandMetSince` Json (`{[severity]: epochMs}`) holds each tier's continuously-satisfied run, which is what makes a wall-clock "sustained for" per-band (business rule 19) — rewritten only when a tier enters or leaves, so the transition-only write property holds. **Nothing may strand a firing row the engine can no longer see:** the engine's vanished-state sweep clears rows whose asset left the rule's scope or whose dimension stopped being reported (`system:out-of-scope`; suppressed assets and in-scope assets with zero readings stay frozen), and the rule service clears active alerts on trigger-identity edit / disable / delete. **Every** interface trigger reads only PINNED interfaces (`Asset.monitoredInterfaces`) — the state trio `ifOperStatus`/`ifAdminStatus`/`poeStatus` and the counter metrics `ifInBps`/`ifOutBps`/`ifInErrorRate`/`ifOutErrorRate` alike, through the shared `interfaceIsPinned` predicate; a device reports every port it has, so the pin is the operator's statement of which ones may alert and there is no opt-out (the builder's interface picker lists the pin set for the same reason). Plus an admin-up gate on ifOperStatus — unplugged or deliberately-disabled ports never alert. `poeStatus` (POWER-ETHERNET-MIB, SNMP only) carries the same shape plus two gates of its own: a NULL reading means "not a PoE port" rather than "PoE is off" and is dropped (otherwise a not-delivering rule fires on every uplink and SVI), and `"disabled"` is excluded as the PoE analogue of the admin-up gate. A *fault* rule is unaffected by that second gate — a disabled port reports `disabled`, never `fault`. The IPsec pair `ipsecStatus`/`ipsecThroughputBps` gates the same way (2026-08) through `tunnelIsPinned` over `Asset.monitoredIpsecTunnels`: unlike interfaces, whose sample table is pinned-only, the IPsec stream still samples EVERY tunnel the gate reports (unpinned rows ride `cadence="slow"`, 24h — they feed the slide-over display), so the engine gate is the only thing keeping a tunnel-down automation from alerting on tunnels nobody selected — and the builder's tunnel picker lists the pin set for the same reason.

#### Contact

**Contact** — an address-book entry: a named email address alerts can route to, whether or not the recipient holds a Polaris account (a distribution list, an on-call rotation, a vendor NOC). `email` is unique and stored trimmed + lower-cased, so the index is case-insensitive and the value compares directly against the normalized set `resolveEmailRecipients` builds. Optional `name` / `description`, plus **device ownership**: `assetCondition` — the SAME nested AND/OR condition tree the automations device filter stores, evaluated by the same `evaluateScopeCondition` — unioned with explicit `assetIds` pins, deliberately NOT intersected with `monitored=true`, since an unmonitored device still has an owner and event/change automations fire on it. It supersedes the flat `assetCriteria` (`tagAssignmentService` vocabulary) it shipped with, so operators aren't asked "which devices?" in two languages: both columns are still READ but only ONE is live per row (a write of the condition nulls the criteria), and pre-cutover rows fold forward through the pure `criteriaToCondition` on read, persisted by the `migrateContactFilterShape` one-shot — the `normalizeRuleToV2` pattern. The tree validates against **`DEVICE_FILTER_FIELD_OPS`**, a strict SUPERSET of the automations scope vocabulary: it keeps the four fields the flat builder carried and the automations scope lacks (`osVersion` / `department` / `location` / `fortigate` = "behind FortiGate", matched against `learnedLocation` OR any sighting — where a NEGATIVE operator must hold for EVERY candidate name, or "not behind gate X" would be true for a device sighted behind it the moment it was also sighted elsewhere) plus a wildcard `matches` operator, because losing them would be a regression in exactly the dimension device ownership cares about, and because it's what makes every stored criteria blob convertible. `fortigate` is deliberately NOT added to the automations scope — that filter runs over the whole fleet on every engine tick and the sighting join would land on the hot path. "All devices" is stored as the empty AND group (true for any asset by boolean identity) but is reachable ONLY through an explicit `assetAllDevices` input flag, so a malformed or half-built empty tree can never quietly hand a contact the whole fleet. `createdBy` backs the ownership dimension on the `contacts` key. Owned by `contactService`; the fire-time lookup (`resolveContactsForAsset`) evaluates each contact's filter against the ONE triggering asset — the pure `evaluateScopeCondition` for a tree (which does its own CIDR math, so a folded-forward address book makes no containment query at all), `assetMatchesCriteria` for a legacy blob — never a fleet scan. Surfaced on Automations → Address Book and in the automation wizard's recipient picker.

#### MaintenanceSchedule

**MaintenanceSchedule** — operator-defined maintenance window definition (Assets page → Maintenance modal, gated `maintenanceManagement`). Targets = union(criteria matches, explicit `assetIds`) ∩ `monitored=true`; `criteria` reuses the tagAssignmentService vocabulary (hostname/model/manufacturer/os contains|exact|pattern, subnet `inCidr` — a bare IP is a /32; `integration` = discovered-by integration id, exact-only, matched against `discoveredByIntegrationId` OR any AssetSource row; `fortigate` = "behind FortiGate" device name with string ops, matched against `learnedLocation` OR any AssetFortigateSighting — contains on a site prefix covers every gate at the site; `status` rules rejected since the feature itself flips status); `schedule` is the recurrence JSON validated by `src/utils/maintenanceRecurrence.ts` (oneshot | recurring daily/weekly/monthly/yearly, optional time-of-day range that may span midnight, optional active date bounds — SERVER-LOCAL wall-clock, evaluated per tick so DST is automatic). Reconciled by the `maintenanceScheduler` job (30s) and inline on every CRUD write (so the ad-hoc pill path takes effect immediately). Per-schedule `suppressChildren` (default true) controls whether in-window assets count as down for child dependency suppression. **Ad-hoc lifecycle:** the pill/edit-modal "enter maintenance until…" path creates a single-asset one-shot with `schedule.startNow: true` (the SERVER stamps startAt — a browser-stamped start lands in the server's future whenever the operator's clock runs ahead, breaking immediate entry); any schedule matching the ad-hoc shape (one-shot + no criteria + exactly one explicit asset) self-deletes once spent — operator ends maintenance early (`operatorReleaseAsset`) or the window ends naturally (reconcile sweep; `nextWindow` guard keeps future-edited one-shots) — with closed window rows keeping the `scheduleName` snapshot for chart bands. Disable is an operator choice and never auto-deletes. See business rule 16.

#### AssetMaintenanceWindow

**AssetMaintenanceWindow** — one realized maintenance window per (asset, schedule): opened when the scheduler enters the asset, closed with `endedAt` + `endReason` (`schedule`/`operator`/`disabled`/`deleted`/`criteria`). Open rows (endedAt NULL) are the restart-safe source of truth for "in maintenance"; closed rows power the chart maintenance bands (`GET /assets/:id/maintenance-windows`; `scheduleName` snapshotted so labels survive schedule deletion). Plain table with a real FK to Asset (the no-FK rule is hypertables-only); rows older than ~400 days pruned by the reconcile.

#### NotificationChannel

**NotificationChannel** — operator-configured outbound delivery integration (Automations → Delivery tab; set up like the Integrations page). `type` ∈ `smtp` | `oauth_m365` | `pushbullet` | `slack` | `teams` | `web_push` selects transport + `config` shape; secrets in `config` are masked on read / preserved on write. `web_push` is a singleton (one server VAPID keypair). Owned by `notificationChannelService`; CRUD gated `automationManagement`. Rules reference channels by id in `targets`.

#### NotificationDelivery

**NotificationDelivery** — one outbound delivery per (notification, channel, concrete recipient). `channelId` → NotificationChannel (SetNull; null on a pending row = permanent fail — EXCEPT `transport="api_call"` rows, whose NULL channel is the designed shape: the whole request spec + fire-time-rendered body ride `meta`, dispatched by `apiCallChannel.sendApiCall` with SSRF re-check and normal retries) + `transport` (email/webhook/web_push/pushbullet/api_call) + `target` (recipient address/endpoint; "" for fixed-destination channels; for a composed email, the joined To list — one row carries the whole send, since the acknowledge link names the alert rather than a person (business rule 25)) + `meta` (web_push keys, or the composed-email snapshot `{ composed: true, to[], cc[], bcc[], subject, text, html?, escalation? }` — rendered content + recipient addresses only, never channel secrets) + `status` (pending/sent/failed) + `attempts`. Destination secrets stay on the channel, read at send time. Expanded at fire time by `notificationRecipientService` (escalation rows inserted by the sweep); drained (≤3 retries) by `deliverNotifications` — rows without `meta.composed` (incl. pre-upgrade pending rows) take the legacy per-address path. Cascades with the Notification.

#### Alert email

**Alert email** — leads with **what fired, in the builder's own words, with the reading in it** (`{trigger.summary}` → "Response time (median over 5 minutes) is 760 ms"; `utils/triggerSummary.ts` mirrors the wizard's `triggerSentence` phrasing, states a hardware sensor's value in the install's display unit, reads an alarm bit as a STATE rather than "is 1", and falls back to the CONDITION when no reading is available rather than a sentence fragment). It covers every trigger type, not just metrics: a device-state alert reads "**Monitor status is down**" (the builder's `FIELD_META` label, never the column name) and an event alert names the **event that actually happened** rather than the pattern that was configured — "integration.discover.error on FMG-Ashfield" — with `{event.action|resource|resourceType|actor|level|message}` tokens behind matching facts rows, which for an event about an integration or a user are the only identifying facts the email has. **`{event.message}` is the event's own text — the REASON** ("Discovery failed: RPC -11 no valid session"), and it rides its own **Detail** row rather than `{message}`: the 12 seeded event automations set `messageTemplate: "{value}"` purely to surface that text, so a row of its own is what keeps the reason in the email when an operator replaces the message template. The chart that explains THAT trigger comes first (`{chart.trigger}` resolves via `chartTokenForMetric` against the new `Notification.metric`, which is stamped for asset_state fields too; the specific token for the same chart later in the body is deduped so it never appears twice). "Asset down" points at the response-time chart — the climb before the device stopped answering — and a **packet-loss chart** (`{chart.probeLoss}`, derived by bucketing `AssetMonitorSample` success/failure — 2-minute buckets scaled up so ~30 points cover the span, empty buckets skipped rather than plotted as healthy) carries the alerts where every probe failed and there is no latency left to plot; **its window follows the automation's own History** (`lossChartWindowMs` in the delivery drain reads the rule's trigger through the shared `probeLossWindowSec`, so the graph spans exactly the period the ratio that fired was measured over — the axis label and summary line state the real span), while CPU / memory / response time stay last-hour context. **Its caption quotes the window's PROBE ratio, not the mean of its buckets** (`probeLossSeriesFrom` returns both; `sparklineSvg`'s `avgOverride` prints the ratio): a mean of per-bucket ratios weighs a 10-probe bucket and a 1-probe bucket equally, so the caption drifted from the alert's own reading whenever sampling was uneven — a polling gap, the anchor trimming a partial bucket, a suppressed asset's 2× interval, or (while it ran) the ICMP loss sampler oversampling the failures that started it. Prod 2026-08-20 mailed "18.3 %" over a chart captioned "avg 6.7 %". The chart applies the ratio's **anchor** to its CAPTION ONLY (samples before the window's first success and before `Asset.recoveryStartedAt` are left out of the number, per (b) below) while the LINE plots the whole window: anchoring the picture too meant a loss graph that began when the device came back, so the outage the operator was paged about was missing from the chart sent to explain it. `probeLossSeriesFrom` returns `measuredFromMs` whenever the anchor excludes plotted samples and `sparklineSvg` draws it as a dashed **measured** rule (same clause on the text summary, for a reader whose client blocks images), so the loss to its left reads as outside the caption's number rather than as a contradiction of it — and with NO success in the window every row is measured and it reads 100 %, the widget's `includeFullyDown` semantics, because an asset-down alert embeds this chart too and a blank one there would read as "no loss". A hardware-sensor automation (**value or alarm — both**) charts the sensor's VALUE with the device's own alarm periods shaded (`{chart.sensor}`, keyed on `Notification.dimension` = the bare sensor name). A metric that reported nothing in the window is dropped from the body entirely rather than printing "no data". **An alert about ONE PORT gets no charts at all** and the port's **LLDP neighbour** instead (`isPortScopedAlert` in alertChartService → `services/alertInterfaceService.ts`'s `{interface.lldp}`): a switch with a dead port is answering probes — that is how the port is known to be down — so CPU, memory, response time and packet loss are all flat and healthy, and four graphs of a healthy device bury the finding. What the reader actually wants is what was plugged into port2, which the switch already told us. Only the interface STATE trio (`ifOperStatus` / `ifAdminStatus` / `poeStatus`) drops its charts — an `ifInErrorRate` / `ifOutBps` alert plausibly correlates with device load and keeps them, while still getting the LLDP block. The block is findable at all only because `persistLldpNeighbors` holds a vanished neighbour for a 48-hour sticky window, which is also why it always prints **Last advertised**: the row predates the outage by definition, so its staleness IS part of the finding. `{interface.lldp}` is DEFERRED like `{chart.*}` (`isDeferredToken` matches the whole `interface.` prefix) and expands to a complete `<tr>` with its own heading or to nothing, so no pruning pass of its own is needed; its plain-text form uses no colons anywhere, since `pruneEmptyTextLines` would otherwise delete the heading as a valueless "Label:" line. The default outbound body is a shared TEMPLATE (`src/utils/alertEmailTemplate.ts`), not server-side string building: a TWO-COLUMN header — severity line / subject / trigger sentence on the left, and the install’s **letterhead** right-aligned opposite it (`{brand.header}` → `services/alertBrandService.ts`: the logo as an inline CID attachment, the application name, the subtitle; a DEFERRED token like `{chart.*}`, so an escalation sent hours later carries the CURRENT branding rather than a fire-time snapshot). Which mark and whether the name prints are business rule 27’s decisions, not the email’s: the card is white so the LIGHT-inked `polaris-horiz-light.png` wordmark is the shipped choice, and because that art already spells the product name the name is printed only beside an operator’s OWN logo (which also picks up the accent composite when one is enabled), while the subtitle renders either way. Note the header is therefore a two-cell row — the exact label/value shape `pruneEmptyRows` deletes — and the one-cell `<table>` wrapped around the token is what keeps that pass from taking the headline along with an empty letterhead. Then severity header, the alert sentence — and **`{message}` is deliberately NOT printed under it in either body**, since the sentence is generated from the automation's own trigger and the message restates it ("Monitor status is down" over a grey "HARBOR-61F-1 is down"); the message keeps its real homes, the in-app alert card and every chat/push body, which carry no trigger sentence. A **recovery** is the one case where the message is not a restatement, so the three reset/resolved paths (`fireResolved` / `fireReset` / the operator-clear `runResetActionsForCleared`) stamp their sentence through `setRecoverySentence`, which writes the HEADLINE as well as `{message}` — re-rendering the recovered reading under a green "resolved" header would otherwise read as a fresh alert about a healthy device — a device facts table (IP, connected switch/AP, location, model, **description** — `{asset.description}`, last of the asset rows because it's the only free-text one and a paragraph must not push the identifying facts out of first glance; on a description-synced install this is the device's own admin description, business rule 14 — automation, raised-at), the **last hour of CPU / memory / response time as inline charts**, and **Acknowledge** + **Open device** buttons. The wizard prefills a new Notify action with those exact strings (`schema.defaultEmailTemplate`) so what Polaris sends is what the operator can edit; any piece left blank falls back to the same template server-side, so stored automations get the new body with no migration. Charts are built at DELIVERY time by `alertChartService` (SVG via `utils/sparklineSvg` → PNG via @resvg/resvg-js → inline `cid:` attachment) and degrade to a now/avg/peak text line whenever samples, the asset, or the rasterizer are unavailable. Rendered bodies are pruned (`pruneEmptyRows` / `pruneEmptyDivs` / `pruneEmptyTextLines` / `pruneDeadLinks` at compose time, `pruneEmptyChartSection` at delivery time once `substituteChartTokens` has decided which charts had data) so an under-populated device never mails blank cells, an empty headline, an `<a href="">` button, or a "LAST HOUR" heading over nothing. **`pruneEmptyRows` may never match across a nested `<table>` or a second `<tr>`** — see the alertEmailTemplate.ts entry in ARCHITECTURE.md: a container `<tr><td>` plus the first fact row's empty value cell reads as a label/value pair, and dropping that span took the facts table's opening tag with it and closed the 600px card early, so every alert about Polaris itself mailed a visibly broken box. **An alert about Polaris itself says so**: a system-scoped audit Event (capacity, backups, updates) names no resource, so `utils/alertSubject.ts` supplies `"Polaris server"` as the subject for the `{asset}` token, the stored `Notification.assetHostname` and the event-path cooldown key alike — before it those alerts had a blank headline and a subject line reading "[WARNING]  — Capacity severity escalated". The facts table's label column is a fixed 140px (auto layout gave the labels most of the card once the device rows pruned away) and "Raised" prints `{time.local}` — the server-timezone form — since ISO-8601 is both unfriendly and a 24-character unbreakable string that wrapped mid-token; `{time}` stays catalogued for operator templates that want the machine form.

#### PushSubscription

**PushSubscription** — a browser/PWA Web Push subscription owned by a User (`endpoint` unique + `p256dh`/`auth` keys). Stored via `POST /push-subscriptions`; the web_push channel sends to a recipient user's endpoints via `web-push` signed with the channel's VAPID keypair; a 410/404 prunes the row. Carries **`surface`** (`desktop` | `mobile`, default desktop — migration `20260807000000`): which Polaris surface enrolled, recorded at subscribe time because that's the only moment it's knowable (on Android the installed PWA and the browser share one subscription). It rides the delivery row's `meta` and selects the push deep link — mobile → `/mobile.html#more/alerts`, desktop → `/automations.html` (`pushDeepLinkUrl` in `src/utils/notificationTemplate.ts`, which — unlike `notificationsPageUrl` — falls back to a RELATIVE path instead of null when `POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL` is unset, so an unset public URL can't force every push to the desktop page). Endpoint rotation (`pushsubscriptionchange`) posts `oldEndpoint` alongside the new one; the retiring row's surface carries forward and the row is retired, scoped to the caller's own `userId`.

#### AutomationScript

**AutomationScript** — operator-authored script registry for Automation `script` actions (name unique, interpreter bash|sh|powershell|cmd|python3, body ≤64KB, runTarget server|agent|either, timeoutSec ≤600, sha256 recomputed every save, enabled). **RCE-equivalent surface**: CRUD + attaching script actions gated by the `automationScripts` key (seeded fullwrite only for admin-equivalent roles); creation + body changes stamp warning Events with old/new sha256. Owned by `automationScriptService`; routes at `/automations/scripts` (mounted before `/automations`).

#### AutomationScriptRun

**AutomationScriptRun** — one execution of a registry script (server- or agent-side): scriptName/sha256 snapshots, notificationId/ruleId/assetId (no FK), runOn, args snapshot, status pending|running|succeeded|failed|timeout, exitCode + stdout/stderr (≤64KB each). Server runs are claimed and executed by the `runAutomationScripts` job (5s) via `automationScriptRunner` (0600 temp file + execFile, args as a single argv, SIGKILL on timeout — never inline in the engine/drain). Two hardening properties of that executor: the interpreter resolves to a known **absolute path** where one exists rather than to whatever the inherited PATH names first (bare name only as a last-resort fallback, so a non-standard layout still runs), and the child environment is `process.env` **stripped of secret-shaped keys** (`buildScriptEnv`: `/SECRET|TOKEN|PASSWORD|PASSWD|DATABASE_URL|SESSION|CREDENTIAL|PRIVATE_KEY|_KEY$/i` — a denylist, so PATH/HOME/proxy/locale stay inherited and existing scripts keep working). The scrub matters because **stdout is STORED on the run row and rendered in the Scripts tab**: before it, a one-line `env` copied `DATABASE_URL` and `POLARIS_SECRET_KEY` into a displayed, backed-up column. Authoring a script is already RCE-equivalent so this crosses no privilege boundary — it removes the accidental copy; agent runs ride the AgentCommand queue (`run_script` payload, sha256-verified by the Go `scriptexec` package, results via `/agents/command-result`); pruned after ~90 days.

#### AgentCommand

**AgentCommand** — the agent command queue. The only queued action is **agent-side script runs** (`action="run_script"`, nullable `payload` Json `{runId, interpreter, body, sha256, args, timeoutSec}` — body inline ≤64KB, sha256 VERIFIED by the agent before executing; queued only for active agents ≥0.13.0 via `requestScriptRun`'s version gate, linked to `AutomationScriptRun.agentCommandId`). Agent polls `GET /agents/commands` (the ≤20s poll is the guaranteed floor; a `commands-pending` WS frame wakes it sooner — see `agentCommandWake`), executes via the `scriptexec` sandbox, reports `POST /agents/command-result` (exitCode/stdout/stderr, ≤64KB each). The agent never self-acts and refuses unknown actions. **Process/service start/stop/restart control was removed** (Satellite-posture change, 2026-07): the `stop`/`start`/`restart` actions, their routes, and the agent-side servicecontrol collectors are gone; the `processControl` RBAC key remains in the catalogue but gates nothing.

#### ManagedAgent

**ManagedAgent** — Polaris Agent install record per Asset (os/arch, agent version, install credential, cert-pin set for dual-pin rotation, `installScriptId` = curated OS-locked install-method variant from the `agentInstallScripts` catalog — null = per-OS default). `privilegeTier` (Linux-only, default `"unprivileged"`) selects the systemd unit: **`unprivileged`** = the hardened `DynamicUser`/`NoNewPrivileges`/`ProtectSystem=strict` unit; **`ptrace`** = that same hardened unit plus `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_SYS_PTRACE CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH`, the pair that lets the agent read other users' `/proc/<pid>/fd` for Application Map connection→PID attribution WITHOUT full root — both are required: the fd dir's open is a DAC check only DAC_READ_SEARCH passes, the readlink is the ptrace check (SYS_PTRACE alone collects zero rows; prod 2026-07-29). Operator opt-in with a warning — the pair also permits reading any process's memory and any file on the host. Unit text is written only at install/reinstall, so pre-fix ptrace agents need a reinstall; the agent (≥0.17.1, Linux) reports its actual CapEff on heartbeat (`ManagedAgent.reportedCapEff`, decoded by `utils/capEff`) so the Privilege surfaces render the VERIFIED state — a stale SYS_PTRACE-only unit shows red "reinstall" instead of looking healthy. Full **root** was retired with service control (Satellite-posture change); `privilegeTier="root"` survives only as a legacy value on pre-migration rows and is never emitted for new installs — reinstalling such an agent downgrades it to `unprivileged`/`ptrace`. Windows agents always run as LocalSystem, macOS LaunchDaemons as root, so the tier is Linux-only. The tier maps to the `[Service]` block in `src/utils/agentUnit.ts` (pure, `linuxServiceBlock`/`normalizePrivilegeTier`). The privilege change on reinstall rides `POST /assets/:id/agent/reinstall` (`privilegeTier` body field).

#### UserTableTabs

**UserTableTabs** — per-user list-page TABS (the Assets page tab strip): one row per `(user, scope)` holding `{version, tabs[{id, name, state, savedFilterId?, savedFilterName?}], activeId}`. Each tab carries its own filter+sort `state` (validated by the same `sanitizeFilterState` a preset uses); a tab opened from a preset keeps only a REFERENCE for its label — editing it never writes back, since the preset may be someone else's. Strictly per-caller, no Event audit, CASCADES with the user (the UserDashboard pattern — nothing here is shared, unlike a public SavedTableFilter, which deliberately outlives its author). Absent row = the default single tab, materialized client-side and persisted only once the operator changes something. ≤20 tabs; a stale `activeId` is repaired to the first tab rather than 400-ing the layout away.

#### SavedTableFilter

**SavedTableFilter** — a named, optionally SHARED snapshot of one list page's table filter + sort state (Assets page → Filters ▾). `scope` names the table ("assets" today) and maps to the RBAC function key that already gates that page (`SAVED_FILTER_SCOPES` in `savedFilterService`) — no new permission key. `visibility` is `private` (owner only) or `public` (anyone who can read the scope; publishing needs `<key>:write`, deleting someone else's needs `<key>:fullwrite`). `state` is the TableSF `getPrefs` shape `{ sfFilters, sortKey, sortDir }`, re-validated by `sanitizeFilterState` on every write because a public preset is replayed into other operators' browsers; column widths/visibility deliberately stay per-browser in localStorage. `ownerId` is SetNull (a shared preset outlives its author; the users DELETE drops only their private rows), with `ownerName` snapshotted for display. Same `(scope, owner, name)` save updates rather than duplicating.

#### TopologyLayout

**TopologyLayout** — SHARED Device Map topology node positions, one row per (siteId = FortiGate Asset id, view = `"flat"` | `computeFloorViews` building/floor key); `positions` = `{nodeId: {x,y}}` pixel coords. Written full-replace by operator drags in the topology modal (debounced PUT, gated `deviceMap=write`, last-write-wins); embedded for every viewer as `savedLayouts` on `GET /map/sites/:id/topology` — server layout wins over the per-browser localStorage fallback. Cascades with the site Asset. Single writer: `topologyLayoutService`.

#### Event

**Event** — audit log, 7-day rolling retention. Four per-asset **change events** are written edge-triggered and **unconditionally** (never behind the `change.*` family's subscription gate, since they're rare and wanted in the audit log regardless): `asset.firmware.changed` (os/osVersion), `asset.switch_port.changed` (`lastSeenSwitch`), `asset.wireless_ap.changed` (`lastSeenAp` — every roam), `asset.gateway_firewall.changed` (the freshest `AssetFortigateSighting` flipped gate). Row builders are pure and centralized in `eventLogService`; firmware deliberately suppresses a null→value first learn (that's identification, already covered by `asset.discovered`/`asset.discovery_updated`) while a connection event reports it. Discovery emits them from an end-of-run baseline rather than at each write, because Phase 7 vs Phase 11 (coarse-then-corrected `osVersion`) and Phase 7 vs Phase 7.5 (two formats for the same switch port) ping-pong within a single run. All four appear in the automations change-trigger picker. See TOUCHES.md → cross-cutting/asset-change-events.

#### DiscoveryRun

**DiscoveryRun** — per-integration discovery-run state (status / actor / progress counts / timestamps); one row per integration (`integrationId` unique). `scopeDeviceName` marks a single-FortiGate scoped re-discovery (`POST /assets/:id/rediscover` — full run machinery narrowed to one FMG device; finalize runs `"finalize-scoped"` = Phase 2b per-controller switch/AP decommission only, never the roster-based sweeps).

#### Setting

**Setting** — key-value config store (`manualMonitorSettings`, `sampleRetention`, `mapRegions`, `agentEventLog`, `branding` (appName / subtitle / logoUrl / **`logoAccent`** + **`logoOnLogin`** + **`logoOnSidebar`** — see business rule 27 — + **`temperatureUnit`** — the install-wide DISPLAY-ONLY °C/°F choice for hardware sensors, Server Settings → Customization → Display Units. Samples are always collected, stored, rolled up and ALERTED ON in Celsius; the frontends convert at render via `public/js/temp-unit.js`, gated on each reading's own stored unit so fan RPM / voltage rails are untouched, and automation thresholds stay °C. It rides branding because that payload is unauthenticated, cached in localStorage for synchronous reads, and reaches the identity-less Dash wallboard), `appMapAutoMap`, `backupSchedule`, `backup_history`, `assetSourcePriority`, `reservationMacPlaceholder`, `loginAccessConfig`, etc.). `assetSourcePriority` (`{order[], integrationPrefix}`, Assets → Settings → Sources) orders which discovery source's learned location wins — see business rule 22. `reservationMacPlaceholder` (`{prefix}`, default `02:0F:5E`, Server Settings → Identification) is the OUI every generated placeholder MAC starts with, and the only thing marking such a MAC as synthetic — see business rule 26. `agentEventLog` (`{enabled, minLevel, windowsChannels, linuxMinPriority, maxPerPush, perAssetHourlyCap}`, default disabled) tunes the OS event-log → audit Event ingest (`osEventLogService`); ingested host events become `os_event.<channel>` Events (resourceType=asset) visible in the Events tab.

#### Tag

**Tag** / **GeocodeCache** — registry tables. `Tag` carries an optional **auto-assignment device filter**; when set, `tagAssignmentService` keeps the tag synced onto matching assets (managed sync — adds AND removes on drift). `assetCondition` is the shape: the SAME nested AND/OR condition tree the automations device filter and `Contact.assetCondition` store, validated against `DEVICE_FILTER_FIELD_OPS` and evaluated by the same `evaluateScopeCondition`, so "which devices?" is asked in one language across all three surfaces (and edited in one place — the shared `PolarisConditionBuilder`). It supersedes the flat `criteria` blob it shipped with (manufacturer/model/os/osVersion/hostname/department/location/assetType/status/subnet + the relation-backed `integration` and `fortigate`): both columns are still READ but only ONE is live per row (a write of either clears the other), pre-cutover rows fold forward through the pure `criteriaToCondition` on read, and the `migrateTagFilterShape` one-shot persists it — the `Contact` cutover repeated verbatim. `integration` is the one flat field with no tree equivalent, so a blob carrying it stays on the legacy predicate rather than being half-converted. Two asymmetries with `Contact`, both load-bearing: an **EMPTY tree is NO filter, never "all devices"** (a contact stores `and([])` deliberately as the form of an explicit All-devices checkbox; a tag has no such control, so an empty tree could only come from a half-built form and honoring it would tag the whole fleet on save), and a **decommissioned asset is skipped unless the filter mentions status** (implicit in the flat resolver's `buildPrefilterWhere`, stated explicitly for the tree so the shape cutover couldn't quietly begin tagging retired inventory). **The "Map Regions" category is locked to the Device Map**: the tag registry refuses creating a tag there and refuses MOVING one in (the same act), and a tag in it may not carry a filter at all — those tag names are already managed by the region reconcile through `RegionTagAssignment`, and a second managed-sync engine on the same NAME would spend every cycle undoing the first. Editing the map's own rows is unaffected. **TagAutoAssignment** is the per-(tag,asset) provenance table that lets managed sync strip auto-applied copies without ever touching a hand-applied copy of the same tag name. **RegionTagAssignment** is the same pattern for `region:<name>` tags (`mapRegionService`): one row per (regionId, targetType asset|subnet, targetId) the reconciler itself tagged, keyed by region id so a rename doesn't disturb it — what lets the daily/6h re-evaluation strip a region tag off a device that MOVED (re-pinned gate, repointed switch, re-served subnet) while never touching operator hand-attachments or tags predating provenance.

---

## API Endpoints

All routes are prefixed `/api/v1/`. Auth guards are applied in `src/api/router.ts`.

### Auth — public
- `POST   /auth/login`
- `POST   /auth/logout`
- `GET    /auth/me`                             — Session probe. Returns `{ authenticated: false }` for unauthenticated callers; otherwise `{ authenticated: true, username, authProvider, role: { id, name, color, isProtected, permissions, updatedAt }, regionTags: { user, role, group, effective }, otherTags: { user, role, group, effective } }` (`color` read live each call; `group` is re-resolved from `User.ssoGroups` via `resolveGroupsToAccess` so a GroupMapping edit shows next page load without re-login). The frontend reads `role.permissions[functionKey]` to gate menu items / buttons (see `permAtLeast()` in `public/js/app.js`).
- `GET    /auth/azure/config`                   — Azure SSO feature flag
- `GET    /auth/azure/login`                    — Initiate Azure SAML login
- `POST   /auth/azure/callback`                 — SAML assertion callback
- `POST   /auth/azure/logout`                    — SAML single-logout
- `GET    /auth/oidc/config`                    — OIDC feature flag (login page button)
- `GET    /auth/oidc/login`                     — Initiate OIDC Authorization-Code login (stashes state/nonce/PKCE in session, redirects to IdP)
- `GET    /auth/oidc/callback`                  — OIDC code exchange + ID-token validation + provision. Top-level GET, so SameSite=Lax session cookies are sent (unlike the SAML POST callback)
- `GET    /auth/entra-proxy/config`             — Entra App Proxy header-SSO flag: `{ enabled, available }` (`available` = this request arrived from an allowlisted connector carrying identity headers → drives the fallback login button; booleans only). Public.
- `GET    /auth/entra-proxy/login`              — Read Entra App Proxy identity headers on THIS request, validate source-IP trust, provision, stamp session, redirect to validated `?next=` (default `/`). Both the login-page button and the app.ts silent auto-login land here; all failures redirect to `/login.html?error=…`. Rate-limited (`entraProxyLoginLimiter`, 60/5min).
- LDAP login uses the shared `POST /auth/login` form (routes to LDAP when the account is an LDAP user or the username is unknown and LDAP is enabled)
- SSO/LDAP config (admin, `serverSettingsSystem:write`): `GET|PUT /auth/azure/settings` + `POST /auth/azure/test`, `GET|PUT /auth/oidc/settings` + `POST /auth/oidc/test`, `GET|PUT /auth/ldap/settings` + `POST /auth/ldap/test`, `GET|PUT /auth/entra-proxy/settings` + `POST /auth/entra-proxy/test`
- `POST   /auth/login/totp`                     — Second step of two-phase login when TOTP is enabled. Body: `{ pendingToken, code, isBackupCode? }`. `pendingToken` is returned by `POST /auth/login` whenever the caller's account has `totpEnabledAt` set — until this endpoint consumes it, the session is not issued.

### TOTP self-management — `requireAuth`
- `GET    /auth/totp/status`                    — `{ authProvider, enabled, enrolling, backupCodesRemaining }`
- `POST   /auth/totp/enroll`                    — Starts enrollment for the current user. Returns `{ secret, otpauthUri, qrSvg }`. Only allowed on `authProvider = "local"` accounts that are not already fully enrolled.
- `POST   /auth/totp/confirm`                   — Finalize enrollment by verifying the first 6-digit code. Body: `{ code }`. Returns `{ ok, backupCodes: string[] }` — shown once.
- `DELETE /auth/totp`                           — Self-disable. Requires a current TOTP or backup code. Body: `{ code, isBackupCode? }`.

### IP Blocks — `requireAuth`
- `GET    /blocks`                              — List (filter by tag, ipVersion)
- `POST   /blocks`
- `GET    /blocks/:id`                          — Get + utilization summary
- `PUT    /blocks/:id`
- `DELETE /blocks/:id`                          — 409 if active reservations exist

### Subnets — `requireAuth`
- `GET    /subnets`                             — List (filter by blockId, status, tag, createdBy)
- `POST   /subnets`
- `GET    /subnets/:id`                         — Get + reservation list
- `PUT    /subnets/:id`
- `DELETE /subnets/:id`                         — 409 if active reservations exist
- `POST   /subnets/next-available`              — Auto-allocate next available subnet of given prefix length
- `POST   /subnets/bulk-allocate`                — Allocate multiple subnets in one call from a template. Body: `{ blockId, prefix, entries: [{name, prefixLength, vlan?} | {skip: true, prefixLength}], tags?, anchorPrefix? }`. Each non-skip entry becomes a subnet named `<prefix>_<entry.name>` (e.g. `Riverbend_Hardware`). **Skip entries** reserve address space inside the packed region without creating a subnet — used to leave gaps between allocations. **Anchor-based, all-or-nothing:** entries are packed into a single contiguous region aligned to `max(anchorPrefix, smallest-block-containing-the-group)`; `anchorPrefix` defaults to 24 if omitted. The whole call happens in one transaction — either every subnet is created or none are. Response: `{ created, anchorCidr, effectiveAnchorPrefix }`.
- `POST   /subnets/bulk-allocate/preview`        — Non-mutating preview of the above. Same body minus `prefix` and `tags`, with a lenient entry schema (no name required) so the modal can live-update footprint while the user is still filling rows. Response: `{ fits, anchorCidr, effectiveAnchorPrefix, assignments, totalAddresses, slashTwentyFourCount, blockCidr, error }`.
- `GET    /subnets/archived`                     *(subnets:read)* — retired subnets, newest first (business rule 41). Query `?cidr=&blockId=&fortigateSerial=&limit=&offset=`; `cidr` is a substring match, `limit` defaults 50 / caps 200, and `total` is the UNPAGED match count. Each row carries `_count.reservations`. MUST stay declared before `GET /subnets/:id`, or `/subnets/archived` is captured as a subnet id.
- `GET    /subnets/archived/:id`                 *(subnets:read)* — one retirement with every `ArchivedReservation` it held, ordered by address.
- `POST   /subnets/:id/archive`                  *(subnets:**fullwrite**)* — retire a subnet: snapshot it + its reservations into the archive, then delete the live row, freeing its CIDR so a replacement gate's identical address space can be recorded. Returns `{ archivedSubnetId, cidr, reservationCount }` and writes one `subnet.archived` Event. `fullwrite` rather than the ownership-aware `write` every other mutation on this router uses: a discovered subnet carries `createdBy: null` so an ownership-scoped caller could never reach one anyway, and retiring a site's address space is not an own-rows action. Deliberately NOT subject to business rule 4's active-reservation protection — that guards against accidental DESTRUCTION, and this preserves everything it moves.
- `POST   /subnets/:id/refresh`                  *(user-or-above)* — Per-subnet "refresh from device" action invoked by the **Refresh** button in the IP panel slide-in. Queries the originating FortiGate for ONE DHCP scope (CMDB reservations + live leases) using whichever transport the integration is configured for (FMG proxy / FMG direct / standalone FortiGate REST), reconciles against Polaris's reservation rows for the same subnet, and bumps `Subnet.lastDiscoveredAt` on success.
