## Multi-process architecture

Polaris can run as one process (default) or split across specialized processes
that coordinate through the shared PostgreSQL + pg-boss queue (the SolarWinds
Orion model: many supervised services + a grouping wrapper). The role is chosen
by `POLARIS_ROLE`; capability gating lives in `src/utils/role.ts` (`roleConfig`),
and `src/app.ts` branches on the capability flags at boot.

| Role | Boots | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `all` (default, unset) | everything | Local dev (`npm run dev`) — runs everything in one process for fast iteration. Not a production deployment target since Phase 3 (no `polaris.service` unit is shipped). |
| `web` | Express/HTTPS/agent-WS, **all singleton schedulers**, one-shot migrations, pg-boss **producer** connection, **sample/probe write buffers** (the Polaris Agent `/samples` + `/probe-now` endpoints ingest here, so the web role must run the flush tick or agent-sourced rows never persist) | Single instance — the control plane. Owns the in-app updater (restarts the whole group). |
| `monitor` | pg-boss **monitor-queue consumers** + floating pool, sample/probe write buffers | Run **N replicas** — pg-boss hands each job to exactly one worker, so replicas never double-execute. |
| `discovery` | pg-boss **discovery-queue consumer** (`runDiscovery`) | Executes discovery runs off the `polaris-discovery-run` queue. |

**Discovery is queue-backed.** `triggerDiscovery` (route + scheduler) validates,
upserts a `queued` `DiscoveryRun`, and `publishDiscoveryJob`s to the
`polaris-discovery-run` queue (singletonKey = integrationId → one active run per
integration). The discovery worker runs `runDiscovery`, transitioning the
`DiscoveryRun` row (queued → running → completed/aborted/error) and flushing a
progress accumulator to it; the web process reads that row for the
`/discoveries` endpoint, `isDiscoveryRunning`, the slow-run check, and renders
cancel by setting `cancelRequested` (the worker polls it → aborts its local
AbortController). When pg-boss is off (cursor mode), `triggerDiscovery` runs
`runDiscovery` in-process — the single code path across topologies. See
`src/services/discoveryRunState.ts` and `DiscoveryRun` in the domain model.

**Cancel has two tiers.** The abort signal is observed natively by every HTTP
transport under discovery (fgRequest 15s cap, FMG rpc 10s cap + bounded
retries, geocoder 8s) and cooperatively by `syncDhcpSubnets`, which throws
`DiscoveryAbortError` at each `phaseMark` boundary (`utils/errors.ts` —
`name="AbortError"` so the terminal handler counts the run as aborted, not
errored; the `__end__` mark is exempt so a fully-committed sync isn't
discarded). For wedges the signal cannot reach — a Prisma query blocked on a
Postgres lock has no statement timeout, ignores the signal, and keeps the 60s
heartbeat ticking so the reaper never fires either (prod incident 2026-07-20:
one FortiGate held a run "running" 5+ hours through a cancel) —
`discoveryCancelWatchdog` is armed on abort and disarmed in runDiscovery's
finally: if the run hasn't unwound 2 minutes after abort, it logs the stuck
devices, finalizes the row `aborted`, writes `integration.discover.force_exit`,
and exits 1 so systemd/NSSM restarts the process (same exit-and-restart pattern
as the operator /restart endpoint). Under `all`/cursor-mode-fallback the exit
takes the whole process — matching /restart semantics. If pg-boss redelivers
the interrupted job, runDiscovery sees `cancelRequested` still set at startup
and aborts cleanly.

**Singletons** (monitor producer ticks, discovery scheduler, reconcilers,
rollups, prune, one-shot migrations) are pinned to `web`/`all` so they run in
exactly one process; monitor/discovery stay pure consumers.

**Connection budgeting.** Each process opens its own Prisma + pg-boss pool, so
the group footprint ≈ `(monitor replicas + 2) × per-process pool`. Size so it
stays under Postgres `max_connections` (PgBouncer absorbs the Prisma pools but
pg-boss pools always hit Postgres directly). Each process emits
`polaris_db_pool_role_capacity{role}`; the Capacity Advisor's max_connections
model multiplies by `POLARIS_MONITOR_REPLICAS` (and `peakObserved` is already
group-wide via `pg_stat_activity`).

**Deployment.** systemd: `polaris-migrate.service` (oneshot, sole migrator) →
`polaris-web.service` / `polaris-monitor@.service` (templated, N) /
`polaris-discovery.service`, grouped by `polaris.target` (`systemctl start
polaris.target`). Docker: one image, per-service `POLARIS_ROLE`, a one-shot
`migrate` compose service the app services gate on, plus an `nginx` service
fronting the stack. The single-process `polaris.service` unit was removed
in Phase 3 — every fresh install via `deploy/setup-*.sh` lands the split-role
+ nginx layout. The `all` role still exists in `src/utils/role.ts` so
`npm run dev` keeps working; it's a runtime mode, not a production
deployment target. See [docs/INSTALL.md](docs/INSTALL.md).

**Per-role metrics endpoint.** prom-client registries are per-process. The
web role exposes `/metrics` on its main HTTPS listener; monitor and discovery
boot a standalone HTTP listener via [src/utils/metricsServer.ts](src/utils/metricsServer.ts)
when `POLARIS_METRICS_PORT` is set. The shipped unit files pin the monitor
template to `910N` (instance N → 9101/9102/…) and discovery to `9110`, both
on `127.0.0.1`. Prometheus must scrape every role endpoint or panels that
depend on consumer-stamped metrics (`polaris_probe_*`, `polaris_monitor_work_duration_seconds`,
`polaris_sample_write_duration_seconds`, `polaris_discovery_*`,
`polaris_fmg_worker_queue_depth` / `_inflight`) silently show no data on the
Grafana dashboard. Dashboard queries already `sum()` across instances, so
panels populate as soon as the scrape job is complete. See
[docs/grafana/README.md](docs/grafana/README.md) for an example scrape job.

**nginx-front HTTPS (only mode post-Phase-4).** nginx terminates TLS for the lifetime of the install. Polaris listens HTTP-only on `127.0.0.1:${PORT:-3000}` and reads nginx's cert at `POLARIS_PROXY_CERT_PATH` to surface the fingerprint each Polaris Agent pins. `POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL` is required — [src/utils/runtimeConfig.ts](src/utils/runtimeConfig.ts) fails fast at boot if it's missing. [src/utils/proxyMode.ts](src/utils/proxyMode.ts) is the single lazy check (no module-load caching, so Vitest tests + runtime config reloads see fresh state). [src/utils/trustProxy.ts](src/utils/trustProxy.ts) resolves the Express `trust proxy` setting — operator override > default `"1"` (first-hop trust) — without mutating `process.env`. [src/services/certInfo.ts](src/services/certInfo.ts) reads the PEM from disk with a layered cache keyed on file-content hash and last-known-good fallback that survives certbot-style atomic-rename windows; public API (`getServerCertFingerprint`, `getServerCertHostnames`, `getServerCertExpiry`) is consumed by the agent-install path and `GET /server-settings/https`. [src/utils/publicUrl.ts](src/utils/publicUrl.ts) parses `POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL` to derive the public-facing port stamped into agent.conf. The nginx reference config at [deploy/nginx/polaris.conf](deploy/nginx/polaris.conf) ships HTTP/2 + HTTP/3 listeners (TCP/443 + UDP/443) on the same vhost with `Alt-Svc` advertising HTTP/3 to browsers; requires nginx ≥ 1.25 (setup scripts pull from nginx.org's mainline repo if RHEL AppStream is older). Fresh installs land split-role + nginx + a self-signed cert via [deploy/setup-rhel.sh](deploy/setup-rhel.sh) / [setup-ubuntu.sh](deploy/setup-ubuntu.sh); existing installs use [deploy/migrate-to-nginx.sh](deploy/migrate-to-nginx.sh).

**Phase 2 dual-pin** lifts the "fleet-wide re-install on every cert rotation" caveat. Each `ManagedAgent` row carries `serverCertFingerprint` (canonical) + `additionalServerCertFingerprints String[]` (staged). The union is the agent's trust set; rotation is operator-driven via the Maintenance card's "Cert pin rotation" pane (`POST /server-settings/agents/cert-pins/bulk-add` and `/bulk-remove`). The agent.conf format gained `cert_fingerprints = pin1,pin2,...` (Go agent parses the union; pre-Phase-2 binaries still read the legacy `cert_fingerprint` line for downgrade safety). When the operator stages a new pin, the server pushes via WS `refresh-config` and online agents apply within seconds (offline agents pick it up on next /config poll); agents Save() the new pin set + exit via `os.Exit(0)` so systemd cycles the process with the new pin set live. See cross-cutting/polaris-agent → "Cert pin rotation" in [TOUCHES.md](TOUCHES.md) for the full lockstep checklist.

**In-app nginx GUI (Server Settings → Certificates).** Operator-facing GUI for six nginx directives (HTTPS listen port, HTTP/3 toggle, TLS protocols, HSTS, Prometheus allow-list — plus cert rotation via the dual-pin stage→swap→retire workflow). Trust model: the polaris OS user has narrow sudo via `/etc/sudoers.d/polaris-nginx` granting only `/usr/local/sbin/polaris-nginx-apply` (shipped as [deploy/scripts/polaris-nginx-apply.sh](deploy/scripts/polaris-nginx-apply.sh)). Subcommands take NO user-supplied paths — staged files live at hardcoded `/run/polaris-nginx-stage/` locations set up by `/etc/tmpfiles.d/polaris-nginx.conf`, and the wrapper holds `flock /run/polaris-nginx-apply.lock` + `timeout 30` for every op. Setup scripts (setup-rhel.sh + setup-rhel-nodb.sh + setup-ubuntu.sh + setup-ubuntu-nodb.sh + migrate-to-nginx.sh) install the wrapper/sudoers/tmpfiles and add the polaris user to the nginx group (or Ubuntu's `www-data` group) so the existing fingerprint pane reads the `0640 root:nginx` cert file directly; existing installs pick the same helpers up through [src/services/updateService.ts](src/services/updateService.ts)'s sync block on every in-app update.

The shipped reference config at [deploy/nginx/polaris.conf](deploy/nginx/polaris.conf) is mirrored by a template at [deploy/nginx/polaris.conf.template](deploy/nginx/polaris.conf.template) that Polaris renders from an operator-settable `proxyConfig` Setting row plus env-derived server_name / upstream port. [src/services/nginxRenderer.ts](src/services/nginxRenderer.ts) substitutes the placeholder tokens and emits the rendered file + sha256 (used downstream for drift detection). [src/services/nginxConfigParser.ts](src/services/nginxConfigParser.ts) is the bootstrap-only counterpart: regex-based extraction of the same six directives out of a live `/etc/nginx/conf.d/polaris.conf` so first boot of this feature seeds the `proxyConfig` row from whatever the operator already has on disk (rather than auto-clobbering). `ProxyConfig` shape lives in [src/types/proxyConfig.ts](src/types/proxyConfig.ts). [src/services/proxyConfigService.ts](src/services/proxyConfigService.ts) is the Setting-table accessor (cached, validated; rejects HTTP/3-with-TLS-1.2-only, port out of 1..65535, etc.). [src/services/privilegedSysadmin.ts](src/services/privilegedSysadmin.ts) wraps the sudo call with output capture + timeout. [src/services/nginxApplyService.ts](src/services/nginxApplyService.ts) is the orchestrator: `applyProxyConfig` renders + stages + sudoes the wrapper + records sha256; `rotateCertAndKey` does libcrypto SPKI cert+key pair validation, atomic-renames, invalidates [src/services/certInfo.ts](src/services/certInfo.ts)'s cache via the new `invalidateCache()` export; `preflightCertRotation` returns the new cert metadata + the current canonical fingerprint (so the GUI knows which old pin to retire via the existing `/agents/cert-pins/bulk-remove` after rotation); `bootstrapProxyConfig` runs once at boot via [src/jobs/bootstrapProxyConfig.ts](src/jobs/bootstrapProxyConfig.ts) (no-op outside proxy mode or when the row already exists); `getDriftStatus` compares the live file hash to `lastAppliedHash` for the refuse-and-banner UX. Beyond the six operator-settable directives the shipped config also carries request-body limits that are NOT operator-settable: `client_max_body_size 8m` at the server level (nginx's 1m default sat below the app's own per-route ceilings and 413'd them at the edge) plus a dedicated `location` for `/api/v1/server-settings/database/restore` that lifts the limit (`0`) and sets `proxy_request_buffering off`, since a restore is a whole-database `pg_dump` streamed to disk with no `fileSize` of its own. The rendered config additionally carries the **`location = /api` docs allow block** (`{{API_DOCS_ALLOW_BLOCK}}`), which is NOT a proxyConfig directive: it renders from the separate `apiDocsConfig` Setting via [src/services/apiDocsAccessService.ts](src/services/apiDocsAccessService.ts)'s `deriveApiDocsNginxAllow`, threaded into `RenderInput.apiDocsAllow` at both render call sites (`applyProxyConfig`, and updateService's restart-time sync — which falls back to the shipped default on a read error rather than aborting). It is defense in depth only — the app-level gate in `src/app.ts` is authoritative on every install type — and the parser deliberately never seeds `apiDocsConfig` from nginx: its `allow`-line collection is scoped to the `/metrics*` location blocks (`extractLocationBlocks`) so the docs block's RFC1918 allows can't cross-contaminate `prometheusAllowIps` at bootstrap. A save of the docs scope best-effort re-applies nginx from `PUT /server-settings/api-docs` when (proxy mode ∧ wrapper installed ∧ managedMode ∧ no drift), reported in the PUT response, never failing the save. These blocks are why `nginxConfigParser` expects **9** location blocks — see TOUCHES.md → cross-cutting/deployment for the lockstep rule.

Routes live in [src/api/routes/proxySettings.ts](src/api/routes/proxySettings.ts), mounted at `/api/v1/server-settings/proxy/*` ABOVE the blanket `serverSettingsSystem:read` gate so each route declares its own permission level (read on GET, fullwrite on PUT / `/apply` / `/adopt-managed-mode` / `/cert/preflight` / `/cert/rotate`). The cert rotation flow is orchestrated by the frontend modal in [public/js/server-settings.js](public/js/server-settings.js)'s `openRotateCertModal`: it calls `/cert/preflight` (libcrypto validate + return new metadata) → `/agents/cert-pins/bulk-add` (stage the new pin on every active agent so they accept both old + new while reconnecting) → `/cert/rotate` (sudo wrapper atomic-renames the cert files + reloads nginx) → `/agents/cert-pins/bulk-remove` (retire the old pin once uptake is verified). Adopt-managed-mode gate: `proxyConfig.managedMode` starts at `false` on every install; the GUI shows a yellow drift banner (with drift markers from the regex parser) and disables the controls until the operator clicks "Adopt managed mode." In-app updates render the template only when `managedMode=true` and refuse-to-clobber on sha256-drift.

## Monitoring Architecture

> Moved from CLAUDE.md's Authentication & RBAC section. Covers polling-method resolution, the Polaris Agent, branch-class FortiGate workarounds, per-class FortiSwitch/FortiAP direct polling, push toggles, and verbose-logging behavior.

**Polling-method redesign (resolved per stream from a four-tier hierarchy).** There is no longer a per-asset `monitorType` column. Each of the six streams (response-time probe / CPU+memory / temperature / interfaces / LLDP / storage) gets a polling method picked from a hierarchy: per-asset `*Polling` columns → `MonitorClassOverride.*Polling` → `Integration.config.monitorSettings.polling.*` (or the manual-tier `manualMonitorSettings.*Polling` Setting for orphan assets) → source default. Source defaults: FMG/FortiGate → **`icmp`** on response-time, `rest_api` on CPU+memory / temperature / interfaces, **`disabled`** on LLDP, **`disabled`** on storage (FortiOS appliances don't expose meaningful mountable storage, so the SNMP storage walk would burn cycles on every scrape — operators flip storage to `snmp` per-asset when they have a device that does); AD / Entra ID / Windows Server / Manual → `icmp` for response-time, null (= "not delivered") on the other five; **vCenter → `vcenter` on response-time, CPU+memory, interfaces AND storage** (temperature + LLDP null), because one batched fetch per integration per tick answers all four for both VMs and ESXi hosts — see "vCenter Discovery Workflow". Response-time defaults to ICMP across every source kind because ICMP is the cheapest universal liveness probe — operators wanting a heavier transport (REST `/sys/status`, SNMP `sysUpTime`) opt in per-asset, per-class, or at the integration tier. The compatibility matrix from `utils/pollingCompatibility.ts` enumerates the methods each source can use plus `"disabled"` (universally allowed; expresses "do not poll this stream") and `"agent"` (Polaris Agent installed locally on the host — allowed on AD / Entra / Windows Server / Manual sources only, never appliances). The storage stream is **SNMP or vCenter** (HOST-RESOURCES-MIB `hrStorageTable` + the vendor disk fallback in `pickVendorProfileMerged`; or the guest filesystems / host-mounted datastores in the vCenter warm cache); operators set `storagePolling=snmp` at any tier to opt in on an SNMP device, and the SNMP collector reuses the asset's interfaces credential (no separate storage credential / MIB column on Asset or MonitorClassOverride). The dedicated storage-only cadence (`runStorageFor`) stays SNMP-only — vCenter storage rides the system-info pass, which is already one Map lookup. Methods that don't apply to the asset's source kind are silently ignored at resolution time; the route layer rejects them at write time with a clear 400.

**FortiOS REST reachability gates the FMG source defaults (2026-08-28).** The `rest_api` defaults above assume Polaris can make a FortiOS call to the device. On a **FortiManager on the proxy transport with no `fortigateApiToken`** it cannot: every FortiOS collector builds its config through `buildFortinetConfig()`, which has **no `useProxy` branch** — it dials the asset's own IP and requires that token — so `rest_api` on CPU+memory / temperature / interfaces threw `409 FortiManager direct-mode API token not configured` on every tick, forever, on an integration left at its defaults. `loadIntegrationTierSettings` now stamps a `tierFortiosRestUnavailableCache` sidecar off the config it already reads (no extra query, invalidated with the tier cache), and `defaultPollingForSource(source, stream, {assetType, fortiosRestUnavailable})` returns `disabled` for those three instead. **Response time is deliberately unchanged (`icmp`)** — moving it would silently change how up/down is decided for every gate on every affected install. The one exception is a managed FortiSwitch / FortiAP's response time, which stays `rest_api`: that read goes to the PARENT gate's controller table via `fetchViaFortinetTransport`, the one monitoring path that honours `useProxy`, so it works on FMG's own credential. The shared predicate is `fortiosRestUsable(stream, assetType)`.

**Compatibility vs capability (2026-08-28).** `utils/pollingCompatibility.ts` says whether a method is MEANINGFUL for a source; `utils/pollingCapability.ts` says whether the COLLECTOR EXISTS. Only the write validators' silence about the second let a stream be configured into permanent quiet — `ssh`/`winrm` on cpuMemory / temperature / interfaces / storage / lldp, `snmp` on processes, `rest_api` on FortiOS storage or on anything beyond up/down for a managed FortiSwitch, and `eventLog` on every transport but the agent all resolve fine and collect nothing, while `runTelemetryFor` records a successful tick. The validators now WARN (not refuse — a 400 would punish an operator re-saving a pre-existing value), the dropdowns stop offering them, and `auditPollingCapability` names what is already stored. The one thing promoted to a hard refuse is **ICMP on a non-response-time stream via `PUT /assets/:id`**: the integration-tier and class-override validators always rejected it and the per-asset path never did.

**Agentless host streams (2026-08-28).** `ssh` / `winrm` now deliver **cpuMemory, interfaces and storage** as well as processes, via `agentlessHostService`. The queue gates that used to drop them before enqueueing are gone (`canTelemetry` in both `computeDueWork` and `jobs/monitorAssets`, and `runStorageFor`'s hardcoded SNMP-only test — that cadence now covers SNMP + ssh + winrm, while the agent pushes on its own schedule and vCenter storage rides the system-info pass). The credential chain is the one `runProcessesFor` already used, lifted into the shared `resolveAgentlessCredConfig` (per-stream asset credential → class override → AD bind fallback) so three collectors cannot drift. Interfaces and storage ride ONE connection when both are on the same transport. Still absent over a shell and correctly reported so by `pollingCapability`: **temperature** (Linux hwmon is readable but `MSAcpi_ThermalZoneTemperature` is unimplemented on most real Windows hardware, so neither side ships rather than working on half a fleet) and **LLDP** (no shell equivalent at all).

**Agentless OS event log (2026-08-28).** `eventLog` had settings at every tier and a working sink — `ingestOsEventLog`, which curates entries into the audit Event table with a min-level filter, dedupe, a per-push cap and a per-asset hourly rate cap — but no server-side collector and no cadence, so only the Polaris Agent ever delivered it. `runEventLogFor` closes that: `journalctl -o json -p warning` over SSH (**line-delimited JSON, not an array**) or `Get-WinEvent` at levels 1–3 over WinRM, into the SAME sink, gated by the SAME global `agentEventLog` master switch — an operator who turned the feature off must not have an agentless poller keep filling the audit log. It is the ninth `MonitorCadence`, with its own queue (`polaris-monitor-eventlog`), pool (`POLARIS_MONITOR_EVENTLOG_WORKERS`, default 8 — smaller than processes because what it collects ships off-host through the syslog / SFTP archivers) and anchor (`Asset.lastEventLogAt`, migration `20260828060000`).

Two decisions worth knowing. The collection window is derived from the stream's own interval (1.5×) rather than a row count: a poll asking for "the last N entries" either misses a burst or re-ingests the same quiet hour, whereas asking for "everything since a bit longer ago than my last run" neither drops nor duplicates — the deliberate overlap is cheap because the sink dedupes. And `lastEventLogAt` is stamped **even on failure**, exactly as `runProcessesFor` stamps its anchors: an agentless stream that re-fires every tick against a bad credential is an AD-lockout risk, and this is the one stream where a retry storm would also flood the table it writes into.

**The `fortimanager` polling method (2026-08-28).** A ninth `PollingMethod`, valid on the **response-time stream only** (`FORTIMANAGER_STREAMS`) and the **`fortimanager` source only** — a standalone FortiGate has no FortiManager to ask, and neither does `manual`, which is why that source's set is now spelled out instead of inheriting `ALL_METHODS`. Instead of touching the device it reads FortiManager's own device database: `fetchRosterConnectivity` issues one NATIVE `/dvmdb/adom/<adom>/device` call (no `fields` list — naming fields makes FMG authorize each one and fail the query with `-11`) and `extractRosterConnectivity` projects it to per-serial reachability, walking the same rows and the same `ha_slave[]` members as `extractRosterIdentities` so the two cannot disagree about which serials exist. Encodings match discovery's: top-level `conn_status === 1` is connected with **absent counting as connected** (an FMG that stops reporting the field must not mass-down a fleet), and `ha_slave[].status` 1/0 per member — the standby's only appearance anywhere.

Cost is the point: native reads are outside the `/sys/proxy/json` concurrency-1 lane, and `fetchFmgRosterCached` (30 s TTL + promise-singleton, the controller/vCenter cache shape) makes one request serve every gate on the integration — ~187 gates for one round trip rather than 187 serialized proxy calls or 187 direct dials. It also reaches a gate Polaris has no route to, since only FortiManager must be reachable. `probeFortimanagerNative` dispatches in `probeAsset` **before the IP guard** and identifies the chassis by **serial, never by name** (`fortinetTopology.deviceName` is FMG's device name, which diverges from the gate's configured hostname on real fleets — the `utils/fortinetParentKey.ts` trap; a name mismatch would read as "gone from FortiManager"). **FMG unreachable ⇒ `ProbeResult.skipped`**, not a failure — the vCenter reasoning in business rule 30: the thing that answers for the device is not the device, so one manager outage must never down a whole fleet at once. A gate FMG answers about and reports disconnected IS a real failure.

What it trades away, and why it is one stream rather than a transport: the reading is FMG's, on FMG's check-in cadence, so it is **lagged and second-hand** — it says the chassis is talking to its manager, not that it is serving traffic. It carries **no uptime**, so it drives no reboot detection. And FMG's database holds nothing else worth polling: no CPU, memory, temperature, interface counters or session count, and no live switch/AP status (those are FortiOS monitor endpoints, which is why they ride the proxy or a direct call). **Not a source default** — response time stays `icmp`, because repointing a default would silently change how up/down is decided for every gate on every FMG install.

The same predicate feeds the resolver's validity gate, so a **stored** `rest_api` (authored in bypass mode, or before the token was cleared) is skipped like any other method the source cannot use and the layer below stays — which is what makes the UI's "locked to inherited" true at runtime. It is **non-destructive**: the stored value is never rewritten and returns the moment a token is supplied. Note the condition is NOT simply proxy mode — proxy WITH a token is a legitimate configuration (discovery and writes ride FMG, monitoring reaches the gates directly) and keeps the normal REST defaults. Mirrored client-side by `_fortiosRestUsable` / `_fmgFortiosRestUnavailable` / `_applyFortiosRestLocks` in `public/js/integrations.js`, which disable the affected dropdowns and render a note naming the token as the thing that unlocks them; the FMG-FortiGate class's stream subtabs are no longer hidden behind the transport toggle, since hiding them explained nothing and left the stored values invisibly in force.

**A per-asset REST API credential is the second token source (2026-09).** The gate above assumes the only FortiOS token is the integration's, which is fleet-wide by construction — the FMG Monitoring tab's own hint says it "must be the same across all managed FortiGates". A fleet where each gate carries its own api-user therefore had no way to be polled over REST at all, no matter which method was selected. `buildFortinetConfig(host, integration, credential?)` now prefers a `restapi`-typed `Credential` over the integration's token, resolved per stream through `utils/fortinetRestCredential.ts` and threaded into all five REST collectors: `probeFortinet` (responseTime, `responseTimeCredential`), `collectTelemetryFortinet` (cpuMemory), the `collectHardwareSensorsFortinet` dispatch (temperature), `collectSystemInfoFortinet` + `collectIpsecOnlyFortinetSafe` + `applyFortilinkLldpExclusion` (interfaces), and `collectLldpOnlyFortinet` + `overlayCrossTransportLldp` (lldp). The FortiAP controller-cache reads (`collectTelemetryFortiapRest` / `collectHardwareSensorsFortiapRest`) deliberately get none — those go to the PARENT gate's `wifi/managed_ap` table and authenticate as the parent, so an AP's own credential would be the wrong one. A stream carrying such a credential is additionally **exempt from the skip in the paragraph above** (`assetStreamCredentialId` → the resolver's `ok()`): a per-asset token is precisely what makes a FortiOS call possible where the fleet-wide one is absent, so discarding the method there would silently throw away the operator's fix for the condition being detected. The credential's TYPE cannot be known without a DB read and the resolver takes none on the hot path, so a wrongly-typed credential surfaces as a collection error naming the missing token rather than as a stream that quietly resolves elsewhere. Before this, selecting that credential persisted, resolved, rendered in the modal — and collected nothing, forever, with the tick reporting success: the `pollingCapability.ts` failure class one layer further in, where the collector exists but reads a different token than the UI offered.

**The `http` method — RETIRED (2026-08).** There WAS an `http` polling method: a responseTime-only GET that decided up/down from a status code and an optional body match. It is gone from `PollingMethod`, from every `COMPATIBILITY` set, from `probeAsset`'s dispatch, from both route enums and from the UI mirrors; `tests/unit/pollingCompatibility.test.ts` asserts it cannot come back silently. The check itself survives and is now a **manufacturer custom widget** (`widgetType: "http"`, business rule 33). The reason is ownership of the DEFINITION: as a polling method the check had to ride an `http`-typed Credential, so the row that answers "how do I log in to this vendor" also carried "which path, expecting what" — a second path meant a second copy of the same password. Keyed by manufacturer + optional `modelPattern` it varies on the axis a check actually varies on, and the credential is authentication only. `probeHttp` is unchanged as the socket owner; what changed is who calls it (`collectAndRecordCustomWidgets`, on the telemetry cadence) and where the result lands (`AssetStateSample` 0/1 + an `AssetCustomWidgetSample` response-time gauge, NOT `monitorStatus`).

**Polaris Agent polling-method (`"agent"`).** Seventh value in the polling-method enum. Represents a Polaris-managed agent installed locally on the target host (Linux/macOS/Windows × amd64/arm64) that pushes samples back via `POST /api/v1/agents/samples` on its own schedule and holds a long-lived outbound WebSocket for on-demand probes. The four streams it produces: **response-time** measures the agent → Polaris RTT via a `/heartbeat` ping (so a TLS / firewall / DNS failure surfaces as a real packet-loss sample — not a process-local liveness noop); **telemetry** captures CPU% + memory bytes via gopsutil per-OS (Linux `/proc/stat`+`/proc/meminfo`, macOS `host_statistics`+`sysctl`, Windows `GetSystemTimes`+`GlobalMemoryStatusEx`) plus host thermal sensors when available; **interfaces** enumerates every NIC with its MAC, IP, link state, and cumulative byte+error counters via gopsutil/net merged with stdlib `net.Interfaces` for MAC/IP association; **storage** walks every local mountpoint via gopsutil/disk and skips network filesystems (NFS/SMB/AFP) by default to avoid stalls when the server is unreachable. Default cadences: 60 s response-time / 60 s telemetry / 600 s interfaces / 600 s storage — operator-overridable via `*_interval_sec` keys in `agent.conf`. A separate **system-info push** (`POST /api/v1/agents/system-info`) fires on the heartbeat cadence (default 300 s) and carries the host's identity (hostname, OS family + version + kernel, DMI manufacturer / model / serial / BIOS, primary MAC + IP, agent version itself). The server upserts an `AssetSource` row with `sourceKind = "polaris-agent"` and `externalId = managedAgent.id`, then re-projects the asset — `polaris-agent` is at the top of the projection priority for hostname / serialNumber / manufacturer / model / os / osVersion, beating AD / Entra / Intune because the agent runs ON the host and reads DMI/SMBIOS directly while inventory sources infer from elsewhere. **MAC is written inline** alongside the projection step — `primaryMac` is normalized to colon-uppercase, reconciled into `AssetMacAddress` with `source="polaris-agent"` (preserving entries from other sources), and the freshest entry becomes `Asset.macAddress`. MAC isn't owned by `projectAssetFromSources` (see "Fields the projection does NOT own"), so every discovery path including the agent writes it directly. Falls through cleanly when DMI fields are unreadable (Linux `product_serial` is often 0400 on hardened deployments; the agent's DynamicUser sees empty and AD / Intune fill in instead). Compatible source kinds: `manual`, `activedirectory`, `entraid`, `windowsserver` (anywhere we can install software via stored SSH/WinRM credentials). Explicitly NOT compatible with `fortimanager` / `fortigate` — Fortinet appliances can't run third-party binaries. When any stream resolves to `"agent"`, the periodic puller (probe + telemetry + systemInfo + fastFiltered) becomes a no-op for that stream — the agent owns its own cadence and the synthetic ticking-loop pass returns success-with-zero-write so the `polaris_probe_total{transport="agent"}` counter increments but no DB sample is created. `recordProbeResult` and the `record*Result` writers early-return on agent-mode so the agent's real pushed samples are the only signal that drives the state machine; the inbound `/api/v1/agents/samples` handler calls `recordProbeResult(..., null, { fromAgent: true })` to bypass that guard for the agent's real RTTs. Per-stream credential pickers on the asset edit modal hide when polling-method is `"agent"` — the agent's own per-asset bearer (issued at install time) is implicit.

**Polaris Agent API surface (Phase 2 — inbound + operator-facing routes).** Three inbound endpoints handle the agent runtime: `POST /api/v1/agents/enroll` is public — body carries the one-shot enrollment token plus the cert fingerprint the agent observed during its TLS handshake. The server cross-checks the pin against the value baked into the `ManagedAgent` row at install kickoff (mismatch → 400 + `agent.install_failed` event + bearer revoke), and on success atomically swaps the enrollment token for a long-lived bearer (atomic via `agentTokenService.consumeEnrollmentToken`), transitions `installStatus → "active"`, auto-enables `Asset.monitored` in the same transaction (unless the asset is decommissioned/disabled or already monitored — `shouldEnableMonitoringOnEnroll`; a post-write `recomputeMonitorOverrideForAssets` keeps `monitorOverride` consistent so the discovery sweep can't flip it back off; emits `monitor.enabled_by_agent`), and emits `agent.enrolled`. `POST /api/v1/agents/samples` (bearer-gated via `requireAgentBearer`) accepts a discriminated-union body keyed on `stream: "responseTime" | "telemetry" | "interfaces" | "storage" | "eventLog" | "processInventory" | "processTelemetry" | "processLog"` — sample rows are enqueued through `sampleWriteBuffer.enqueue*` (same 2 s batched-flush path the periodic puller uses) with `req.managedAgent.assetId` stamped server-side so a stolen bearer cannot write samples for a different asset. The probe stream additionally calls `recordProbeResult` with `fromAgent: true` to drive the five-state machine; telemetry/interfaces/storage bump the corresponding `last*At` stamps directly; the process streams persist via `persistAssetProcesses` / `enqueueProcessSamples` / `enqueueProcessLogSamples` and `eventLog` flows through `osEventLogService.ingestOsEventLog`. `GET /api/v1/agents/config` (bearer) returns the resolved cadences + which streams are agent-mode + an `ETag` so the agent can issue `If-None-Match` to short-circuit polls when nothing changed. The handler **self-heals polling-method drift on every call** — `consumeEnrollmentToken` already stamps the asset's per-stream polling columns to `"agent"` at enroll time (the seven agent-owned streams: response-time / CPU+memory / temperature / interfaces / LLDP / storage / processes — `eventLog` is deliberately excluded so it stays opt-in/OFF for PII), but assets enrolled before a given stream landed in that list, or assets where an operator manually cleared a column afterward, would otherwise inherit source defaults (ICMP / not-delivered) and the agent's pushes for that stream would be ignored by the resolver. When `/config` sees any of `responseTimePolling` / `cpuMemoryPolling` / `temperaturePolling` / `interfacesPolling` / `lldpPolling` / `storagePolling` / `processesPolling` is not `"agent"`, it re-stamps all seven in a single update, invalidates the monitor-settings cache for that scope, and writes one `monitor.polling_overridden_by_agent` Event with the prior values for audit. Idempotent — once stamped, subsequent /config polls find no drift and skip the write. **The heartbeat ETag (`computeConfigEtag`) hashes every agent-owned stream's resolved (polling, interval, timeout) plus the monitored-process pin count** — a running agent only re-fetches `/config` when this ETag changes, and the self-heal above only fires on that re-fetch, so omitting a stream from the ETag (storage / processes / eventLog were originally left out) deadlocks that stream's collection on already-running agents until a restart. `POST /api/v1/agents/heartbeat` (bearer) bumps `lastSeenAt` + refreshes `agentVersion` + (agent ≥0.17.1, Linux) stores the raw `capEff` mask from the agent's /proc/self/status into `ManagedAgent.reportedCapEff` — the VERIFIED privilege state, decoded server-side by `utils/capEff.decodeCapEff` (surfaced as `caps` on `GET /assets/:id/agent` and `/server-settings/agents/installed`; a ptrace-tier agent whose mask lacks CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH renders as "stale unit — reinstall" since it collects no Application Map connections). The three operator-facing endpoints on `/api/v1/assets/:id/agent` are: `GET` (any auth role) returns the redacted `ManagedAgent` row (hashes stripped) or 404; `POST /install` (assets-admin) validates the credential type matches the chosen OS (ssh for linux/darwin, winrm for windows) and validates the optional `scriptId` install-method variant against the target OS (`resolveInstallScriptId` — the server-side OS-lock; persisted on `ManagedAgent.installScriptId`, re-checked in `runInstall` before executing), captures the live Polaris HTTPS cert fingerprint via `certInfo.getServerCertFingerprint()`, creates the `ManagedAgent` row in `pending`, mints a 10-min-TTL enrollment token, emits `agent.install_kickoff`, and (Phase 2) returns the enrollment token in the response so an operator can stand up the agent by hand — the SSH/WinRM file-push that automates this work lands in Phase 4 via `agentInstallService`. `DELETE` (admin-only) is a two-phase op: synchronous `revokeBearer` is always immediate; `?force=true` additionally hard-deletes the row and emits `agent.force_removed` (for unreachable hosts). Without force, the row is left in place with `installStatus="revoked"` so the Phase-4 async remote-uninstall job has something to drive.

**Polaris Agent remote install (Phase 4a — SSH).** `src/services/agentInstallService.ts` fires the async background work when the operator clicks Install Agent: open ssh2 connection → SFTP upload binary + agent.conf + installer script to `/tmp/` → `sudo -n bash /tmp/polaris-agent-install.sh` → cleanup. The installer script (embedded as a string in the service, not shipped alongside the binary so it stays version-locked with FortiOS-style "Polaris release == one bundle" semantics) writes `/usr/local/bin/polaris-agent` + `/var/lib/polaris-agent/agent.conf` (Linux — under systemd's `StateDirectory=` so the agent can rewrite it after enroll; `/etc/` is read-only via `ProtectSystem=strict`. **The installer chowns `agent.conf` to whatever owns that state directory, never to root**: with `DynamicUser=yes` systemd chowns the state *directory* to the dynamic UID but leaves files already inside it alone, so a `root:root` conf written on a **reinstall** — where `/var/lib/polaris-agent` is already a symlink into `/var/lib/private/` owned by the dynamic user — leaves the agent crash-looping on `load config: permission denied` with the row parked at `enrolling` and no error surfaced, since the installer itself exited 0. First installs mask the bug because systemd migrates the brand-new directory and chowns the whole tree. Prod incident 2026-07-27) or `/etc/polaris-agent/agent.conf` (macOS) + a systemd unit (Linux) or launchd plist (macOS). The systemd unit uses `DynamicUser=yes` so the agent runs as a non-root system-managed user; the macOS plist runs the agent as root (operators tighten this in a follow-on if needed). State transitions: `pending → uploading → enrolling → active` (the last step happens when the agent's first POST /enroll lands). The `ManagedAgent.installCredentialId` column stores which SSH credential was used, so the default DELETE path can reuse it for the remote uninstall mirror — `sudo -n bash /tmp/polaris-agent-uninstall.sh` stops + disables the service, removes the unit/plist/binary/config, and on success hard-deletes the ManagedAgent row (audit trail lives in Event). Binaries live under `<STATE_DIR>/data/agents/<version>/`; the manifest at `<STATE_DIR>/data/agents/manifest.json` names the current default version + maps platform-arch tuples to filenames. The URL stamped into `agent.conf`'s `server_url` resolves in this order: (1) `Setting.agent.serverUrlOverride` — operator-settable from Server Settings → Maintenance → Polaris Agent card via the **Server URL stamped into agent.conf** input (PUT `/server-settings/agents/server-url` with `{url}`; empty string clears the override and falls back to the cert-derived default); (2) `POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL` env var (legacy operator override, still honored for scripted deployments); (3) first DNS SAN on the running HTTPS leaf cert + live HTTPS port — the natural default, since operators generate the cert with the hostname they expect Polaris to be reachable at and the agent's pin is verifying that exact cert; (4) cert CN + port; (5) first IP SAN + port (covers IP-only certs in isolated networks); (6) `POLARIS_PUBLIC_HOST` env + PORT; (7) `localhost` + PORT. The install kickoff route guards against producing `https://localhost:<port>` for a non-loopback target. Reverse-proxy / TLS-termination shops set either the UI override or `POLARIS_PUBLIC_URL` so the agent dials the proxy's public hostname rather than the upstream's internal IP. The Polaris Agent card surfaces the **effective** URL pre-filled (so operators can see what install would use right now) and the **cert-derived default** as helper text so it's obvious what they'd inherit if they cleared the override.

**Polaris Agent remote install (Phase 4b — WinRM).** Windows hosts install via the same agentInstallService entry point but use a different transport: instead of SFTP-uploading the binary, the PowerShell installer running on the host **pulls the binary over HTTPS** from a new public endpoint `GET /api/v1/agents/binary/:filename` (filename whitelist-checked against `data/agents/manifest.json`, directory-traversal protected, no-store cache). The pull is gated by a server-cert pin: `[Net.ServicePointManager]::ServerCertificateValidationCallback` is wired to compare the leaf SHA-256 against the pin embedded in the PowerShell command, then restored after the download. We avoid implementing the WS-Management `Send` verb (chunked stdin file upload) entirely — saves ~1000 lines of XML envelope code that's only used here. The WinRS shell verbs we DO implement live in `src/utils/winrm.ts`: `CreateShell` → `RunCommand` → `Receive` (polled loop until `CommandState=Done`) → `DeleteShell` (always in a `finally`). PowerShell is invoked via `-EncodedCommand` (UTF-16-LE base64) so command-line escaping never bites. The installer creates the service via `New-Service` (canonical, ships in every Windows since 5.1) and stamps recovery actions via `sc.exe failure`. Deliberately avoids `Get-WmiObject Win32_Service` (DCOM-based, removed in PowerShell 7+) and `Remove-Service` (PowerShell 6+ only, missing from stock Server 2019); uses `sc.exe delete` for the uninstall. The host's `%ProgramFiles%\Polaris\Agent\polaris-agent.exe` + `%ProgramData%\Polaris\agent\agent.conf` are written with admin-only ACLs (the bearer is in agent.conf so it must not be world-readable). Same install lifecycle as SSH: `pending → uploading → enrolling → active`, with the agent's first POST /enroll flipping to active. WinRM needs to be enabled on the target host on port 5986 (HTTPS preferred) or 5985 (HTTP fallback); the credential must have local admin rights.

**Polaris Agent in-app build (Server Settings → Maintenance → Polaris Agent).** Operators click Build to produce all six platform binaries (linux/darwin/windows × amd64/arm64) right from the web UI; no shell access needed. Driven by `src/services/agentBuildService.ts` which spawns one `go build` per platform serially (parallel calls thrash the shared GOCACHE), writes binaries under `<STATE_DIR>/data/agents/<version>/`, and writes `manifest.json` atomically (`.tmp` + rename) only after all six succeed. Version comes from `getAgentVersion()` (reads `agent/VERSION` text file with a 5s mtime cache) — DECOUPLED from `getAppVersion()` so Polaris patch releases that don't touch `agent/` produce zero build noise. Install scripts (`deploy/setup-rhel.sh`, `setup-ubuntu.sh`, `setup-windows.ps1` and their `-nodb` variants) install Go alongside Node; the Dockerfile pulls `golang-go` from bookworm-backports. UI gates the Build button on `goAvailable()` and surfaces a clear "install Go and reload" notice when missing. The card shows a per-platform inventory grid (size / built-when / present-✓), a drift hint when `manifest.currentVersion` lags `agent/VERSION`, a queued-builds strip (FIFO depth 3; 4th simultaneous click 409s with "queue full"), per-build × cancel buttons, and an Auto-build toggle. **Build queueing:** two operators clicking near-simultaneously land in a stable FIFO order (Node's single thread guarantees no interleave between the queue-length check and the enqueue); each build re-reads `getAgentVersion()` at start-of-run so a queued build picks up a VERSION bump that landed during its wait. **Cancellation:** `state.activeChild` holds the running `go build` ChildProcess; DELETE sends SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 5s grace. The `manifest.json` is only written after ALL platforms succeed so a cancelled build leaves partial binaries under `data/agents/<version>/` but the previous manifest still points at the previous version's files (operator-visible: nothing happened). **Per-version retention:** after every successful build the helper prunes deletable version directories — deletable = NOT `manifest.currentVersion` AND NOT in use by any live `ManagedAgent` AND NOT within the most-recent N (env `POLARIS_AGENT_KEEP_VERSIONS`, default 3). A manual "Clean up old binaries" button on the card fires the same helper. **Auto-build:** `src/jobs/autoBuildAgents.ts` fires 60s after boot, refuses unless `manifest.json` exists (operator opted in), Polaris's `getAgentVersion()` differs from `manifest.currentVersion`, Go is available, AND `Setting.agent.autoBuildOnVersionMismatch !== false`. Actor stamped as `"system:auto-build-on-version-change"` so the audit trail distinguishes this from operator clicks. Skipped builds emit `agent.build.auto_skipped` with the reason so operators see the staleness on the Events page.

**Windows binary code signing (internal-CA PKCS#12, opt-in, FAIL-OPEN).** When the `agent.codeSigning` Setting is enabled (Integrations → Polaris Agents → Code signing), `agentBuildService.signWindowsBinaries()` runs between the platform loop and the manifest write: it invokes `java -jar tools/jsign.jar --storetype PKCS12 --keystore <pfx> --storepass env:POLARIS_SIGNING_PASSWORD [--alias <alias>] --tsaurl <tsa> --tsmode RFC3161 <exe>` per Windows binary — the keystore password rides the child env, never argv, and `scrubSecrets` keeps it out of step errors/Events. There is NO credential-exchange step (a PKCS#12 store is read directly), so unlike the prior hosted-service path there is no whole-phase token failure mode before the per-file loop. **Timestamping is explicit and required:** jsign auto-enables RFC3161 only for hosted store types, so `tsaUrl` is part of `isSigningConfigured()` and a cleared field falls back to the default rather than silently disabling it — without a countersignature every signature in the fleet goes invalid the moment the signing cert expires, all at once. A public TSA is correct with an internal-CA cert (a TSA attests to *when*, not *who*). Progress strip gains `sign/windows-{amd64,arm64}` step rows under phase `signing`; cancellation rides the same `state.activeChild` SIGTERM path as `go build`. **Fail-open:** any signing failure marks the step failed, stamps the durable `agent.signing.lastFailure` Setting, and emits `agent.build.sign_failed` (warning) — but the build completes and ships unsigned; `agent.build.completed` carries `signed: true|false|"disabled"`. The stamp drives a dismissable sidebar alert (`#signing-failure-alert` in [public/js/app.js](public/js/app.js), 30s poll of `GET /assets/agent-signing-alert`, visible to `assets:write` roles, per-user-per-failure localStorage dismissal) and clears on the next fully-signed build or when signing is disabled. Host tooling (Java 17 headless + the SHA-256-pinned jsign 7.4 jar at `<app dir>/tools/jsign.jar`) is provisioned by the setup scripts + Dockerfile; `signingAvailability()` re-probes uncached so "install Java and reload" just works. The two Windows exes also carry a committed VERSIONINFO resource (`agent/cmd/polaris-agent/winres.json` → `rsrc_windows_{amd64,arm64}.syso`, regenerated by `make -C agent winres` on VERSION bumps) so the PE shows publisher/product/version metadata independent of signing. **Trust is fleet-scoped, not public:** an internal CA contributes nothing to SmartScreen reputation; what it buys is a deterministic allow via a Defender for Endpoint certificate indicator (leaf certs only, ~3h to propagate) or an App Control publisher rule, and any host that does not trust the internal root sees an UNTRUSTED signature. PKI-side setup + operator walkthrough: docs/INSTALL.md → "Optional: Code signing for agent Windows binaries".

**Polaris Agent upgrade-already-installed (`POST /assets/:id/agent/upgrade` + bulk).** `startUpgrade` in `src/services/agentInstallService.ts` does an SSH/WinRM-driven binary swap that preserves `agent.conf` — bearer + cert pin survive, agent reconnects with the same identity. SSH path SFTPs the new binary to `/tmp/polaris-agent.new` and runs an embedded upgrade shell script that stops the systemd unit / launchd job, `install -m 0755`s over the old binary, restarts. WinRM path runs an embedded PowerShell `-EncodedCommand` that re-uses the install-flow's cert-pin-verified `Invoke-WebRequest` to pull the new binary from `/api/v1/agents/binary/:filename`, then `Stop-Service` → atomic `Move-Item` → `Start-Service`. State transitions: `active → upgrading → active` on success, `active → upgrade_failed` on remote error — and `upgrade_failed` is itself an upgradeable status (`UPGRADEABLE_INSTALL_STATUSES` / `canUpgradeFromStatus`, exported from the same service and used by the guard, the bulk filter and the two `outOfDate` flags alike), because every failure path leaves the old binary and `agent.conf` untouched. That is what lets a host asleep during one fan-out be retried by the next build instead of needing an uninstall/reinstall. Per-asset Upgrade button on the asset details modal Agent panel (Retry Upgrade on a failed row); bulk Upgrade-all line on the Maintenance Polaris Agent card with a Promise pool of 4. The bulk path's "N of M out-of-date" line is backed by `GET /server-settings/agents/installed-summary` which returns a per-version histogram (cheap groupBy on `ManagedAgent.agentVersion`).

The `ManagedAgent` table tracks each install (lifecycle: pending → uploading → enrolling → active → revoked / uninstalled / upgrading / upgrade_failed; one row per asset, FK cascade). See the plan at `~/.claude/plans/the-app-needs-a-glowing-knuth.md` for the implementation roadmap.

**SSH deployment (Integrations → Polaris Agent → "SSH Deployment" card).** Installing the agent on Windows over SSH rather than WinRM has been supported since the `installTransport` split (`sshWindowsInstall` / `sshWindowsUninstall` / `sshWindowsUpgrade`), and the `ssh` credential type has always accepted a `privateKey` in place of a `password`. What this card adds is everything around them: Polaris now GENERATES the deployment keypair and emits the script that authorizes it fleet-wide, instead of the operator running `ssh-keygen`, pasting the private half into the credential form, and hand-writing the push. That hand-written step is the error-prone part — Windows OpenSSH ignores `%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys` for anyone in the Administrators group (it reads only `%ProgramData%\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys`) and refuses that file unless it is owned by Administrators/SYSTEM with inheritance disabled; neither mistake produces a client-side error, authentication just fails.

Four routes under `/api/v1/server-settings/agents/windows-ssh` (beside the agent-build routes, matching that card's existing UI-on-Integrations / routes-on-serverSettings split): `GET` (card state — `serverSettingsSystem:read`), `PUT` (accountMode / username / polarisServerIp — `fullwrite`), `POST /generate` (mint or rotate the keypair) and `GET /script?kind=remediation|detection`. **`/generate` carries a CHAINED gate** — `serverSettingsSystem:fullwrite` **AND** `credentials:write` — because it creates and mutates a Credential row; without the chain a custom role holding system settings but no credential access could mint a fleet-wide admin key. Same chaining shape as `PUT /application-map/discovery`.

`SshConfig` gained `publicKey`, deliberately **not** in `SECRET_FIELDS_BY_TYPE.ssh` so it survives `stripSecrets` — otherwise the onboarding script could not be re-rendered without rotating the key and re-touching every endpoint. The private half is sealed at rest by the `db.ts` extension and returned by no read path.

**Linux (Phase 1b)** works the same way with three platform differences that matter. The key goes into the USER's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` (700 dir / 600 file, correctly owned) rather than one group-wide file; `restorecon` fixes the SELinux context, which RHEL-family sshd otherwise refuses just as silently as a bad Windows ACL; and the script installs a **NOPASSWD sudoers drop-in**, because the agent installer runs `sudo -n bash /tmp/polaris-agent-install.sh` — SSH key auth alone does not install an agent, so onboarding without it would just move the manual step. The drop-in is validated with `visudo -cf` BEFORE being installed: a malformed one locks sudo out for every user on the host, which is far worse than a failed onboarding. Deliberately NOT installed: `openssh-server` (distro-specific package management, and a host you cannot already reach over SSH is not one the script was delivered to) — it detects and reports instead. The Linux detection script also checks the account and the sudoers drop-in, unlike the Windows one, because both are prerequisites the install genuinely fails without and both are cheaply observable.

Account settings are **per platform** (`config.windows` / `config.linux`); `polarisServerIp` is shared. Polaris maintains **one managed credential per platform**, both carrying the same keypair — a `Credential` holds exactly one username, and a Windows `DOMAIN\user` is meaningless on Linux, so a single shared row would leave one platform unable to log in.

The generated scripts are **delivery-neutral and fleet-generic**: no machine-specific values (public key, username, account mode and server IP are fleet constants; `administrators_authorized_keys` is one group-wide file authorizing any local Administrator presenting the key), so the identical body runs under an Intune Remediation, a GPO startup script, an SCCM Configuration Baseline, Azure Arc, an RMM job, or a one-off `Invoke-Command` loop. The **detection** script is what makes rollout self-healing when paired with the remediation one — a plain Intune platform script runs once per device and never retries, so machines offline at assignment time or reimaged afterwards stay unconfigured. Note that Intune does not manage traditional Windows Server, so the Servers class needs GPO/SCCM/Arc even on an Intune estate. An unsupported Windows build (pre-1809 / pre-Server 2019, no OpenSSH capability) reports `unsupported:` and exits **0** from both scripts on purpose: returning non-zero would loop the pair forever against a device remediation cannot fix.

**SSH host-key verification (opt-in, all SSH paths).** Until 2026-08 Polaris passed no `hostVerifier` to ssh2, so **every** SSH connection accepted whatever host key was presented — the server was never authenticated to the client. That covered agent install/upgrade/uninstall (which SFTPs a script and runs it as root), agentless process collection, and the SSH monitor probe alike; anything able to answer on the target's address could impersonate it and, on an install, be handed a credential.

`SshConfig.verifyHostKey` turns on trust-on-first-use pinning against the `SshHostKey` table. It is **opt-in, default OFF**, defaulting ON only for newly created credentials — the exact shape of the WinRM `verifyTls` remediation (2026-06-03 review, H1), because enabling it globally would break every install whose hosts have never been pinned. `buildHostVerifier` in [remoteExec.ts](src/utils/remoteExec.ts) is shared by BOTH `ssh2.connect` call sites (`withSshClient` and `monitoringService.probeSsh` — the only two in the tree) so they cannot drift on whether the server is checked, and it **fails closed**: an operator who asked for verification gets a refused connection on an internal error, never a silently unverified one.

Pins live in their own table rather than on `Credential.config` because host keys are per-HOST while one credential legitimately spans a fleet. The operator surface (list + Delete) is on the Windows SSH Deployment card, since deleting a pin is the documented recovery after a legitimate rebuild or re-key — and it is audited at warning level precisely because it re-opens first-use trust. **TOFU is only as good as the moment you pin:** enabling this against a running fleet pins whatever currently answers, so it detects a key *changing* rather than a host that was already impersonated. It is genuinely strong for a greenfield rollout, where the pin is taken at deploy time.

**Where the polling method comes from.** Per-stream dropdowns appear at four tiers in the UI:
- **Manual tier** — Assets page → Monitoring Settings modal → Manual Monitoring section. Accepts any method (covers any source).
- **Integration tier** — each integration's edit modal → Monitoring tab → Cadence & Retention section. Methods filtered to the integration's source kind.
- **Class override** — Assets page → Monitoring Settings modal → Class Overrides. Methods re-render when the source picker changes; integration-scoped overrides are pinned to the integration's source kind.
- **Per-asset** — asset edit modal → Monitoring tab. Methods filtered to the asset's source kind.

`/api/v1/assets/:id/effective-monitor-settings` returns the resolved values plus per-field provenance (`asset` / `class` / `integration` / `manual`) so the asset edit modal can render tier badges. Each "Inherit" option in every dropdown is labeled with the resolver's expected fallback ("Source default: REST API" / "Source default: ICMP" / "Not delivered for this source") so operators see what they'd inherit without clicking through.

**Credential resolution.** A polling method that needs authentication (`snmp`, `winrm`, `ssh`, `rest_api`) walks four tiers, most-specific first: per-stream asset credential (`Asset.responseTimeCredentialId` / `telemetryCredentialId` / `interfacesCredentialId` / `lldpCredentialId`) → asset's generic `Asset.monitorCredentialId` → class-override per-stream credential (`MonitorClassOverride.responseTimeCredentialId` / etc — surfaced by `resolveMonitorSettings` onto the resolved `*CredentialId` fields, looked up in the dispatcher via `loadClassOverrideStreamCredential`) → integration fallback. The integration fallback is FMG/FortiGate-discovered firewalls reading `Integration.config.monitorCredentialId` (SNMP) or the stored API token (REST API), and AD-discovered hosts reading the integration's `bindDn` / `bindPassword`. The asset's monitor credential picker is type-agnostic — the operator pairs it with their chosen polling method. Credential / method mismatches fall through silently at probe time to a clear error; setting a SNMP credential on an asset whose `responseTimePolling` is `winrm` is allowed but the probe will report "No WinRM credential selected" until one is attached.

**Branch-class FortiGate workaround.** Small-branch FortiGates (60F/61F/91G class) sometimes 404 the FortiOS REST sensor-info / interface endpoints on FortiOS 7.4.x. Operators flip the relevant streams to `snmp` at the integration tier (covers the whole fleet) or per-asset (one box at a time) — the resolver routes the affected streams over `FORTINET-FORTIGATE-MIB::fgHwSensors` + IF-MIB while leaving the working streams on REST API. **IPsec tunnels always go via REST** regardless of the interfaces polling method — SNMP has no equivalent and we don't want flipping "Interfaces" off REST to silently kill IPsec history. LLDP is decoupled from interfaces because the FortiOS REST endpoint and SNMP LLDP-MIB don't always agree on coverage; the transport resolver dispatches LLDP independently in `collectSystemInfo`, overlaying a `collectLldpOnlySnmp` / `collectLldpOnlyFortinet` call when the LLDP method differs from the interfaces method.

**REST API telemetry + temperature for managed FortiAPs.** The same `/api/v2/monitor/wifi/managed_ap` row that the probe path consumes carries `cpu_usage`, `mem_free` / `mem_total` (in MB), and `sensors_temperatures` per AP. `fetchFortinetControllerInventory` parses those fields once at fetch time into `entry.apTelemetry` so the 30 s controller-inventory cache absorbs all three consumers (probe + telemetry + hardware sensors) — one upstream call per controller serves N APs on every telemetry tick. When the resolved `cpuMemoryPolling` is `rest_api` on an `access_point` asset, `collectTelemetry` dispatches to `collectTelemetryFortiapRest` which converts MB → bytes (`memTotalBytes = memTotalMb × 1024²`, `memUsedBytes = (memTotal − memFree) × 1024²`) and writes the standard `AssetTelemetrySample` shape; `memPct` is left null because the bytes form is more useful for charts across AP models with different RAM sizes. When the resolved `temperaturePolling` is `rest_api`, `collectHardwareSensors` dispatches to `collectHardwareSensorsFortiapRest` which projects `sensors_temperatures` into the `HardwareSensorSample[]` shape (one row per sensor, all `sensorClass="temperature"` — the controller cache only exposes AP temps). APs whose model doesn't publish CPU/memory/temperature (some older indoor units) come back with `data: []` or null fields rather than an error — the System tab renders "no sensors" instead of a failure pill. Managed FortiSwitches still have no REST telemetry path (the controller-status table reports up/down only); operators wanting switch telemetry flip to SNMP at the integration or per-asset tier.

**REST API probe path for managed FortiSwitches / FortiAPs.** Managed FortiSwitches and FortiAPs aren't directly REST-able — the only authoritative up/down signal is the parent FortiGate's `managed-switch/status` (switches) or `wifi/managed_ap` (APs) inventory table. When the resolved `responseTimePolling` is `rest_api` AND the asset's `assetType` is `switch` or `access_point` AND the asset was discovered through an FMG or FortiGate integration, `probeAsset` dispatches to `probeFortinetController` instead of hitting the asset's own IP. The helper resolves the controller via `Asset.fortinetTopology.controllerFortigate` (FMG) or the integration's own host (standalone FortiGate), fetches the appropriate inventory once, and looks up the asset by serial. `status === "Connected"` (switches) or `status ∈ {"online","connected"}` (APs) is success; everything else (including "not present in the controller's table") is failure. The **per-controller inventory cache** is module-local in `monitoringService.ts` with a 30s TTL keyed on `(integrationId, deviceName, "switches"|"aps")` — N switches or APs sharing one controller make exactly one controller call per cache window, important for FMG proxy mode (concurrency=1). The result flows through the standard `recordProbeResult` → five-state machine → `failureThreshold` → `monitor.status_changed` Event pipeline like any other probe, so a switch that goes Disconnected and stays that way for `failureThreshold` consecutive probes (default 3) ends up as `down`. Cadence implication: at the default 60s `intervalSeconds` and threshold 3, "down" detection takes ~3 minutes; operators on slower cadences should adjust accordingly.

**Per-class FortiSwitch / FortiAP direct polling and auto-Monitor flag:** The FMG/FortiGate integration's `config` JSON accepts `fortiswitchMonitor` and `fortiapMonitor` blocks, each `{ enabled: boolean, snmpCredentialId: string | null, sshCredentialId: string | null, addAsMonitored: boolean, autoMonitorInterfaces: AutoMonitorSelection | null, streams: ClassStreamsBlock }`, plus a `fortigateMonitor: { addAsMonitored: boolean, autoMonitorInterfaces: AutoMonitorSelection | null, pullSnmpLocation: boolean, pushGeocodedCoords: boolean, latitudeMetavar: string, longitudeMetavar: string, addressMetavar: string, streams: ClassStreamsBlock }` block. The three metavar-name fields (FMG-only) name the per-device metavariables used for the coord read + write-back (`latitudeMetavar`/`longitudeMetavar`, default `Latitude`/`Longitude`) and the opt-in address geocode source (`addressMetavar`, blank-disabled); edited from the **Geographic Location** tab. **Phase 2** added the `streams` field on each class block — the per-stream config consumed by the resolver under that class's assetType (see "Monitor Settings Hierarchy" above). AD / Entra / Windows Server gained matching `workstationMonitor` / `serverMonitor` blocks with the same `streams` shape. Shape per stream cell: `{ polling: PollingMethod | null, credentialId: uuid | null, intervalSeconds: number | null, timeoutMs: number | null, mibId: uuid | null, failureThreshold?: number | null }` (failureThreshold only honored on `responseTime`; FortiAP omits the `storage` stream entirely). The integration-tier resolved `responseTimePolling` decides which credential gets stamped on a freshly-discovered switch/AP — `ssh` picks `sshCredentialId`, anything else falls back to `snmpCredentialId`. The `autoMonitorInterfaces` field is the "Auto-Monitor Interfaces" selection — see the dedicated subsection below for its three modes. Edited from the **FortiSwitches** and **FortiAPs** subtabs (full block) and the **FortiGates** subtab (auto-Monitor checkbox only) of the Monitoring tab. The two switch/AP flags are independent and drive these discovery-time outcomes:

| `enabled` (direct polling) | `addAsMonitored` | Stamped on new switch/AP |
|---|---|---|
| false | false | ensure monitored=false (sweep off) |
| false | true | `monitored=true`; resolver picks ICMP source default |
| true (with credential) | false | `monitorCredentialId=<id>`; ensure monitored=false (sweep off) |
| true (with credential) | true | `monitorCredentialId=<id>`, `monitored=true` |

Discovery always stamps `discoveredByIntegrationId=<integration>` on any of these "non-empty" rows so the resolver can pick the source default polling method. Existing switch/AP assets are *only* re-stamped with a credential when their existing `monitorCredentialId` is null OR matches the integration's class credential — operator-pointed credentials are preserved. The `monitored` flip is gated by `Asset.monitorOverride`: discovery enforces `monitored = addAsMonitored` on every cycle EXCEPT when override is true (an explicit operator pin). `monitorOverride` is an **explicit operator-intent bit** — it is written ONLY at the moment of an operator action (the asset write paths compute `monitored XOR addAsMonitored` for the touched ids; re-aligning monitoring to the flag clears it on the same write; the Reset-to-integration-default action clears it). It is **never re-derived from incidental divergence** by a boot job or integration save: an asset that ends up `monitored=false` for a non-operator reason (decommission clamp, created-before-flag-enabled, HA standby) keeps `monitorOverride=false` and self-heals — the next discovery sweep retakes it to the flag's value. (This replaced an earlier convergent model whose every-boot/every-save re-derivation wrongly stamped incidental divergence as an override and stranded those assets unmonitored.)

For **FortiGates**, `fortigateMonitor.addAsMonitored` drives a bidirectional sweep on the same model — `buildFortigateMonitorStamp()` runs on both create and update paths and sets monitored to match the flag (skipping asset rows with `monitorOverride=true`; it reads the override but never writes it). **HA standby members are actively swept to `monitored=false` (+ `consecutiveFailures=0`)** rather than skipped — a standby isn't probe-reachable (its IP is nulled; the cluster IP routes to the active member), so polling one is guaranteed-failure waste, and the per-cycle sweep is what un-monitors an ex-primary after failover. The standby's effective default is `false` at every point that consults the class flag: `recomputeMonitorOverrideForAssets` + `sweepMonitoredForIntegration` (nested `haRole='secondary'` CASE in the SQL), the monitor-override reset endpoint, and the auto-monitor preflight counts — so a deliberate operator opt-in on a standby computes `monitorOverride=true` and sticks. The polling method comes from the resolver (REST API source default for fortimanager / fortigate sources).

For **AD / Entra / Windows Server** integrations, `workstationMonitor.addAsMonitored` and `serverMonitor.addAsMonitored` carry the same semantics on workstation- and server-typed assets. The Entra and AD sync paths call `buildMonitoredSweep()` from `src/services/monitorOverrideService.ts` on every asset write to enforce the flag.

**Integration save sweep.** When the operator changes any per-class `addAsMonitored` value on an integration's edit modal and clicks Save Changes, the PUT /integrations/:id handler runs `sweepMonitoredForIntegration()` (bulk SQL UPDATE that sets `monitored = addAsMonitored` on every **non-override** asset under this integration matching the affected class). It deliberately does **not** recompute `monitorOverride` — a flag flip respects existing operator pins (operators re-align a pinned asset per-asset via the Reset-to-integration-default action, `POST /assets/:id/monitor-override/reset`). Writes one `integration.auto_monitor_swept` Event with the touched-asset count when the sweep was non-trivial. Pairs with the frontend confirm modal (see "Operator confirm flow" below) that protects against accidental fleet-wide disables.

**Operator confirm flow.** The Add/Edit integration modal's Monitoring tab → per-class subtabs render an **Enable Auto-Monitoring** (blue) / **Disable Auto-Monitoring** (red) button instead of a checkbox (`_classAddAsMonitoredHTML` and `_fortigateAddMonitoredHTML` in `public/js/integrations.js`). The button toggles a hidden checkbox of the same id the save path already reads, so persistence is unchanged. On Save Changes the frontend POSTs the proposed flag map to `/integrations/:id/auto-monitor-assets/preflight` and, when any class reports `wouldDisable > 0`, surfaces a confirm modal listing the per-class impact ("Disabling Auto-Monitoring will sweep monitoring OFF for N FortiSwitch(es) — P protected by per-asset override"). Decline aborts the save with no API call.

**Auto-Monitor Interfaces (per-class):** Each `*Monitor` block above also carries an `autoMonitorInterfaces` field that pre-selects which interfaces on every discovered asset of that class are added to the "Poll 1m" fast-cadence pin-list. Real interfaces land in `Asset.monitoredInterfaces` (IF-MIB); synthetic IPsec-tunnel rows land in `Asset.monitoredIpsecTunnels` (the IPsec sampler's list) — the apply pass routes by provenance via `splitPinsByProvenance`. Multi-block union — each block is optional, presence = on, and the apply pass takes the **union** across whichever blocks are present:

```ts
autoMonitorInterfaces: {
  byNames?:    { names: string[] }                                                    // explicit ifNames from the aggregated checklist
  byPatterns?: { patterns: string[]; regex: boolean; onlyUp: boolean }                // wildcards (* and ?) when regex=false, raw anchor-free regex when regex=true
  byTypes?:    { types: Array<"physical"|"aggregate"|"vlan"|"loopback"|"tunnel">; onlyUp: boolean; includeDownTunnels?: boolean }
  byLldp?:     { neighborTypes: Array<"firewall"|"switch"|"access_point"|"server"|"workstation"|"router"|"printer"|"other"> }
} | null                                                                              // null (or all keys missing) = feature off
```

Edited from a card on each Monitoring subtab (FortiGates / FortiSwitches / FortiAPs). Each block has its own master checkbox so operators can mix and match (e.g. "By pattern: `wan*` + By LLDP: switch" on FortiSwitches). `onlyUp` filters candidate interfaces to those with `operStatus === "up"` on their latest `AssetInterfaceSample`; available on byPatterns + byTypes, intentionally not on byNames (explicit names always pin even when the link is down). Default `onlyUp: true` for byTypes, `false` for byPatterns. **`byTypes.includeDownTunnels`** is a tunnel-only exception to `onlyUp`: when both are set, fully-`down` IPsec tunnels still pin (a down tunnel is often exactly what an operator wants to watch). No-op on non-tunnel types and moot when `onlyUp` is false. **Dead-parent exclusion** overrides everything above: an IPsec tunnel whose phase-1 parent interface (`AssetIpsecTunnelSample.parentInterface`, e.g. `wan2`) is currently down AND holds no usable IP (null / `""` / `0.0.0.0`) can never establish, so `mergeTunnelsIntoInterfaces` stamps its row `parentDownNoIp` and `resolvePinnedInterfaces` excludes it from EVERY block — byNames, byPatterns, byTypes (even with `includeDownTunnels`), byLldp. A parent that is down but still addressed does not trigger it (that's a flapped link, the `includeDownTunnels` use case), nor does a missing parent row or unknown operStatus. Hand-pins on the asset are unaffected (apply is additive). The UI renders an **"Include down tunnels"** checkbox inline to the right of the `tunnel` type row, shown only when `tunnel` is checked (`_amonTypeRowHTML` + `wireInclDown` in `public/js/integrations.js`; the check state survives the post-aggregate type-list re-render via the `inclDownState` closure). **By LLDP** semantics (UI label: **By LLDP (includes inferred interfaces)**): for each interface on the discovered asset, look up its `AssetLldpNeighbor` row AND any peer-inferred edge from `Asset.fortinetTopology` and pin if any match resolves to a Polaris asset whose `assetType` is in the selected set AND `monitored=true` — automatically tracks fleet topology (a new FortiGate uplink to a managed switch gets pinned on the next discovery, no operator action). The inferred half (`loadInferredLldpByAsset` in `autoMonitorInterfacesService.ts`) covers managed FortiAPs whose FortiSwitch consumes LLDP without re-publishing via SNMP LLDP-MIB — same data source as the inferred Neighbor column on the System tab (see `peerInferredLldpService`). Class-aware: `fortigate` walks switches whose `controllerFortigate` names this FortiGate and pins on `switch.uplinkInterface`; `fortiswitch` walks APs whose `parentSwitch` names this switch and pins on `ap.parentPort`; `fortiap` resolves the AP's own `parentSwitch` + `uplinkInterface` and pins on the AP-local port. Apply logic lives in `autoMonitorInterfacesService.ts` (pure resolver `resolvePinnedInterfaces` + DB-bound `applyAutoMonitorForClass`); the apply pass runs as Phase 2c at the end of every successful discovery and from the integration edit modal's **Save Changes** button via `POST /integrations/:id/interface-aggregate/apply` (which now fires the apply in the background and returns `202` so the modal doesn't block on the fleet-wide resolve), once per per-class block whose selection is non-null so operators don't have to wait for the next discovery cycle. **Strictly additive**: never strips operator-pinned interfaces, only adds. Removing a name from the selection on subsequent saves doesn't unpin it on existing assets — operator-owned. The "By name" UI pulls its checklist from `GET /integrations/:id/interface-aggregate?class=...`, served from `Integration.interfaceAggregateCache` (precomputed at end-of-discovery by `computeAndCacheInterfaceAggregate`, with a live-compute fallback before the first post-feature run) and returns one row per distinct ifName with a device count. A client-side filter box above the checklist (`applyNamesFilter` in `public/js/integrations.js`) substring-matches the ifName (case-insensitive) and hides non-matching rows — view-only, so a row hidden by the filter keeps its checkbox state, and the filter re-applies whenever the checklist re-loads. **The "By interface type" checklist is sourced from the same aggregate response** at lazy-load time (frontend filters `rows[*].ifType` against the canonical `IF_TYPES` set in `autoMonitorInterfacesService.ts`) so operators only see ifType values that actually appear on this integration's discovered devices — a fleet whose tunnels register as FortiOS `ipsec` (normalized to `tunnel` in `normalizeFortiIfType`) shows `tunnel`; a fleet with no tunnels won't show it at all. **IPsec tunnel augmentation (fortigate class only):** the data loader `loadLatestInterfaces` is called with `includeIpsecTunnels = klass === "fortigate"`; when set it also pulls the latest `AssetIpsecTunnelSample` per `(asset, tunnelName)` (same 72h-bounded DISTINCT ON, run in parallel) and merges each tunnel in as an `ifType:"tunnel"` interface via the pure helper `mergeTunnelsIntoInterfaces` (status maps to operStatus with only fully-`down` → `"down"`). This exists because FortiOS phase1-interface tunnels are real `config system interface` entries but the REST `/api/v2/monitor/system/interface` endpoint omits them, so on REST-polled FortiGates they never reach `asset_interface_samples` and would otherwise be invisible in both pickers. Each tunnel row is tagged `isIpsecTunnel`. **The IPsec SA status is authoritative:** if a tunnel name collides with a real interface row (e.g. an SNMP-polled gate whose IF-MIB reports the tunnel's `ifOperStatus` as always "up" regardless of SA state), the merge OVERRIDES that row's operStatus with the SA-derived value and tags it `isIpsecTunnel` rather than skipping the synthetic — without this, `onlyUp` would pin a tunnel whose SA is down (the bug that surfaced once tunnel pins started fast-polling). The merge augments the resolver feed too, so By name / By type selections of a tunnel actually pin — and `splitPinsByProvenance` routes those pins to `Asset.monitoredIpsecTunnels` (read by the dedicated IPsec sampler → `asset_ipsec_tunnel_samples` for SA-status + throughput), NOT `Asset.monitoredInterfaces`. This is what makes a "By type: tunnel" selection fast-poll IPsec tunnels on REST-polled gates, where an IF-MIB pin would yield nothing. Switches/APs have no IPsec and skip the extra query. Saved-selection types not present in the latest aggregate are preserved across renders so a stored value isn't silently dropped.
